x: Tolkāppiyar, our fatherly author of Tamil grammar, wrote down the title ‘The Letters of the Alphabet’, and remained engrossed in deep thoughts. The great treasure of the grammar of Tamil language and literature started taking shape in his dreams. Even as his eyelids remained closed, the white of the eyeballs was sending out streaks of lustre through the corners of the eye just as rice peeps out of the grain that remained soaked in rain waters for long. Before ploughing the stylus through the palm leaves, there was his mind ploughing deep within. Are not letters essential for one to make a book, just as one needs the chisel for carving out a statue and the brush for painting? Because sounds lie at the base of language and because the chapter on hand is titled ‘Chapter on Letters’ (Eḻuttatikāram), the first verse begins with the letters of the Tamil alphabet. Perhaps following in the line of Tolkāppiyar, our sage poet Tiruvalluvar too begins his Tirukkuṟaḷ with the line “ ‘a’ stands at the head of all letters.” As we examine the sprawling corpus of words in Tamil, we find that they all are made up of thirty phonemes, which constitute the orthographic tradition in Tamil beginning in the period before Tolkāppiyar. As such, it is the letters that come marching aloud in the vision of Tolkāppiyar. All the primary letters of the alphabet prostrated before him and stood in a row in order: a, ā, i, ī, u, ū, e, ē, ai, o, ō, au formed the head of the row. They were followed by k, ṅ, c, ñ, ṭ, ṇ, t, n, p, m, y, r, l, v, ḻ, ḷ, ṟ, ṉ. At that juncture, a shade appeared near the wall which was followed by yet another shade. Since the sounds raised by these two shades were low, Tolkāppiyar realized the difference and opened his eyes wide. One of the shades identified itself as ikaram. Another shade introduced itself as ukaram. Tolkāppiyar looked at them and pronounced strictly that they would be a part of the secondary letters taking the names kuṟṟiyalikaram and kuṟṟiyalukaram. They could not be placed among the first thirty primary letters. At that time, the figure of a new letter clenching a stick (āytam) appeared and roared, “Do you agree to put me among these thirty?” Tolkāppiyar retorted promptly, “What, do you threaten me? Just because you appear with a weapon, do you think I will shiver with fear and allot a place for you in the first row?” Realizing Tolkāppiyar’s wrath, the ‘āytam’ letter said meekly, and with all humility, “Sir! Kindly put me in any place as you wish. Even if I don’t get placed in the front row, I will offer my assistance whenever a need arises.” Tolkāppiyar smiled in jest after writing the first verse and said, “You are offering assistance! Quite funny.” The āytam letter said ecstatically, “See how talented I am! You have given me a chance in your very first verse.” Tolkāppiyar read his verse again: > Thirty are the phonemes > From /a/ through /ṉ/; > Excluding the three, the secondary ones, > So has it been handed down. > > (Eḻuttatikāram : Nūl Marapu, verse 1) He was surprised to note that the āytam letter has found a place in the word muppaḵtu (thirty) of his first verse. The thirty letters of the Tamil alphabet thus begin with ‘a’ and end with ‘ṉ’. > The secondary phonemes are > The shortened /i/ (kuṟṟiyalikaram), the shortened /u/ (kuṟṟiyalukaram), > And the three-dotted āytam [ஃ], > Which too partake of a phoneme’s nature. > > (Nūl Marapu, verse 2)

The teacher asked the students in the classroom, “How would you remember the vowels in Tamil?” “Sir, shall I answer?” said student Maṇivācakaṉ. The teacher nodded ‘yes’. “I would remember the twelve-handed Murukaṉ to give me the cue”, pat came the reply. “Oh, good! You evoke spirituality”, smiled the teacher. “Sir, kuṟiñci flowers blossom once in twelve years. That would remind me of the twelve vowel letters”, was the reply of Pūṅkōti, a girl student. The teacher took turns to question a farmer’s son, “O boy! What would you do to remember the vowels?” “Sir, the month of Thai ushers in the Poṅkal festival which is marked by new clothes, cleaning houses, worshipping paddy and decorating bullocks. After celebrating the festival this year we would have to wait for twelve long months for its recurrence. In the same manner, the twelve vowels would be etched on my mind.” The teacher posed his next question, “Okay, how would you remember the consonants?” “The eighteen sacred steps of Lord Sabarimalai Ayyappa shrine would remind me of the eighteen consonants, sir”, was the reply of student Maṇivācakaṉ. Pūṅkōti got up to speak wisely, “The great Cēra king Ceṅkuṭṭuvaṉ vanquished the Aryan kings Kanaka Vicayar at Kuyilāluvam to get the stone for carving Kaṇṇaki’s statue. He made them carry the stones on their heads. At that juncture, an elated Ceṅkuṭṭuvaṉ roared, ‘The war between gods and demons lasted for eighteen years. The great Rāmāyaṇa war spanned out for eighteen months. The Mahābārata war went on for eighteen days, whereas Cēraṉ Ceṅkuṭṭuvaṉ’s war against the Himalayan kingdom finished within eighteen nāḻikai (one nāḻikai = 24 minutes).’ Since I remember this inspirational speech, the fact that consonants are eighteen would remain deeply embedded in my mind.” The teacher patted Pūṅkōti proudly and concluded, “Though based on spirituality and rationality, which are poles apart, your answers are appropriate.” The teacher conveyed his greetings to the students. > The twelve phonemes (from /a/ through /au/) > Are known to be vowels, > So has it been laid down. > > (Eḻuttatikāram : Nūl Marapu, verse 8) > The eighteen phonemes (from /k/ through /ṉ/) > Are called consonants, > Thus goes the usage codified. > > (Nūl Marapu, verse 9)

I was enjoying the pleasant caressing of breeze, sitting on the beach. The darkness of night was slowly swallowing the dusk, when a friend said, “Oh! The lights are already on,” forcing me to wake up from the trance. Sitting near Gandhiji’s statue, I turned towards the northern direction to look at Aṇṇā’s statue and my mind raced back in memory lane. The electrical poles erected near Aṇṇā’s statue were spilling light over me. My poetic elegy on the All India Radio on the eve of Aṇṇā’s demise rushed back to my memory. Or rather, I am sorry; when did I forget it for me to remember it? > We looked up to you as our shade of life, > but you went in search of solace in the land off the sea. > Is this fair? > Establishing your supremacy among the > pearls underneath sea, > You sleep peacefully on the beach! > > Your tongue had mothered > Many a speech sweet like nākaswaram’s strain; > Why is it tied up now? > You wished to possess a heart > which could weather any shock. > But can my frail heart > bear your loss added! > > ...... > ...... > > I know, it is conspiracy of Nature, > Aṇṇā .... you! > > Till the time I join you in > the abode you repose in, > kindly lend me your mighty heart, Aṇṇā! > I swear to present it at your lotus feet > When I join you, Aṇṇā. Beads of tears swept my cheeks even when I was reciting the verse. On observing my melancholy, my friends tried to divert my attention by broaching sundry stories. At last, they came to square one. A friend noted, “Just observe the peach of a gift Tamil has presented us. Aṇṇā with ‘a’ as the first letter in his name was our leader. Now it is Kalaiñar Karunanidhi with ‘ka’ as the first letter in his name.” I intervened, “Sir, I am just the consonant /k/. It becomes the consonant-vowel ‘ka’ only when it combines with the vowel /a/ that begins Aṇṇā’s name.” > A consonant-vowel is said > With vowel following the consonant. > > (Eḻuttatikāram : Nūl Marapu, verse 18)

In a classical dusky scenario enacted in the West, the Golden Apollo was being slowly swallowed by darkness of night. Consequently, the crescent moon resembled the part of a broken coconut in Lord Ganesha’s temple. In that hamlet’s temple-tank even the croaking of toads sounded distant and low. Two men -- both middle-aged with torn, black hat, gaping khaki shirt and folded dirty dhoti-- were lurking in the bushes near the hutments. Both of them were holding shining knives. The hamlet was predominant with hutments, the sole bungalow standing apart being the only exception. The two shady characters were prowling near that bungalow. In that hamlet, predominantly inhabited by poor masses, thieves were probably eyeing that lone bungalow. Both of them kept gesticulating to each other. At last one of them gathered courage to peer inside the house through the balcony. Nothing seemed obvious in the house dimly illuminated by a lantern. Though the eyes failed him, his ears came to his rescue. The distinct mumbling sound a-i-u-e-o emanated from a young female. The man on the balcony opined, “Seems a pregnant woman is in travail.” Both of them listened intently even as the grumbling stretched on. It was followed by an elderly woman’s voice, “One māttirai! One māttirai!”* The startled thieves remarked, “Seems the midwife is asking the woman to have a tablet.” Even when the thieves were lisping, the young woman’s grumbling hit their ears: ā-ī-ū-ē-ai-ō-au. “Now two māttirai for this”. Prescribed the elderly woman. *The word māttirai representing a unit of time in the pronunciation of sounds is homonymous with the word ‘tablet’ in English. “Ay, the pain hasn’t subsided in one tablet; the midwife has prescribed two”, concluded the two lurking men and decided to abandon their nefarious mission in order to leave the pregnant woman alone. “Look here, girl! The five sounds a, i, u, e and o take one māttirai each, while the seven sounds ā, ī, ū, ē, ai, ō and au are elongated taking two māttirai each. In the same manner, consonant sounds take half a māttirai each.” “Madam! You have clearly explained the classes of letters. But I have a doubt.” “Okay girl! What is your doubt?” “You spoke about one māttirai, two māttirai and half a māttirai. What are they?” “Well, the winking of eyes or the snapping of fingers forms one unit of time called māttirai. Do you understand it now?” “I understand, madam. The units of sound (māttirai) in Tolkāppiyam have evoked sympathy among the thieves as they mistook them for the grumbling of a pregnant woman and left the place.” “Is it so? How do you know?” “Madam, your vision is a bit low; but I saw them in the balcony and overheard their conversation.” “Look, girl! Tamil grammar has come to our rescue. Medicine could be consumed in tablet form but Tolkāppiyar has described the duration of sounds in terms of māttirai. Let me elucidate further: > The five among the thirty — > /a/, /i/, /u/, /e/ and /o/ — > Are known to be short vowels > Articulated by single phonic measures (māttirai) > So do the learned hold. > > (Eḻuttatikāram, Nūl Marapu, verse 3) > The seven among the thirty — > /ā/, /ī/, /ū/, /ē/, /ai/ and /au/ — > Are known to be long vowels > Taking two such phonic measures, > Thus has the authority ruled. > > (Eḻuttatikāram, Nūl Marapu, verse 4) > Half a phonic measure do consonants mark, > Thus goes the norm by usage set. > > (Eḻuttatikāram, Nūl Marapu, verse 11) > As discerning minds have seen it right, > A wink of the eyes or a snap of the fingers > Does constitute a phonic measure (māttirai). > > (Eḻuttatikāram, Nūl Marapu, verse 7)

It was a glorious hall, adorned with the portraits of illustrious Tamil kings, renowned poets and filled with audience eager to taste the manna of Tamil discourse. Vaḷavaṉ, a Tamil scholar and an intellectual with a broad forehead, penetrating eyes, slightly grey sprouting beard and blessed with ideas like an ever-flowing river, was lecturing on the title ‘Race’ (iṉam).* The origin of various races in the world, the way they prospered, and the interaction and conflict between them were detailed with precision and historical evidences along with the researchers’ unambiguous views. Vaḷavaṉ’s discourse proved to be a feast as well as a medicine for the audience. “Now let me explain the rise and fall of our Tamil race”, announced Vaḷavaṉ after stealing a glance at the audience who were unconsciously drooping their heads like a bunch of lotus flowers in stooping posture due to the weight of their own petals. Vaḷavaṉ spoke, “The Tamilians are one race, but Tamil itself constitutes three races. The speakers of the language form one race. How then is their language divided into three races? Yes, gentlemen, what this humble man of yours states is an irrefutable truth! In our Tamil language the consonants could be divided into three races (categories): k, c, ṭ, t, p, ṟ --> are vallinam (hard consonants) ṅ, ñ, ṇ, n, m, ṉ --> are mellinam (soft consonants) y, r, l, v, ḻ, ḷ --> are iṭaiyiṉam (medial consonants) *The Tamil word iṉam, among others, means race, and a section or class of something. Here, the author plays pun on the meanings of this word. Thus our Tamil consonants are divided into three classes. That is why I said, “The Tamilians are one race, while the Tamil language is of three races.” After hearing this, a group of youth who were yet to be fully initiated into Tamil grammar stood up agitatedly and raised war-cries. “What is this , sir? Wouldn’t our Tamil language’s fame get tarnished if her letters stand apart in three groups?” An unperturbed Vaḷavaṉ’ came forward to allay their doubts in a balanced manner: “Young men of valour! That you are apparently agitated with fears about the slight of the language makes me thrilled. But then, a five-footer like me would feel elated like a six-footer if you channelize your energy to oppose men smearing our Tamil language. You see, unlike the Tamil race, the Tamil language in her own characteristic style unites vallinam, mellinam and iṭaiyiṉam in itself and stands lofty.” “How? How?” enquired the youth. “Brothers! Sisters! In Tamil, /t/ is vallinam, /m/ is mellinam and /l/ iṭaiyiṉam. In this way, our classical Tamil language unites three diverse races of consonant letters to make a harmonious whole. But then, the practitioners of the Tamil language are split into various groups and stand apart. Do think about this. When vallinam, mellinam and iṭaiyiṉam blend together and make a lustrous entity called Tamil, is this correct on the part of the Tamilians to be divided into so many groups?” The gathering dispersed and the youth took leave of each other after discussing among themselves, this nagging question: “When the word Tamil is formed by the blending of letters from three different classes, should the Tamil race stand divided?” There was only a deep sigh. > /k/, /c/, /ṭ/, /t/, /p/ and /ṟ/ are called hard consonants. > /ṅ/, /ñ/, /ṇ/, /n/, /m/ and /ṉ/ are called soft consonants. > /y/, /r/, /l/, /v/, /ḻ/ and /ḷ/ are called medial consonants. > > (Eḻuttatikāram : Nūl Marapu, verses 19, 20 and 21)

t: Production of Speech Sounds - How Admirable!
x: This is an imaginary scene depicting Paṉampāraṉār credited with composing the prologue to Tolkāppiyam, the great work composed by Tolkāppiyar to preserve the glorious culture of the Tamils. Tolkāppiyar’s work had been presented in the court of the Pāṇṭiya king before the learned bards headed by Ataṅkōṭṭācāṉ. Even when he was strolling leisurely, the debate in sweet Tamil, which sounded melodious like the music of the veena blended with the sea wind, hit his ears. Paṉampāraṉār turned back and stared intently. A few poets, five or six seated in the hall near the beach, were engrossed in a discussion. Upon seeing him, they stood up in obeisance and welcomed him. “What is the discussion about? Is there any debate?” Enquiring thus, Paṉampāraṉār sat among them in the hall. A poet replied, “There is no debate as such. We were just talking about the doubt arising from the Eḻuttatikāram section of Tolkāppiyar’s Tolkāppiyam, presented recently in the royal court.” “What is that doubt?” questioned Paṉampāraṉār. “In the section describing the articulation of the sounds of letters under the title ‘Production of Speech Sounds’, Tolkāppiyar has stated scientifically that each class of letters possesses specific characteristics”, a poet said at the outset. A smiling Paṉampāraṉār replied, “Quite correct. In language, sounds appeared first and the corresponding letters followed only later. Description of the speech organs for the production of these individual sounds has a scientific basis for sure. This holds true while pronouncing the Tamil words vā and pō. The word vā is pronounced as the upper teeth ridge comes into contact with the folded lower lip, while the word pō is pronounced with the airstream forced out between the lower and upper lips closing and opening. This is what Tolkāppiyar refers to as airstream originating right from the navel, getting upwardly mobile to reach the head, neck and chest, and passing through teeth, lips, tongue, nose and hard palate. On the whole, airstream passes through eight human organs to produce relevant sounds. Among them, the twelve vowel sounds come from the pharynx: a and ā are articulated by opening the mouth. The five vowel sounds u, ū, o, ō, and au are said with lips rounded. The tongue touches the lower palate to produce k and ṅ. Some people don’t differentiate between l and ḷ and pronounce kulam, wrongly as kuḷam, and kaḷam as kalam which strike a jarring note. That is why Tolkāppiyar tells us to pronounce l with the tongue touching the hard palate and ḷ with the tongue stroking the palate. Such systematic articulation through organs of speech either touching each other or gently stroking each other sounds sweet to the ear. If wrongly pronounced, as kol for koḷ or moli for moḻi, it will feel like the strike of thunder, won’t it?” Paṉampāraṉār’s explanation evoked a vociferous laugh among the poets. One poet intervened, “Respected sir, all the linguists have formulated such detailed phonetic explanations for their languages, especially the Sanskrit scholars, which Tolkāppiyar too refers to in the lines: > The phonic measure of each distinctive sound (māttirai) > Even as it is so shaped within > Is examined and shown in terms unimpeachable > In the scriptured treatises of the brahmins (Antaṇar).” On hearing this, Paṉampāraṉār got agitated and retorted, “No sir, no! It is wrong. Antaṇar does not refer to the Aryans; nor maṟai points to their vedas. Among the Tamilians, the intellectuals are referred to as Antaṇar while their great works are held as works of scripture. Therefore, kindly don’t give credit to somebody else for the work of our scholars. It is wrong, a sin even, to forget our unique achievements ourselves, and to stand by others who gloss over such achievements.” Thus saying, Paṉampāraṉār left the hall leaving an atmosphere of silence behind. > The egressive airstream originating at the lungs, > Inflated by the action of the diaphragm, > Abides and is reinforced at the larynx and the buccal cavity, > Reaches the teeth, lips, tongue, nose and palate, > Gets duly modified within these eight organs > And comes out in forms distinctive; > Thus are the phonemes all produced - > Which a discerning mind can mark. > > (Eḻuttatikāram : Piṟappiyal, verse 1)

She was an exquisite beauty, full moon of the month of Cittirai. Her curvaceous form could break even the celibacy vows of Lord Siva. She was a blossom by age but her body was not past a bud. She stood before a cascade and her eyes lusted upon the well-built figure of a handsome male bathing nude. Unaware of her presence, he bathed nude in the cascade which changed her flustering to a flare-up of passion. Without bothering about her neat dress, she pounced upon the bathing man to his dismay. “My dear, why are you quivering?” The cheeky girl enquired and made her mark upon his lips. Pushing her away, he gathered sense to wrap up the towel lying on the bank. “What did you do?” He enquired angrily. “What wrong did I do? I was just practising the lesson learnt from the teacher!” “Look, girl! I might be your teacher; but I am not the poet Utāraṉ of Pilkaṇīyam, nor are you Amutavalli whom Utāraṉ taught.” “My Lord! Our names might have changed, but who would prevent us from playing the roles of Amutavalli and Utāraṉ?” She spoke thus and embraced him again. “Fie upon you! Leave me! Is this the way a student behaves with a teacher? Are you not ashamed?” “That I possess in abundance - but then Cupid’s arrow burns me like fire.” “Get away! Don’t speak irrationally!” “Well, you only taught...?” “What did I teach? Speak up.” “ ‘If a word ends with a vowel to be followed by another word beginning with a vowel, uṭampaṭumei (intrusive consonant) would ensue; that form would not be disapproved by anybody but rather accepted’. This is what you taught with the example mā + ilai --> māvilai. Just have a look at us. Aren’t we a fine example of this phenomenon? When grammar endorses coalescing of uyir (vowels), why cannot it be extended to our bodies?” “You stupid girl! Are you trying to put into practice the lesson taught? I spoke of the grammar of letters but you extend it to my neck.” “Don’t worry, dear! I have learned my lessons in the right sense. Was there anything wrong in my understanding of Tolkāppiyam?” “It was impeccable, but is this the place to practise it?” “Oh! Pardon me, If place is what bothers you, there is a hall nearby.” She dragged him and he followed her to the hall. > Where the preceding word’s final > And the succeeding word’s beginning > Are both vowels, > The intervention of an intrusive consonant [/y/, /v/] > Is not forbidden. > > (Eḻuttatikāram : Puṇariyal, verse 38)

Explaining grammar is not my sole objective in this work. It is an attempt at aiding learners of Tolkāppiyam to retain in mind the significant aspects of grammatical norms and principles. As a part of this, I seek to explain here cāriyai (empty morph) which unfolds in the form of a scene. Wordbooks define aikāram as chest, ornament worn on the shoulder, rebuke, snake, falsehood, elephant’s food, etc. In the same manner, māṉam means self-respect, haughtiness, pain, guilt, love, affection and chastity. The grammatical term cāriyai is not only a word of the closed system but also a kind of dance of the puṟam mode. āṭūu denotes a male and makaṭūu denotes a female. Bearing these in mind, it would be useful as well as amusing to read this ‘blossom’. Now, Nallatampi and Nallataṅkai - brother and sister - were taking leave of their parents for staging a dance performance. A learned Tamil teacher - Cellaiyā, marked with a confused mind, met the siblings on the way. On encountering their parents, the teacher once again enquired, “Where are your children off to?”, completely forgetting his meeting with the children earlier. “Isn’t today āṭipperukku? The rivers would flow to their fill marking the greatness of the regime. In such a joyous function, which men and women enjoy to the hilt, my son and daughter are going to enjoy themselves by entertaining the people through a dance”, was the explanation offered to the teacher. “What role are the brother and sister going to play in that dance?” “Nallatampi would don the role of Kōvalaṉ, while his sister pairs opposite to him as Kōvalaṉ’s mistress Mātavi.” “Brother and sister playing the characters of Kōvalaṉ and Mātavi?” exclaimed Cellaiyā, the scholar. After a momentary pondering, he commented laughingly, “māṉamillai” meaning ‘dishonourable’. It was enough to provoke the parents, “Teacher! How dare you say such a defaming and offending word to us!”. The agitated parents lost no time to arm themselves with a sickle and a log. It sent shivers down the spine of the teacher who muttered, “Why such agitation? Now, what offensive thing did I utter?” “Then what? You enquired about my children and dismissed them as shameless! How can I tolerate this?” “Well, I am just returning from the school after teaching Tolkāppiyam to children. Since my mind was still preoccupied with what I taught in the classroom, I stammered something. In retrospect, there is nothing wrong with my remark.” “What? Is there nothing wrong?” “Kindly bear with me! Let me offer my explanation first. In Tolkāppiyam’s Eḻuttatikāram there is a verse on cāriyai: > For the intervening empty morpheme iṉ to occur > After the two preceding terms āṭūu and makaṭūu > [Besides the hard consonant augmentation] > Is no failing in use. Cāriyai doesn’t mean dance alone; it also refers to morphemes of closed word class. The relevant verse states clearly that in ‘āṭūu’ and ‘makaṭūu’ which refer to man and woman respectively, not only hard consonants but even if cāriyai occurs, it is not wrong. ‘āṭūu’ and ‘makaṭūu’, that is, brother and sister playing the roles of Kōvalaṉ and Mātavi respectively is not erroneous. This is what I wished to state. Māṉam means wrong, māṉam illai means that it is not wrong.” The parents sighed with relief and looked at the teacher, “Sir, though brother and sister are paired opposite to each other, it is after all a form of art. Therefore, it is not a sin. Didn’t you get a simpler word to express the same opinion? Why did you perplex us by uttering the seemingly offending word ‘māṉam illai’?” “That is what I am reiterating: in between ‘āṭūu’ and ‘makaṭūu’, not only hard consonants but even if cāriyai appears, it is not a mistake. Since I was engrossed in what I taught in the classroom, I uttered the word māṉam illai in that sense. This is the cause of all the misunderstanding. My apologies.” Thus pleasing the parents, the teacher took their leave, with the satisfaction that he was able to throw light on a verse of Tolkāppiyam. > For the intervening empty morpheme iṉ to occur > After the two preceding terms āṭūu and makaṭūu > [Besides the hard consonant augmentation] > Is no failing in use. > > (Eḻuttatikāram : Uyir Mayaṅkiyal, verse 69)

Ten years ago, an old woman was seen staggering with a stick on the bank of the Koḷḷiṭam river, being unable to walk with an upright gait due to scorching heat. A cowherd youth sitting under a tree took pity upon the ageing woman and approached her with some fruits. The youth held her famished hands and enquired, “Grandmother! Where are you going in this hot sun? You are hardly able to walk. Here, have these fruits.” He offered the blackberries to her. The old woman scrutinized the fruits carefully and remarked rather mockingly, “Are these fruits hot or cold?” “The aged don’t lose their sense of humour, do they? I am no Lord Murukaṉ. First, have these fruits!” The old woman tasted the fruits, touched the shoulders of the youth affectionately and questioned, “Son! Why are you rearing cows at this age instead of going to school?”. “Well! I am studying. I do this work only during holidays.” “Is there nobody at home?” “My father is afflicted with tuberculosis. When I go to school, my mother rears the cows and milks them to make our both ends meet.” “It is quite pathetic! How do you concentrate upon your education, amid such gruelling poverty? What are you studying and what do you want to become?” “I am studying Tamil. My ambition is to work as a Tamil teacher!” “Is it so? Quite good! Is your Tamil teacher tutoring you in literature?” “Oh yes! He is teaching Tirukkuṟaḷ, Tolkāppiyam and all.” “In that case, I know a little of literature, as I happen to be a retired Tamil teacher. I would ask you a question. Would you answer?” “Please do ask, grandmother. I will answer!” “Suppose I say that Cōḻaṉ would come (varum) to take me, is Cōḻaṉ here human or non-human class?” “Grandmother, if Cōḻaṉ referred to by you happens to be your son or grandson, it is human! In case Cōḻaṉ points to the bus, it is non-human class.” “Son, how do you say so? What is its grammatical explanation?” “Grandmother, look! Tolkāppiyam’s Eḻuttatikāram is crystal clear in this regard: > There is non-change coalescence too > Where > Nouns that designate > Both the human and non-human generic classes > Are the preceding words. The noun that takes both human and non-human classes is called a common noun. That is how my explanation holds good. The human masculine Cōḻaṉ normally becomes non-human.” “Dear grandson! You are more talented than Lord Murukaṉ himself who proved his mettle before Avvai, in those days. While he demonstrated his Tamil proficiency only with regard to a fruit, you have revealed your talent in age-old Tamil grammar. May you flourish in your life! May you flourish in your life!” The Cōḻaṉ came (vantuviṭṭāṉ) during the shower of greetings. No, no, it came (vantuviṭṭatu). The old lady planted a kiss upon the forehead of the youth and boarded the bus with his assistance. > There is non-change coalescence too > Where > Nouns that designate > Both the human and non-human generic classes > Are the preceding words. > > (Eḻuttatikāram : Tokaimarapu, verse 13)

I have entered the garden of Tolkāppiyam with a resolve that there be no politics in this literary study. I am all enjoying the flowers in the garden of this treatise. But then, inevitably, in the natural course of writing, a few illustrations are drawn in from the world of politics in general rather than party politics. In the second world war, the nations owing allegiance to America were pitted against Hitler-led Germany and its friendly countries. That the Axis countries and the Allied countries each were dependent upon the dominant partners which possessed enormous power at their disposal is an irrefutable fact. History could neither forget nor deny it. The situation is related to the bygone era of the second world war. In the modern age, though not at the level of nations, the political parties in a country invariably form alliances with like-minded parties to capture power or to elect the President. Though the major parties possess the resources to face the electorate on their own, since there is nothing wrong in adding strength to their alliance, they take precautions to forge alliances with various small organizations. Therefore, political fronts consisting of various parties emerge. Minor parties sans individuality find themselves compelled to join such fronts. That the three letters, kuṟṟiyalikaram, kuṟṟiyalukaram and āytam, are in a similar condition is true. Caught in a piquant situation, wherein they are dependent upon and possess no individuality, the three letters - kuṟṟiyalikaram /i/, kuṟṟiyalukaram /u/, āytam /ḵ/ take the origin of letters upon which they are dependent as their own origin, thereby functioning as secondary letters. > The three secondary phonemes > [Shortened /i/, shortened /u/ and /ḵ/] > Discerned to be dependent and sans distinctiveness, > Have for their places of articulation > The organs of their respective primary phonemes; > And yet speaking relatively, > They are marked by natures of their own. > > (Eḻuttatikāram : Piṟappiyal, verse 19)

It was a mutt looking like a palace, adorned with a front hall that resembled Hari engrossed in deep sleep over the mythical athiseshan snake. A young ascetic was sitting on the veranda of that mutt looking forward to the arrival of somebody. Not just that. His ears were keenly expecting the unlocking sound from the adjacent prayer room, while the eyes kept a vigil on the door of the room. The door did not open. But then the Tamil teacher, teaching literature to the chief priest of the mutt, appeared well before the expected time. With the sacred Vaishnavite religious mark on his forehead and a book in his hand, the teacher came near the young monk. “What Ciṉṉaccāmi (junior monk), how are you?” asked the teacher. “Teacher, sir! I am the junior pontiff of this mutt. You are referring to me as if I were Kiḷappāḷuvūr Ciṉṉaccāmi who self-immolated.” “Pardon me. He was but a lion-hearted Tamil.” “Since I am keeping guard here, am I then an ugly Tamilian?” “Okay, leave it. The nocturnal chic would have come. Have they fled off?” “You, teacher! How come you ask of such things without any inhibition?” “Why should I be afraid? Are the pontiffs devoted to God in deep sleep after exhaustion, or are they taking a rest? Is this an unbroken meditation? That is what I am asking.” “That does not allow you to raise questions breaking the rules of grammar!” “It is a long time since some monks have forgotten and abandoned the norms of ascetic life. Well then, junior monk! Pray, which grammatical rule have I broken?” “You used the plural verb while referring to one nocturnal chic, and in the same vein you referred to the single pontiff in the room using a plural suffix. According to your statement, how many pontiffs are there in the room? How many nocturnal chics? One pontiff and many nocturnal chics? Or, one nocturnal chic and many pontiffs?” “Junior pontiff, don’t be confused! My question was based on a sound grammatical principle. The plural suffix is used for referring to a single man or woman. Singulars being referred to by plural suffixes are used as honorifics. It is indeed based on established grammatical rules which Tolkāppiyar calls admissible deviations.” “Is that so!” exclaimed the junior monk with a gaping mouth, just as the door of the room opened. The colourful damsel released from the bedroom staggered her way out through the backdoor of the mutt. The teacher caught hold of the junior monk and recited the relevant verse from Tolkāppiyam: > Plural suffix to a noun denoting human species singular > And plural suffix to a noun denoting non-human species singular > Are part of worldly usage in honour clothed, > Not permitted they are by norms of grammar though. > > (Collatikāram : Kiḷaviyākkam, verse 27)

The lover urged his beloved, “My dear, you have received coveted awards in the art of painting. Why don’t you draw us in an embracing posture and put it in a place not frequented by others, so that both of us can attain ecstasy by viewing it?” “I will certainly draw such a picture. You are a sculptor. Kindly chisel a statue depicting the posture you mentioned.” “Painting first; statue next.” The lady gracefully obliged her lover. Later, she led him to the retiring room and showed him the painting. It was a poetic depiction of a lover embracing his love. The tight hug revealed only one of her breasts. Of the two eyes, one of the eyes was concealed by the cheek of the lover which was brushing against her cheek. Her unbridled locks were spread all over the shoulders of the lover like the jasmine creeper, which brought only one of his shoulders to the fore. The painting showed her other shoulder being hugged tightly by his hands. “You have painted by adhering to the grammatical norms”, was the crisp reaction of the lover. He further elucidated, “Of the two eyes, only one eye is visible in the painting. In the same manner, the painting doesn’t unravel two bosoms; only one of them is visible. You have represented your shoulders also in a similar way. I am able to view only one eye, one shoulder, one breast, instead of two eyes, two shoulders and two breasts. In a nutshell, the painting is a true reflection of Tolkāppiyam’s grammatical norm.” “What does Tolkāppiyam prescribe?” “Let me throw light upon that. Though eye, shoulder and bosom signify plurality, they need not be referred to as two eyes, two shoulders, two bosoms. They, or for that matter other words like them, can be stated in singular which would very well imply their plurality. If the context demands, they could be presented in plural form as well.” “Is that so? Is my painting a telltale example of this grammatical norm? Kindly recite the relevant verse.” “Yes! I will recite it verbatim. What I am going to say is related to words, while your painting is its pictorial representation.” > Limbs in pairs > Such as eye, shoulder and breast > Need no plural suffix > Unless they are followed by plural verbs. > > (Collatikāram : Kiḷaviyākkam, verse 62)

He was clad in a pure hand-woven dhoti, with a customary towel on the shoulder. He was immune to sweat and shiver. Beside him were his middle-aged wife in Ciṉṉāḷapaṭṭi sari, and their darling daughter Kaṇṇaki with a few books in her hands, a girl pursuing her education in a college. This compact family entered the busy Gokhale Bookshop after visiting some other bookshops on the street. Incidentally, the name of the owner of the shop was also Gokhale. He gave an appearance of a staunch nationalist. His son Aruṇaṉ with a silk shirt and a costly watch was frequently combing his curly hair with his hands. He was also assisting his father actively in his business. But then, ever since Kaṇṇaki entered the shop, he paid hardly any attention to the business. His father Gokhale seized the initiative from him and enquired Kaṇṇaki’s father enthusiastically, “Which book do you want?” “Do you have Nehru’s Glimpses of the World History?” Gokhale pondered for a few minutes by stroking his hair and replied: “We have Gandhi’s My Experiments with Truth.” Kaṇṇaki’s father responded, “I have that. Therefore, I don’t need it! It is okay. What about Aṇṇā’s Iru Paramparaikaḷ?” Gokhale went back to stroking his hair. “The latest edition has arrived. Aṇṇā’s Veḷḷai Māḷikaiyil. Would you need it? We have that book.” “So you don’t possess Iru Paramparaikaḷ? Doesn’t matter’. Veḷḷai Māḷikaiyil referred to by you is available in our own Kaṇṇaki library.” “Well, so you own a library? Do you have at least a thousand books?” Aruṇaṉ posed the question to Kaṇṇaki and ogled her. She couldn’t bear it. She turned the other way round and searched for books! At that juncture, Aruṇaṉ’s father determined to clinch the business deal, briefed Kaṇṇaki’s parents, “Tirukkuṟaḷ commentaries are available!” “Kindly get us Pulavar Kuḻantai’s Rāvaṇa Kāviyam, if at all you possess it!” “Well, Rāmāyaṇam is available, which is widely read by everybody!” Kaṇṇaki intervened, “Not that. Do you have Pāratitācaṉ’s Pāṇṭiyaṉ Paricu?” As if waiting for this opportune moment, Aruṇaṉ replied wearing a flustered face, “We have Etirpārāta Muttam (Unexpected Kiss). Do you need it?”. He looked at Kaṇṇaki and winked. Kaṇṇaki retorted sternly, “I have Tamiḻacciyiṉ Katti (Tamil Woman’s Knife)” and after a pause, she said, “Even that is authored by Pāratitācaṉ.” Her eyes spit fire. Aruṇaṉ was subdued. Her irritated father questioned the shop owner, “Well, you have been mentioning about some other books instead of the ones asked for! What joke is this?” Proprietor Gokhale smiled and clarified it, “Sir, this is the advice of Tolkāppiyam. A businessman should follow only that. One should never say ‘No’ to a customer; instead, whatever is available in the shop should be made known. Then only would business prosper. This is what he says.” Kaṇṇaki’s mother who remained tightlipped so far, enquired, “Well then! Do you at least have Tolkāppiyam commentary?” Pat came the reply from Proprietor Gokhale, “The cheap edition of Mahābāratam is available.” > If one has to say > ‘It is but unavailable’ > When a certain commodity is asked for, > One must do so > By pointing to something else that is available. > > (Collatikāram : Kiḷaviyākkam, verse 35)

The cart-driver holding on the Mayilai bullocks and saying “We’ve arrived at Karuṇaiyānanta Press”, Kaliyaperumāḷ leaning comfortably in the cart, alighted with a bag in his hands. As soon as Kaliyaperumāḷ entered the room of the manager in the frontier of the printing press, he was greeted by the saluting manager with the chants of “Welcome! Welcome!” and was offered a chair. Kaliyaperumāḷ extricated five or six big papers from his bag and said, “An auspicious event is slated to take place in our house. That is why I have come here.” “I am very happy. Seems like son’s marriage. You are here for printing invitation. Went through the news!” “Yes, the marriage was fixed in a hurry. One thousand invitations must be printed. Groom’s name - Bride’s name and other details are there in these papers! You yourself can make necessary corrections.” The manager scanned through the papers handed to him and remarked, “Okay! Though it is a self-respect marriage, the Ayyar who wrote this seems to have smeared customary turmeric powder on it and noted down the auspicious time for marriage along with astrological details as in the conventional marriage.” “Is that so? Has he written the auspicious time? The Ayyar has shown his true colours! It is okay. Though the Ayyar has set an auspicious time for the marriage, it would be conducted on line with the principles of Periyar. Therefore, let the title of the invitation be ‘Wedding Celebration Invitation’.” “If it is a self-respect marriage, then why are you sticking to auspicious date and stars?” “Don’t you know? On certain occasions, vedic rituals would be insisted upon by bridegroom’s side, whereas, at times, bride’s side would take turns to sticking to them. Here, for the sake of the bride’s family - the astrological details. And in accordance with our wish, self-respect marriage.” The manager smiled and scrutinized the marriage invitation given to him by Kaliyaperumāḷ for printing. “Is everything okay? Do you know as to why I am asking this? You possess proficiency in Tamil with a knack of rectifying even minor mistakes! That is why we prefer this press!” “Everything is correct except for one mistake!” “What is it?” “Not exactly a big mistake. While writing bridegroom’s name, you have mentioned it as ‘my son’ (eṉatu makaṉ).” “Yes, the bridegroom is my son...” “Sir, that is exactly the mistake.” “What are you saying, Meyyappaṉ? He is my son, otherwise, who else is he?” “That is not correct.” “You give back that paper! What blabbering is this?” Kaliyaperumāḷ snatched the paper from the hands of Meyyappaṉ. Just then, Meyyappaṉ caught hold of his hand and pleaded: “My apologies. You only commended my Tamil proficiency, then how come you get agitated?” “Okay; What do you want to say? Speak out!” “The sixth case marker atu in eṉatu makaṉ is wrong. We must use the fourth case marker ku and write eṉakku makaṉ.” “I hardly know anything about case markers and distinctions of human and non-human classes. Because you say this, it must be correct.” “I don’t say that! Tolkāppiyam states so!” “Whosoever might say so, there is no denying the fact that he is my son! Kindly finish the invitation printing work soon. And here is your advance amount. Now, let me take your leave.” > Where the succeeding word > Is the human generic class [kinship denoting] noun, > The sixth case declension atu of the preceding word > Gets dropped, > And the fourth case morpheme ku takes its place. > > (Collatikāram: Vēṟṟumai Mayaṅkiyal, verse 11)

In the prebifurcated North Arcot District, all the bisexuals from various parts of the country converged for the annual Kūvākam festival commemorating the sacrifice of Aravāṉ. In the festival marked by gaiety, eunuchs, dressed in colourful makeups and dresses, performed the traditional kummi dance in various groups, much to the amusement of gasping youngsters and oldies alike. The mythology goes that Aravāṉ was sacrificed at the commencement of the Mahābāratha war, and the bisexuals mourned his death with the beating of breasts and the rituals of removing their sacred thread and the sindhur mark on the forehead. The festival characterized by joyous revelry came to an end as if the end of a storm and the bisexuals all exhausted retired to their restrooms to sleep. A bisexual named Rātā, who was in deep sleep marked by high decibel snoring, had a dream. The eunuch bore the name ‘Rātā’ - common to both male and female persons. The scene in the dream figured Lord Kaṇṇaṉ and the five Pāṇṭavas with their consort Pāñcāli. As per the condition, the Pāṇṭavas had to live incognito in which they had to be in disguise so that nobody could identify them. Otherwise, they would not regain the countries lost to Turiyōtaṉa by Tarumaṉ in gambling. Therefore, each of the Pāṇṭavas was studiedly sporting the guise by which to hide from public gaze. Among them, Arjuṉaṉ, who was under the cloak of a bisexual, met Lord Kaṇṇaṉ, separately. Yes, all this happened in eunuch Rātā’s dream! “Kaṇṇa! I have a doubt!” “What is it Arjuṉā? Do come out with it!” “Am I a male or a female now?” “Why do you have such a grammatical confusion, all of a sudden?” “Would I be called he or she?” “Hold on! Let me refer to Tolkāppiyam!” Thus saying Kaṇṇaṉ stretched his hands towards the opposite direction and from nowhere Tolkāppiyam’s palm leaf manuscript came into his hands. Arjuṉaṉ, who was in the guise of a eunuch posed a question to Kaṇṇaṉ: “What is this Kaṇṇa? How come Tolkāppiyam exists in this age?” “O the holder of the bow! In the make-believe world of dreams, everything is possible.” So saying, Kaṇṇaṉ referred to Tolkāppiyam. “Look! Tolkāppiyam has an answer to your question!” “What is the answer? Am I a male or a female?” “None of the two. Eunuch is the answer.” “But then, I am a man.” “Arjuṉā, Tolkāppiyam prescribes that a eunuch deprived of manliness should not be represented by the musculine gender. That is, in expressions like ‘eunuch came, went, spoke, etc., only feminine gender should be used, using the proform ‘she’.” “What is the verse on that?” “Here! Listen to me as I read! > Words denoting > Hermaphroditic ones of effete musculinity > Will not be words with musculine gender endings.” With disappointment writ large on his face, Arjuṉaṉ beseeched: “Kaṇṇa! Everything is okay. As per Tolkāppiyam, anybody sans manliness should be referred to by feminine gender. But then, in my case, I haven’t lost my manliness to become a bisexual like milk spoilt. I am under the guise of a eunuch only to fulfil the condition imposed by gambling.” “Therefore, you suppose, you are qualified to be addressed as a man, using the musculine suffix; if that be so, you would be easily identified! Therefore, forbear to be referred to in feminine terms meant for the eunuch.” “Great Lord! At least in my case it is an ephemeral phase. But then, how would thousands of eunuchs sans manliness tolerate being referred to in feminine terms?” “Arjuṉā! Why do you consider feminine gender as degrading? Poor thing, you don’t like women - but Pāñcāli, Alli, Pavaḷakkoṭi, Cupattirai..., the long list of your wives, which certainly doesn’t end with them, all belong to feminine gender!” An embarrassed and shy Arjuṉaṉ bent his head. Kaṇṇaṉ was quick to retort, “Well then! Tolkāppiyam’s grammar suits you ninety out of a hundred per cent.” A startled bisexual Rātā woke up and her mixed dream dissipated. > Words denoting > Hermaphroditic ones of effete musculinity > Will not be words with musculine gender endings. > > (Collatikāram : Kiḷaviyākkam, verse 12)

Perched beside the greenish bushes of the garden, Marakatam and Taṅkam were discussing sweet nothings. “You, Taṅkam, do you know the scoop! It is widely believed that our Aṉṉam is mentally disturbed, of late.” “Why? Is there any heartbreak due to love failure? As far as I know, she has not fallen for anybody and none is in love with her, either.” “I also suspected on the same lines and paid her a visit yesterday.” “You saw her in person? How is she? Is she blabbering anything?” “Yes. I saw her in person! She was in the midst of a junk of books!” “Junk of books? Or useless books?” “Aṉṉam is never known to have even touched them! She completely abhors such books and for that matter, even odd perverted stories published in weeklies. She discards them, even if they are offered by somebody.” “Let it be so. Though men and women feign to dislike them, they never miss any opportunity to read them, unnoticed by others. Okay, Marakatam! Aṉṉam always remains engrossed in literature. What has happened to her now?” “That is why she is afflicted with literature craze.” “You are also a connoisseur of literature,” “Not to such an extent as to confuse myself and others too.” “Please tell me, what is the matter?” “A bisexual deprived of manliness should not be referred to using musculine verbal suffixes; we should, according to norms of grammar, use feminine suffixes.” “That is correct! So what? What does Aṉṉam say?” “She says the term female son (peṇ makaṉ) could be used.” “How could it be? Female son? Are you referring to a eunuch?” “No, no! Seems, it was in vogue to call the girls in pre-pubescent stage by the term female son. That is why Aṉṉam says ‘female son came’ (with feminine verbal suffix) could very well be used.” “Okay, okay. There is no denying the fact that she has gone bonkers! She is fantasizing quite interestingly. Lunatic, lunatic! She is no doubt a lunatic!” “Who is mad? You Taṅkam! Marakatam! It is not my own concept!” A shouting Aṉṉam made her appearance with Tolkāppiyam in her hand. She opened the relevant page and said sarcastically, “Here, open your eyes properly and read this: > The nominal terms ellārum and ellīrum > And the term makaṉ that follows peṇ > Are of the same kind too, > [They mark distinctions of gender within the human-class], > So do the learned say. Again, > The aberrant feminine gender designation peṇmakaṉ > Takes the verb concord > In the manner of a feminine gender denoting term. Do you know what this verse in Collatikāram means? To put it in a nutshell: The expression female son, which is a breach of gender, would take feminine gender—‘the girl came’(with the feminine verbal suffix).” Aṉṉam elucidated further: “Terms like ‘everybody’. ‘all persons’ and female son are human class words. In the past, it was in vogue to call girls in pre-pubescent phase by the term female son.” Taṅkam and Marakatam were completely astonished and listened to Aṉṉam without blinking their eyelids. “Here is the Tolkāppiyam verse. Read it as well as its commentary first and decide as to whether Aṉṉam is really mad.” Thus thundered Aṉṉam and made her exit. > The nominal terms ellārum and ellīrum > And the term makaṉ that follows peṇ > Are of the same kind too, > [They mark distinctions of gender within the human-class], > So do the learned say. > > (Collatikāram : Peyariyal, verse 10) > The aberrant feminine gender designation peṇmakaṉ > Takes the verb concord > In the manner of a feminine gender denoting term. > > (Collatikāram : Peyariyal, verse 40)

He had invited friends to a feast. Two of the friends arrived even before midnoon. His wife feigned anger, “What dear! You have invited your friends without intimating to me in advance.” “I bought murrel fish. I would be only too happy to share them with my friends. Since you would also like the gesture, I invited those two friends. Hurry up! Look after the cooking.” The mistress of the house was activated immediately. She cleaned the rice, put it in boiling water, lighted the stove, chopped the fish into equal pieces, and after mixing the requisite amount of spice, salt, and tamarind, put them one after another into the boiling curry. She kept herself focused upon the food being prepared on both the stoves. It is indeed a joyful thing for her to serve food to the guests and sit eating with them. The husband, seated on the veranda of the house, repeatedly asked his wife, “Is the food ready? Why is it taking so long? Why is it taking so long?” She didn’t relish his loud reminders. The Tirukkuṟaḷ verse on hospitality, > The anicham flower withers away when smelt; > The guests would turn sullen when looked at with a frown. kept ringing as a caution in her heart. Just as she was rushing through with cooking, she heard her husband’s harsh query, “At what time would you finish cooking? At what time would it be served? At what time would we be eating it?” The lady wearing a smile on her face placed the plantain leaves on the floor and said, “Let me state the present time and future time in past tense -- here, I finished cooking. I am right here for serving. You three could come and start eating.” One of the friends was all praise for her: “Looks the mistress of the house has a sound mastery over grammar also, as she reigns like a queen!” “Well, I am no queen - I am an ordinary woman discharging my household duties and of course with some knowledge of literature. That is all.” Her proud and loving husband enquired, “Isn’t this Tolkāppiyam? You can as well recite the entire verse.” “Let the feast be over, then recitation can follow.” After finishing the feast, she didn’t forget to serve the delicacy of Tolkāppiyam: > To attribute the action of a verb to the past > While it bears on the present and future > Is to suggest exigency, > So do the literate hold. > > (Collatikāram : Viṉaiyiyal, verse 44) Note: An event that links the present and the future times can be expressed in the form of past tense.

Darwin’s theory has succeeded in scientifically explaining the human being’s evolution from the monkey. Among this teeming sea of humanity, growing in their multitudes, owing to diversification development and witnessed in this world, somewhere around five thousand years ago, the Tamil race was gradually preparing itself for a systematic form of life. Leading an unorganized life is poles apart from leading a planned course of living. In order to formulate such a structured life, communication tools are mandatory. Among these communication tools, language has stood the test of time and stands as numero uno. The races emerging from various parts of the world had been using their languages, but the Tamil race has had the distinction of standardizing its language and developing literature and grammar at a very early stage. The historically renowned Tamil race is credited with providing sheen and glitter to their language two thousand years ago, though the development process itself started some three thousand years earlier. Tolkāppiyam’s Poruḷatikāram section, the grammar of literature and life, is a perfect telltale example of that feat. Though the modes of living and patterns of behaviour mentioned in Tolkāppiyam were very much in practice much before the Tolkāppiyam’s era, we can always recollect with pride that the arduous task of piecing them together and presenting them in the form of a poetic garland was effortlessly accomplished by Tolkāppiyar. It may be debatable as to how many of the principles, beliefs and practices of that era are relevant to the contemporary milieu. But there is no denying the fact that we would be woefully missing the mirrors of the past in the absence of landmark books like Tolkāppiyam. In this context and background, let’s enjoy a few of the blossoms from the Poruḷatikāram section of Tolkāppiyam. Of the three components of structure and content in literature, mutal poruḷ, karupporuḷ and uripporuḷ, mutal poruḷ has been divided into two, viz., land and time. > Mutalporuḷ is > Aspects of land and time, > So do men of discernment find. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Akattiṇai iyal, verse 4) The land has been classified into pastoral tract (mullai), hilly tract (kuṟiñci), agricultural tract (marutam) and maritime tract (neytal). Each one of them has been assigned a presiding deity. And these deities supposedly protected and blessed the respective divisions of the Tamil land. Here is the Tolkāppiyam verse: > The forest tract which Māyōṉ tends, > The hilly tract which Cēyōṉ tends > The fertile cultivable tract which Vēntaṉ tends > And the littoral tract which Varuṇaṉ tends > Are known to be > Mullai, kuṟiñci, marutam and neytal respectively. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Akattiṇai iyal, verse 5) \*Gods equated with Tirumāl, Murukaṉ, Intiraṉ and Varuṇaṉ respectively by the commentators.

Given that the types and modes of love behaviour of the hero and the heroine and the attendant situations and sub-situations as prescribed in Tolkāppiyam are being discussed in the succeeding chapters, it is necessary to briefly introduce them here. Pastoral tract (mullai): Season--rainy season; time of the day - evening. Hilly tract (kuṟiñci): Season--winter; time of the day - midnight Agricultural tract (marutam): Season--all seasons; time of the day - dawn Maritime land (neytal): Season--all seasons; time of the day - sunset. The desert tract, not included among the four above, has the hot summer season and the midday hour for its season and hour of the day. > The rainy season and evening > Are assigned to the forest tract. > The learned find > The cold season and midnight hour > Assigned to the hilly tract. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Akattiṇai iyal, verse 6) > The early dewy season > Does also go with the hilly tract, > So has it been said. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Akattiṇai iyal, verse7) > The wee hours just before daybreak > Are assigned to the cultivable tract. > The day’s close before sunset > Belongs to the littoral tract. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Akattiṇai iyal, verse 8) > As we see it, > The hot season and midday hour > Go with the centrally placed [arid] tract. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Akattiṇai iyal, verse 9) > The last dewy season > Is also held to be proper to the arid tract. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Akattiṇai iyal, verse 10) After having described all these, Tolkāppiyar shows that it is inevitable that the nature of love behaviour may change, and not the nature of land and its characteristics. > That > Aspects of love behaviour > Assigned to a given tract > Do get mixed with those of another tract > Is no deviation unacceptable; > Yet, > No commingling is permitted among the tracts themselves, > So goes the norm by men of discernment. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Akattiṇai iyal, verse 12)

Having discussed the features of land and time and the modes of love behaviour, it is now necessary to explain the distinctive regional features of the five tracts of land (karupporuḷ). The deity worshipped, food for the stomach, animals, trees, plants, creepers, birds, leather instruments, occupation, the lyre and other string instruments and things of these sorts would come under karupporuḷ. Place, water, flower, etc., would also come under karupporuḷ. > God, food, animal, tree, > Bird, drum, occupation and the lute > And such of these > Constitute the distinctive physical features of the given tract of land. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Akattiṇai iyal, verse 18) Though, in this list of karupporuḷ, flowers and birds are allotted to specific divisions of land, they might be shown to belong to other divisions of land. > Where the flora and fauna occur > Not marked proper to the land and season in question though, > They be deemed > Characteristic of that land and that season. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Akattiṇai iyal, verses 19) Just as mullai land is inhabited by shepherds and hunters, the other types of land also have farmers, etc. engaged in occupations characteristic of those geographical divisions: > Cowherds and huntsmen > Designate region-specific persons of the masculine gender; > There are other names of principal characters such as these two > Drawn that they are on the region’s occupation. > We find on reflection that > Inhabitants of other regions too > Have their names derived from the mores of their region > And from the occupation of that region. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Akattiṇai iyal, verses 21, 22) > Such representation of kaikkiḷai and peruntiṇai > Does mark men of other menial occupations too. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Akattiṇai iyal, verse 24) Tolkāppiyar does not go by the social status, and assigns the position of the hero and heroine even to those folks engaged in lowly occupations. There are, however, some scholars amongst us who tend to misinterpret ēval marapu (menial work) as that of ordering others.

t: Land and People: A Study in Excellence
x: We get to know that Tolkāppiyar designates land by the term world, which points to his universal perspective to human existence, though it conspicuously lacked individual features related to the Tamiḻ race. In spite of specific characteristics and vocations allotted to each type of land, there are overlappings with regard to certain features. But in general, the characteristics pertain to the type of land mentioned. Each type of land has people bearing two categories of names, viz., conventional names and occupation-related names: > The persons that people a tract of land > Have names specific to that region; > These names fall into two categories: > Names in tune with the mores of the region > And names derived from occupations of that region. > (Poruḷatikāram : Akattiṇai iyal, verse 20) > Pursuit of learning > And ambassadorial mission > Are proper to men of superior social classes. > (Poruḷatikāram : Akattiṇai iyal, verse 26) In both these activities, men of excellence and character took the responsibility. Tolkāppiyar says that it is the prerogative of the king to either go on war himself, or entrust the responsibility to his commanders. > Going on war himself against his enemy > And entrusting the job > To those associated with him > Are given to the king. > (Poruḷatikāram : Akattiṇai iyal, verse 27) The implication is that the duties of governance, fighting, learning and ambassadorship were assigned to men of character, intelligence and valour. Further, in all types of land, there were people who excelled in the performance of specific tasks and duties. > Conduct of prayers and festivities > For those of abiding note other than the humans (i.e. deities); > Restoration of righteousness where it turns deviant > In all regions extending through the forest tract; > And to make riches through virtue abroad - > Are occasions too > For the hero to remain parted from the heroine. > (Poruḷatikāram : Akattiṇai iyal, verse 28) Therefore, the performance of duties proper to a given type of land goes to the nobility, the inhabitants of the land, men from lower strata and workers. > The conduct of prayers and festivities > Stands enjoined on the inhabitants of the four regions. > (Poruḷatikāram : Akattiṇai iyal, verse 29) A few commentators misread ‘the four types of people’ as ‘four castes of people.’ That the classification of men meant for the management of the given type of land was misinterpreted as a classification on the basis of caste is but the product of perverted thinking.

The Tamiḻ professor made an announcement in the classroom of the college: “Students, I announce a competition to commemorate the birth anniversary of the Tamiḻ scholar Thiru V. Ka. The best among you who scene scripts a characterizing a man and a woman in a beautiful manner, in sweet, charming Tamiḻ by conforming to the established rules of old Tamiḻ tradition and history would bag a prize of literature books worth rupees five thousand. Well then! You can as well start now and read out your work to me before the end of this class”. The students welcomed this announcement and raced against each other to write the script in order to bag the prize. “There is yet another condition for winning the competition! You should finish it first, and further your work should be prize-worthy.” Within an hour of the announcement, Mukilaṉ finished his work and he approached the professor with the papers. He said, “Sir, I have finished writing.” “Is that so! I am quite happy! Why don’t you read it aloud to others?” Student Mukilaṉ started rushing through with his presentation: The lover sits by his beloved wearing a sad countenance. She enquires, “Why are you sorrow-worn? Why does your face look withered?” “Sulking”, is the crisp reply. “Sulking? What does it mean...?” “O my goodness! You don’t know what sulking means! Among the verses in Iṉpattuppāl section of Tirukkuṟaḷ, those under “sulking” are the best. The man and woman have a feigned quarrel against each other, which ultimately gets resolved leading to ecstasy.” “In the first place, why should they sulk and then settle down to reconciliation?” “Sulking is entering into a quarrel with the sole aim of getting reconciled.” “Okay then, what are you waiting for? Start the quarrel.” “I am going to break a piece of news, most disliked by you.” “What is it?” “The dawn tomorrow would see me sailing to Rome.” “Oh, no. Don’t tell me you are off to a foreign land once again.” “Yes, we need to carry the pearls of Tamiḻ Nāṭu for sale in Rome.” “Alas! Was I born to be tossed like a catamaran by the ebb and tide of the sea waves? No, I am determined to stop your voyage.” “No obstacles please! Let there be no embers in your eyes! If I sell pearls overseas, gold coins would pile like a flood unshuttered. So dear lady, let me take leave of you.” “When I, like the lamp of the house, wait for you here with my fingers crossed, you tear apart the tumultuous sea to go for trading. I would have breathed my last by the time you returned.” “Come on! Look here! You are soon going to break into pearls of laughter, which certainly doesn’t grow in the shell. Oh chaste Tamiḻ, which abide in my heart! You are going to accompany me to Rome. Is that okay?” After hearing this sweet news she planted some mighty kisses and embraced her lord. Everybody in the classroom appreciated Mukilaṉ with a thunderous applause. The Tamiḻ professor said, “What students? Shall we confer the first prize on Mukilaṉ? But one thing. This script doesn’t completely belong to Mukilaṉ. It reads like part of a dialogue in the play Pūmpukār!” Student Mullaikkoṭi intervened: “Professor sir! Friend Mukilaṉ’s work doesn’t conform to the norms of ancient Tamiḻ literature and culture. Nor is it completely like the dialogue in Pūmpukār.” “What is your objection? If you could reflect what is in my mind, you will get the prize.” “Sir, last week while teaching Tolkāppiyam, you explained the Akattiṇai iyal verse 34 as meaning that the ancient Tamiḻ culture did not permit men taking their wives with them during voyages to foreign lands. And what Mukilaṉ has written runs contrary to this practice.” “Yes Mullaikkoṭi! You have said exactly what I thought. Dear Mukilaṉ, your script is excellent! The pen-portrait you have done remains a feast for the eyes! But then, the award should rightly go to the objection raised by Mullaikkoṭi! Once again, the students expressed their happiness by their clapping of hands. > The hero does not take the heroine with him > While he undertakes a voyage on the seas. > (Poruḷatikāram : Akattiṇai iyal, verse 34).

Mukilaṉ approached Mullaikkoṭi, when she was coming from the classroom with hands full of the books, received as a prize. “I am so happy! Congratulations on your winning the prize!” Mukilaṉ said with a smile on his face but he made no attempt to hide his anger. “Mukilaṉ! Help me with these books. I am unable to carry them.” “Oh! Do you take me for an aide?” So saying, Mukilaṉ took the bundle of books she received as a prize. “What Mullai? What sort of a feminist are you? You were advocating male chauvinism!” “What, me advocating male chauvinism?” “Exactly! Didn’t you argue in favour of Tolkāppiyam prohibiting women from accompanying men on voyage?” “Who said that it was Tolkāppiyam’s idea? In the ancient era, such a practice was in vogue. Tolkāppiyar merely reflected it, without concealing anything.” “I didn’t want to subscribe to that retrogressive principle, which is why I didn’t mention it. But you managed to receive appreciation by holding up views against your own gender. A worst form of female subjugation! Is this how Tolkāppiyam depicts women?” “These historical facts, lifestyle of people of the yesteryears, their beliefs and their activities based on these beliefs - everything is represented without any concealment by literature. Do you know something, Mukil? The Tolkāppiyar, who refers to the prohibition of women from undertaking voyages, has also spoken about an advantage conferred on women in those days.” “What was that Mullai?” “In order to win his beloved by any means, the hero used to ride on a horse made of palmyra leaves in the ancient days.” “Quite correct! The practice of riding on palmyra horses involved men sitting on horses made of palmyra leaves, going down the street of the town of the heroine and persuading the elders of the town to get him the heroine. The dried leaves of the palmyra would cause bruises all over his body. In order to save women from experiencing such an excruciating pain, women were prevented from undergoing this process in those days!” “To realize our love we men underwent maṭalēṟutal; but you women--to achieve the objective of your love...” “We need not undergo the practice of maṭalēṟutal; instead a mere maṭal (letter) would do the trick.” “Is that so? Is that so easy? Shall I give it a try?” “I am sure you mean our marriage invitation!” a blushing Mullaikkoṭi started leaving, taking the books back and holding them tight to her bosom. “Wish I had been those books!” Though Mukilaṉ didn’t exactly utter these words, his mischievous glance looked like saying so. > No strand of Akam love behaviour > Does enjoin on the heroine > To ride on the horse of palmyra stems > As it goes contrary to the norms of feminine propriety. > (Poruḷatikāram : Akattiṇai iyal, verse 35).

t: A Simple Point in the Middle
x: It is a common trait among scholars - of the past as well as the present -- who have penned commentaries on the old Tamiḻ words and phrases to overlook the comprehension potential of the readers. Instead of providing simple explanations, they prefer to tread on rough terrain, by being pedantic like classical musicians, who flaunt all the finer nuances of music in a concert, to be appreciated by only a hundred people among multitudes of laymen. To be precise, how many presons know as to what exactly tiṇai means? Tiṇai is the term related to aspects of behaviour, land division and classes of beings. While uyartiṇai refers to human beings, akṟiṇai denotes things non-human. Akattiṇai signifies the love career of the hero and the heroine through the phases of union, separation, patient waiting, sulking, etc., and deals with the pre-marital and marital relations of these two, with akam, the heart, standing at the base. There is also the unrequited love and abnormal sexual passion. Aintiṇai is the fivefold love career of the hero and the heroine -- kuṟiñci (the union of the lovers), pālai (separation), marutam (feigned love quarrels), mullai (patient waiting of the heroine), and neytal (the lamentation in separation). Even as union, separation, etc., may occur in all classes of land, we need to look at tiṇai as a place or land of occurrence of an event of love. Puṟattiṇai is the parallel, the counterpoint of Akattiṇai. While Akam is the intimacy of love behaviour and conjugal life between a man and a woman, Puṟam signifies aspects of life in the society at large such as war, governance, learning, friendship, etc. The Puṟam events, like the Akam ones, are both land-specific and universal. This simple explanation would be useful in understanding the issues of akam and puṟam life in their complexities - the breeze, the storm, the tremors of the earth in the life of men and women.

Love is a ticklish phenomenon which binds the lovers together but prohibits union and attainment of ecstasy. A girl entangled in love is sleeping beside her mother. Her mother’s hand, like a creeper swept by the breeze, is moving around her body, making the girl realize that she is still wide awake. It is the winter season, specific to the mullai land. The time of the day is midnight. The prayer song sung to appease the presiding deity Kaṇṇaṉ, echoing itself in the hills and trees of the forest, hits the ears of the mother and the daughter, though the actual song ended long before. All of a sudden, the girl wakes up and sits. The mother without revealing that she is awake turns to the other side. The daughter prays, “Kaṇṇa! Thanks for your mercy! Just as I wished, he has agreed to forget me. On my part, I will not think of him either.” A satisfied mother goes to sleep with happiness thinking that the mullai deity Kaṇṇaṉ has changed the minds of the lovers. Realizing that her strategy has succeeded, the girl pretends to sleep for some time, only to nimble-footedly walk her way to the handsome man hiding behind the tree outside. She touches his shoulders and both of them set out on the journey. The cock which heralds the breaking of day seems to tell tales of elopement of the lover and his condescending lady, without parents’ knowledge, making a startled mother wake up, and realize the disaster. The friend of the girl, who abets the elopement, joins the mother in her grief. My finely-jewelled girl—nourished by me since infancy, through breast-feeding and intake of jackfruit, banana, mango, and millet mixed with honey—remained under my shadow till attaining puberty, but eloped with an abject novice like cotton popping out of its seed flying away. Friend, shouldn’t we consult the auguries and omens for the wellbeing of the one who left me (though I protected her like a couch shell) and the one who led her away from me? Shouldn’t we seek divine soothsaying? Shouldn’t we take vows to the mullai’s presiding deity Kaṇṇaṉ? Wonder what might happen to them on the way! Wonder what might be their condition right now! Wonder what sort of problems might await them in the future! Thus, instead of getting furious with the eloped lovers, the kind-hearted mother is murmuring her concern that they should not be haunted by any evil, whomso-ever she has gone with: > As the heroine goes on elopement with the hero, > The utterances appropriate to her mother are: > She would pour out her anguished concern > To the confidante and to those who had seen the lovers on the way; > She would speak > Referring to predictions unsought and divinations and prognostications, > Weighing the good and the bad that might befall the lovers, > Expressing apprehensions about the path they trod > And about the help that might come their way, > Reflecting on the past, the now and the future of her daughter. > (Poruḷatikāram : Akattiṇai iyal, verse 36).

t: Great is the Aid of the Confidante
x: Poruḷatikāram codifies the responsibilities of the heroine’s confidante, when the hero prepares himself to take leave of the heroine. “How is it fair on your part to start off for attaining either a personal or social goal leaving your lady alone? Just as fish cannot live without water, it is illogical to think that she would live without you. You better take her also with you”, requests the confidante. In the meantime, she tries to console and get ready the heroine, who sheds tears for departing from her near and dear relatives. But, all of a sudden the friend has a doubt. Even though he seems to love her truly, on that eventful day, in the garden of the Kaṇṇaṉ temple he fetched a seemingly inaccessible fruit for another damsel and smiled meaningfully at her, directing an equally mischievous question, “I have got that fruit. Would I get these fruits?” Shouldn’t she recognize his true colours from his appearance of being an embodiment of truth and falsehood? Thus ponders the friend. But there comes a change of heart. While thinking about the lover and the heroine’s mother, the friend is reminded of the Kaṇṇaṉ temple incident. But she has to focus upon the plight of a disconsolate, grief-stricken, pining heroine. She tries to cheer her lady up with the pep talk of her lover, but then that attempt proves futile. As she retorts, “Shall I get roasted in the embers of loneliness like a pacalai (also meaning pale yellow spot supposed to appear on the body of a woman due to lovesickness) creeper?” She seems to be under the embers even while asking. The friend comes forward to console and encourage the lady to accompany her lover. The friend’s deeds of thoughtful intercession between the hero and the heroine and her words of reasoning with the heroine’s foster mother are worth admiration: > Perceived rightly, > The contexts that mark the utterances of the confidante > Who abides in heart-like intimacy with the heroine are: > Bringing home to the hero > The distress and despondency > That might befall the heroine > Were he to go leaving her languishing at home; > Entreating the hero to take to elopement with the heroine; > Leaving the heroine in his hands > As he consents to elopement; > Reflecting on the distress of her kin > As the heroine leaves them on elopement; > Bringing home to the hero the delusive nature of his conduct; > Consoling the heroine’s mother > Who stays distressed at her daughter’s elopement; > Uttering words of comfort to the heroine > Who remains distraught in solitude > By recalling the hero’s words of assurance; > And such situations as these. > (Poruḷatikāram : Akattiṇai iyal, verse 39).

The hero elopes with the heroine, bound by the spell of love. Their journey extends from the sylvan tract through the arid wastes. This is a scene from Kalittokai, seen in the backdrop of Tolkāppiyam. In the early morning, being parted from the mother, she accompanies her lover by holding his hand. She comes across deer and rabbit frolicking among koṉṟai, kāyā and kuruntam trees. Blossoms of mullai, kullai and paṭavam are spreading fragrance all around. The peasants rush to sow common millets like cāmai and varaku. She beholds all the scenes while continuing the journey. Since the dawn replaces early morning darkness, they can no longer remain hidden from others. The twinkling stars scattered profusely on the sky gravitate us to see them. Even among those innumerable stars, don’t we view the moon first? This most beautiful damsel is that moon! She is like a statue in beauty! She moves like an exquisite art! When she goes along with her lover equally matching in charm and valour, nobody could miss an opportunity to admire that perfect pair. When they travel a long distance in the desert land, they are trailed by the foster mother, anxious to trace them. In that land, where are seen emaciated elephants and wolves moving around and parched ponds and wells, the foster mother travels listening to the music of the paṟai (a percussion instrument) and the yāḻ (a stringed musical instrument) even while she eagerly enquires about her daughter and her lover. “Mother, why are you treading the fearsome path looking for them? We saw both of them. Our village is nearby, you can take a sojourn in our place’. As we said thus, they stayed with us for a while and resumed their journey towards a far-off village.” Though the news conveyed by the residents of that hamlet tastes like honey, her daughter’s separation stings her like a scorpion. “Mother, we could appreciate your position. Being a mother, you are delighted to hear about their wellbeing; so it is only fitting on your part to facilitate their marriage and thereby be more happy”. Thus saying they try to restrain the mother: > The patterns of utterance > Enjoined on those > Who meet on the way > The lovers in elopement are: > Warning the hero and heroine on elopement > Against the perilous nature of their journey > At such a time and along such a tract > As would be wrought with fright; > Telling them through words of kindness and concern > To stay in the village nearby > Since their destination stands removed afar; > Exhorting the couple united in love > Through words of compassion > Against the course of deed they took to; > Forbidding the foster-mother to pursue the lovers > As she has set out in search of them; > Guiding the foster-mother’s pursuit of the lovers; > Speaking of the long distance the lovers traversed, > And speaking of the return of the lovers, > So goes the norm of utterance types in Akam poetry. > (Poruḷatikāram : Akattiṇai iyal, verse 40). “Is it a far-off place? Doesn’t matter. I will retrieve my daughter by treading the turbulent path, however difficult the journey might be”. The mother vows and starts off. Isn’t it a mother’s heart? It would naturally be tumultuous. Though she has learnt of her daughter’s wellbeing, she desires that the girl should stay in her parental protection. Otherwise, the efforts to nourish her so long would vanish into the thin air. So saying, the frustrated mother runs towards the direction where the lovers are supposed to have gone. The sun is scorching. On the way, she is encountered by some sage men treading the desert path. She discloses her predicament to them. “Have you seen my daughter along with a broad-shouldered man?” so saying she trembles in anxiety. “We did see them, mother.
