The flag of love flies aloft in their hearts. Don’t think of cutting it off, mother.” “What are you saying? When her own mother and me, her foster-mother, are grieving thus, is it proper for you to support the girl who has gone away to our grief?” “Mother, listen! Though sweet-smelling sandal sprouts and grows in the mountain, it doesn’t belong to the mountain. It is meant for applying on the body. Being born in water, can the pearl remain wedded to the water? It will add to the beauty of the one who wears it. The music emanating from the yāḻ gives pleasure not to the yāḻ but to the auditors or the one who plays it. Mother, your daughter is like sandal born from the mountain, pearl born from the sea, music from the yāḻ. Therefore, it is best for her to be with her loved man.” Here is that Kalittokai poem: > Not unseen by us they were, > We did see them tread this torrid path; > You seem to be the mother of that maid > Decked in grace with resplendent ornaments, > Who this desert path braved > With a youth of quintessential bearing. > > On reflection we see that > Your daughter is to you > What the fragrant sandal mixed with myriad things > Is to the mountain where it’s born; > It’s beneficial to those only who apply it on them. > > On pondering it we find that > Your daughter is to you > What the choice white pearl is to the ocean > Where it’s born; > It serves those only who wear it on them. > > Weighing it right we find that > Your daughter is to you > What the enchanting melody, > The seven strings in unison issue, > Is to the yāḻ where it’s conceived; > It’s beneficial to the songsters only. The lover and his love after surmounting the difficult problems settle down in life. Realizing that they were leading a virtuous life, the foster-mother abandoned her search. It is natural that she would visit them, stay with them and attain heartfelt pleasure. Such would be the collective essence of Tolkāppiyam Poruḷatikāram and Kalittokai.

t: The Call of Duty and the Predicament of the Hero
x: There might be many reasons for men to leave women. Separation means unbearable anxiety for women. The man takes much pains to console his woman and take leave of her. Separation is inevitable for men. They must go to train in warfare or to acquire knowledge for enriching their minds. If trained in these skills, separation happens on account of protection of the state leaving behind the object of one’s love. The woman doesn’t take the parting for good, though her loneliness is rather short. Since both of them live so intimately as not to let a thread to pass through their embrace, she regards each day of separation as a sword chopping her heart. Even though he parts only to learn Tamiḻ literature and grammar and receive training in warfare after explaining the benefits of his activities to the home and the country, she bids adieu only after shedding copious tears, waterfall like. If the hero happens to be a king bound by the responsibilities of the state such as aiding a friendly ruler, or if he goes on an ambassadorial mission, he has to be valorous or wise as the occasion demands. He measures his own strength, his army’s strength, and ally’s strength, while the superiority of his foe in foot-soldiers,cavalry, and elephant force also does not escape his thoughts. In spite of all these reflections flashing across his mind, and in spite of his resolution to encounter the odds and triumph over them, he marches ahead only after seeking farewell from his darling. Since it involves the responsibility of protecting the country, the lady bids farewell wishing him victory, though her eyes shed tears like the Ganga and the Cauvery. In the warfield, caught like a tiger in the midst of elephants, he comes unscathed due to strength of determination. The war still persists, and the hero demonstrates that he is second to none. Then, at night, in the war-camp, his fair lady disturbs him in the dream. Since even the act of pining for her in dreams would dampen his heroic vigour, he avoids it. The war ends, with the hoisting of the flag of victory. He hastens the chariot driver. “The sweet lady of mine would be waiting; her passionate kisses would heal my injuries. Go fast”, he says. “Horses, may God bless you to run like a storm and convey me to my wife”, he requests from the core of his heart. On the way, occasionally, on encountering a prostitute he makes merry. Since this news would reach the ears of his love waiting at home, it would lead to sulking. He should resolve that sulking also and row the boat of marital life in the river of happiness. The poetic hero has many such responsibilities and duties, and predicaments as well: > As he intends going after mind’s enrichment and physical prowess > And the rewards attendant therein; > As he dilates to the heroine > Upon the abiding note such quests yield, > And upon the ignominy keeping off these quests would result in; > As he responds to the calling of being a royal emissary; > As he takes to aiding an ally in need; > As he sets out to take on hostile foemen > Who pride over their might, the might of their allies and the difficulty of > invading their forts > And over the secured unapproachability of their fortresses; > And as he remains in a war-camp away from his love; > As he, > Returning after the task accomplished, > Addresses his charioteer urging him to make it swift; > As he parts from his love > For purpose of security and protection of the state; > And, > As he importunes her > After his return from prostitutes > And seeks resolution of her sulking. > (Poruḷatikāram : Akattiṇai iyal, verse 41)

Tolkāppiyam unfolds the rose of a poetic device called ‘implied simile’. The reason why it is called a rose is that it is a rose among thorns and is a literature of a grammatical concept. To draw parallels between two things is known as a simile. The implied simile suggests things rather than explicitly compares them. A Marutakkali poem provides a fine illustration of this mode of simile where it looks like providing a relish of a spectacle in nature that forms part of a village: > O the lord of the virtuous land with fountains abounding, > Where > The beetle drones about the blue water-lily, > Which the vendors plucked > From the fields of copious waters > And are carrying to town; > Once in town, > The beetle moves off > To feast on the fragrant juice > From the temples of the elephant grand and stately; > Come the hour of the eve, > It seeks its craving appeased > By feeding on the scented jasmine opening up > On the honey-smelling tresses of women, > Who hold their loved ones in embrace, > So fast with their plump forearms > As to leave their men bruised by their bracelets; > The pain of hunger gone > The beetle goes oblivious > Taking off its mind for ever > From the blossoms of the pond > Which it feasted on ere in passion. While bringing the blue water lily flowers for sale from a field filled with an abundance of water, the bees also accompany, swarming around the flowers. These bees happen to taste the juice of the rutting elephant on the way. The bees, indulging in drinking the fluid during the day resort to enjoying mullai flowers at night. Later, without even thinking about any other flower, they tend to forget their abode, which is a beautiful pond filled with water. Since blue water lily flowers, bees, elephant’s juice, mullai flower and pond filled with flowers are there to see, this would seem like a verbal portrait of bees and flowers. But in the context of the heroine’s separation from the hero, there are subtle parallels between the hero and the bees, prostitutes and the rutting elephant’s fluid, concubines and the mullai blossoms, and the pond and the home where the heroine suffers in loneliness. There is no explicit comparison of such things by the heroine. It is the evocation of this spectacle in nature by which the heroine bares out her hurt. And the following Tolkāppiyam verse provides the grammar of the Kali poem above: > The suggestive simile is one > Where > The tenor comes revealing > As it draws implicitly on the vehicle described. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Akattiṇai iyal, verse 48).

t: The Heroine of the Agricultural Tract
x: There is the fourfold division of land, along with a fifth, viz., the arid tract, a forced addition though it seems. Each type of land has a specified presiding deity right from the era of Tolkāppiyam. The agricultural land’s presiding deity ,Vēntaṉ, that was in vogue from the days of Tolkāppiyar was incidentally transformed into Intiraṉ after a few hundred years, owing to the onslaught of other cultures. Be that as it may, the kaikkiḷai (unrequited love) theme of Akam love, though unknown today for its grammatical significance, makes its presence felt in day-to-day life. That has been picturised as a dramatic scene here: The inhabitants of the agricultural tract celebrate the festival of Intiraṉ. Decked in lotus and water lily flowers, people gather under the shade of the groves of kāñci, marutam and vañci trees, play marutam melody on their marutam lutes, take bath in the freshets and enjoy themselves. A drama stage comes into existence and the Cakuntalam play is enacted. Lo and behold! King Dushyandhan and the sage’s daughter Cakuntalai meet by a wild stream in the forest. “Cakuntala, this memorable meeting is the foundation of our immortal love.” “You are the king, here in the forest for hunting. You took me for a deer and hunted me. How could an ascetic’s hut bank upon palace’s word of treating this meeting as love’s base?” “I have encountered a number of animals while hunting. But I feel that you and the love induced by you have become a fetter to me. Now I won’t move even a foot towards the palace.” “No. Don’t relinquish your duties towards the country. And don’t wash your hands off this forest flower either.” “You are certainly not an emerald flower; instead, you are the flower of my life. Yes, you are the essence of my life!” “Hope you won't forget me!” “Forget? How can I forget this embodiment of beauty? Here, have my signet ring as a symbol of my love unforgettable.” Dushyandhan puts his signet ring on Cakuntalai’s finger and kisses. (During the break, they both come to the dressing room for change of make-up). The artiste playing Dushyandhan approaches the actress taking Cakuntalai’s role and speaks to her, “What Tāmarai! I planted a sizzling kiss on your fingers, while putting on the ring. How did it taste?” he bared his teeth and smiled. “In the drama only, I was Cakuntalai! You were Dushyandhan!” “Why can’t we remain so in real life?” “Kindly watch your manners. What is your age? And what is mine?” “I am a well-built young man and you are a bud today! But the bud would soon become a flower, dear girl, provided you fall for a man like me.” “Don’t nurse unrealistic dreams. Go away.” “The next scene in the play would be my forgetting you.” “That scene appears, only after the signet ring is lost.” “Before the ring gets lost, what about embracing you and planting a kiss?” “Let that ring be lost right now.” So saying, she throws away the signet ring in the dressing room itself. She walks off in a huff and disrobes her ascetic guise, even while going outside.” “Oh girl! The signet ring should be swallowed by the fish. Isn’t that the real story of the play?” “Before that, you might gobble me!” “I am the tank most suitable for a lotus like you to float on.” He grabs her and pulls her towards him. But in a defiant fury, she pushes him aside and makes good her escape. Dushyandhan of the drama stands stupefied relishing even her anger. This one-sided love is what is called kaikkiḷai. The defining features of unrequited love conduct (kaikkiḷai) are: > One falls in for a lass > With the passion of sex unformed yet > And yet, > One turns incurably afflicted; > One enters into conversation with that lass > Which alternates between praise and dispraise; > No reciprocity on her part marked though, > One persists indulgently in one’s address. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Akattiṇai iyal, verse 50).

Maṭalēṟutal, the public practice of men riding on the horse made of dried palmyra leaves that cause bruises all over the body with blood oozing, by which to compel the parents of the girl to give her in marriage to him; Men and women in the evening of their life, being filled with abnormal desire to enjoy union, which assails them like a poniard; The extreme of carnal desire remaining unbridled like a truant child, in spite of all attempts to restrain it; and The violent pursuit of passion that surges up like a turbulent sea - All these four are acts of peruntiṇai (abnormal sexual passion) and they are not totally alien to those of kaikkiḷai. The practice of riding on the palmyra horse is not confined to the front of the house of the hero. In fact, the man comes to the street and all through the village. This act would persist until the parents of the heroine consent to hand the girl to him. Where it does not happen, the man would threaten to give up his life. Once the man and woman are sapped of youth, they should contemplate activities to be undertaken for the welfare of the society and the future generation. They should continue their service to humanity by realizing that sex is not an end in itself, taking the cue from the placement of the section on sexual love in Tirukkuṟaḷ where Tiruvalluvar implies that sex must end at a point in life, and should not persist as an end in life. Owing to unbridled sexual desire and by giving vent to their carnal cravings, certain folks plunge into socially ostracized activities like murder and rape. They push themselves into these socially degrading deeds, without fully realizing their enormity. The concept of peruntiṇai then is an invaluable treasure in so far as it serves as a warning against such deeds. Tolkāppiyar has chosen to treat this concept as a thing to be excluded. The four defining features of abnormal sexual passion (peruntiṇai) are: > Taking to riding of the horse made of palmyra stems; > Man and woman past their youth drawn to each other; > The passion of lust growing uncontained and out of proportion; > And excessive lust seeking gratification through forced union. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Akattiṇai iyal, verse 51).

t: Warriors who Protected Honour and Valour
x: The Puṟattiṇai chapter in Tolkāppiyam speaks of seven thematic situations (tiṇais) of Puṟam corresponding to the seven Akam situations. They are 1. Veṭci (counterpart of kuṟiñci) is the seizure of the cattle of an enemy king in secret by the vassals or officers of his rival (and taking the animals under the latter’s protection), an act provoking war in ancient times. The counter-attack in the form of fighting and recovery of the seized cattle by the enemy king’s men is also part of this tiṇai. 2. Vañci (counterpart of mullai) is the march of one king with his forces against another, causing fear to the subjects of the kingdoms; it is motivated by the ambition of seizing territory through conquest. 3. Uḻiñai (counterpart of marutam) is the siege by an attacking king of a fort, along with its defence by the king remaining within. 4. Tumpai (counterpart of neytal) is the heroic attack of the invading king met with equally heroic resistance in battle by the defending king. The focus here is on deeds of exceptional valour and heroism in battle performed by warriors of either side in an attack; the tumpai situation can occur with other situations involving fighting, e.g., veṭcippuṟattumpai, dealing with exploits of bravery in cattle seizure preliminary to war. 5. Vākai (counterpart of pālai) is the excellence achieved by different social orders as well as sages and ascetics-in-penance, performing their functions by themselves and in complementation or confrontation with others. 6. Kāñci (counterpart of peruntiṇai) treats of the instability of human life, youth, wealth, etc. 7. Pāṭāṉ (counterpart of kaikkiḷai) speaks the praises of a male patron (āṇ) by a suppliant poet seeking the former’s benefaction. > Veṭci is > Men at the border-posts, > Charged by their ruler, > Capturing the cows of the hostile king by stealth > And keeping them right under guard. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Puṟattiṇai iyal, verse 2) Coming to veṭci situation, there are fourteen types of activities (called sub-situations (tuṟais)) attendant on it. These activities in their order of occurrence are enumerated in Tolkāppiyam as under: > The fourteen substrands of the veṭci theme are: > The clamour > That marks the army’s movement to lift the foeman’s cows; > The utterances of townsfolk around > Coming for good omens for the marching men; > The men’s march > Being unknown to the foeman’s spies > That infiltrate into their midst; > The marching men’s spying > Unnoticed by the foeman; > Lying in wait for the moment opportune to lift the cows > Encircling the foemen’s positions spied right; > Slaying of foemen that offer resistance; > Capturing the cows therein; > Putting to rout the foemen in pursuit; > Being back home > With no affliction to the cattle captured; > Home that they are > To witness cheer and accolade; > Securing the herds of cows at home; > The cows captured being shared; > Revelry marking the victorious seizure of cows > And gifting away of cows to others too. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Puṟattiṇai iyal, verse 3) What is important here is not the victory or the defeat of one king or the other, but the acts of prowess and courage and honour displayed by the warriors of both sides. Here is a poetic illustration of Tolkāppiyar’s exposition in a Puṟanāṉūṟu poem (269) by Avvaiyār: > Wearing a garland of wild jasmine full of seeds and a few blossoms and > buds as sharp-tipped as a kuyil’s beak resplendently bedecking our thick > black hair, you drank once, and again, of liquor as amber as a tiger’s eyes > poured out in a new cup, and then because a tuṭi drummer wearing a > chaplet of dried leaves and drumming the call to battle on his drum had > come, you refused to praise and accept the filtered, intoxicating toddy > they then offered you, but instead took up this sword, they say, into > your powerful hand and with it, after tracking bowmen who had seized > the many long lines of cattle in combat where the warriors wore > fragrant basil, you cut down those enemies while the red vultures > screeched, sailing on their curving wings!

t: He Who has Turned a Hero-stone
x: The wars waged by the ancient Tamils to either capture the cows or to retrieve the cows were fought with codes of conduct. From which direction is he throwing the spear or for that matter, from which direction is he shooting the arrows? In the event of the warrors confronting each other in the warfield, what was the method employed to distinguish between our men and the enemy? > Wearing of palmyra, morgosa and mountain ebony, > The [totemic] flowers of towering note, > That mark identity and distinctiveness > Among soldiers who make the massive armies > Which the great monarchs of burning hostility commanded. To distinguish between the enemy and one’s own soldiers, during face-to-face confrontation, the soldiers were made to wear the garlands of male palmyra tree, neem tree and common mountain ebony tree. > Rout of foemen in a fierce battle; > Recovery of the cows captured; > Singing the praises of the monarch of lasting note; > The warrior taking lofty vows > On account of his exceeding prowess in war; > Apart from these > Which the karaṇtai theme characterizes, > The others proper to veṭci are: > The twofold piḷḷainilai of > Resisting the vanguard of the opposing army > And being felled by the enemy’s sword; > The people rejoicing at the valour of the warrior > Who withstood the strike of the enemy’s sword, > To the accompaniment of drum-beat, > And bestowing the land on him; > The choice of the proper stone > For erecting the memorial of the fallen warrior; > Commencing the sculpturing of the dead warrior’s image; > Giving the stone a ceremonial bathing; > Erecting the stone thus sculptured; > Bestowing honours right in accord with tradition; > And praise and worship extended to the stone. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Puṟattiṇai iyal, verse 5) What follows is an imaginative illustration of this Tolkāppiyam exposition: They made the enemy run for cover showing their back. The cows captured by the veṭci soliders were retrieved. They trumpeted and hailed their king for his deft strategy which fed valour and strength, culminating in a glorious victory. The veṭci soldiers boasted that cows captured by them could not be retrieved, just as milk - the food from the udder of cows - cannot be restored to the cows. But our king shattered all the tall claims of these warriors. Thus they hailed their king and sang hosannas about him. In the meantime, the prince in the prime of his youth thundered, “O king, issue your command! In order to sing accolades of our victory not merely confining to retrieval of the cows but for the act of capturing the entire lot of enemy’s land, issue command unto me. I would shatter the strong fort of the enemy and ruin the front ranks of the army, which guard that land. I will make the enemy subservient to us, through the might of my sword. I salute and await your orders, with a vow to accomplish this task. You nourished me affectionately during my childhood days. Now, I am a grown-up man, how can you be afraid of issuing orders?” He spoke in a voice, which sounded like an explosion. “I am proud of parenting a brave son. My arms swell up in excitement, to see you stand seeking permission, with a sword in your hand. My heart quivers in excitement. Yes, proceed towards the fort. Annihilate all the wings of foe’s army, be it the front rank, cavalry, infantry or the elephant wing. You have obtained the permission, dear prince. March on!” After getting the king’s permission, the elite wing of the army raised the war cry “Victory is ours” and marched forward to the beating of the drums. The doors of the fort got shattered! The flag pole fell down! With nobody left to save the country, the nation of veṭci men became a virtual hunted ground for the karaṇtai warriors. “We are unparalleled” was the song on the lips of the karaṇtai soldiers. The prince raised the sword, which fetched victory to him and his army and entered the fort riding his horse. At the time of entry, a spear flying from nowhere pierced through his chest. He held the fatal spear and breathed his last, but not before accounting for ten to twenty heads of the enemy soldiers. “Dear son! You declined the golden crown and rather chose the aura of fame through bravery,” a visibly perturbed king kissed his forehead. The soldiers, unable to celebrate their victory fully, erected a hero-stone for the immortal prince in tune with the practice of raising hero-stones in memory of the warriors dying undaunted in the field of battle.

Even while ruling over the entire land, people would go for reigning supreme over the water. After possessing the land and the water, they would like to venture for the sky and capture that also. The bees swarming around over the honeycomb would fly up and above and think the land and the sky are well within their reach. It is no wonder then that a chieftain no longer remains content with being under the overlordship of a king. Further, the coveted fame of possessor of many a fortress also gets satiating. When the land comes, he retorts, “You alone? Let the sea also assemble here to obey my orders!’ If that improbable also happens, then he desires for the eastern sky of the morning and of the western sky of the dusk to extend a red carpet welcome to him! Tolkāppiyam’s vañcittiṇai focuses upon such persons of overvaulting ambitions. Further, to extend the boundaries of their kingdoms, they desire large tracts of land and consequently invade the neighbouring countries. It then also happens that the invaded stand up in prowess and humble the aggressor. > It (veṭci) is > The vanquishing of a king > Marked by uncontained hunger for other’s soil, > By another king > Through a frightful display of prowess. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Puṟattiṇai iyal, verse 7) The columns of opposing soldiers appear like the winged ants from groves to make one wonder: Is the country too small for the army? Or is the army too large for the country? They march on as if they are unbridled horses, and with eyes burning like tigers’. “Let fire engulf the way we pass through! Let it spread in all directions! And let it reduce the flower garden-like fields to ashes.” They say, “Our king has earned undeclining fame by his valour”. They praise the king of their country for his chivalry of liberally donating the prize articles in the form of battle-arms. The soldiers compose songs and sing them to the accompaniment of stringed instruments. “Victory greets our king in all the places, whereas other kings are doomed to destruction.” They would even say it was their king who added lustrous embellishment to the word ‘victory’ itself. So go their unabashed hyperboles of flatteries. Like the mighty dam, which stops the overflowing waters of a river threatening to breech the banks, due to unabated rain marking the peak of the rainy season, there is also the one who singlehandedly defends his land against the aggression of the seemingly never-ending columns of invading army, out to conquer the land. He shatters their overvaulting avarice and leaves them dejected. The conqueror is at the same time not bloated over the ruin of the vanquished. He believes in the cultured doctrine of civility that it is always better to regard victory and defeat in the same manner. Therefore, he provides aid and food to those injured in the war. He exempts the vanquished from paying tribute and stands with no desire to seek vengeance. He remains tall as an epitome of marvellous fame. The greedy king, who sought to invade, beats a hasty retreat to his country by declaring that he doesn’t need an enlarged kingdom, instead whatever he is left with is good enough. > The vañci puram theme > Ramifies into thirteen substrands of worthy note: > The clamour that marks the army’s march; > Setting the foemen’s land on fire; > The radiant glory that attends the feats of prowess; > The acts of liberality extended by the monarch; > The acts of valour > With which the enemy is charged at close quarters > And is sent to his doom; > The boast of the warriors > As recipients of the ruler’s gifts and honours; > The dauntless daring of foemen as if they were a trifle; > Holding in single-handedly > The advance of the hostile forces > As does a rocky dam > That contains surging floods; > The king gives a grand feast > To his warriors on the eve of battle; > The pervasive radiant note of fame > That attends the victorious king; > The decline and debility > That go with the vanquished; > The inexhaustible prowess of the king in war > And the great prosperity that it brings > Praised in the pestle song; > And the king tending and embracing his warriors > Wounded through acts of valour in battle. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Puṟattiṇai iyal, verse 8)

In the Hindu temples, the presiding deity has two statues - mūlavar, the stone statue fixed inside sanctum sanctorum and uṟcavar , the statue made of five types of metals. Of them, mūlavar is worshipped in the place of its location, whereas uṟcavar is taken in procession outside the temple, as the representative of mūlavar during festivals. This practice is seen observed in all the temples of Tamiḻnāṭu. But the exceptions are the six temples at Tiruvārūr and the adjoining Tirukkuvaḷai, Tirukkōpuravāsal, Tirumaṟaikkāṭu, Tirunākai and Tiruvāymūr, where the mūlavar and uṟcavar statues are not made of stone and metal respectively, and they look alike. The same Tiyākarāja statue is fixed in the sanctum sanctorum and taken in procession also. It is also used in chariot processions. In these shrines, the procession deity has a more pronounced honour of worship. The devotees and priests carry the statue on their shoulders every year on auspicious days to mark the advent of the festival. They place it on a chariot and celebrate festivals drawing the chariots. At the culmination of the festivals, the statue is reinstated inside the temple. In the uḻiñai situation of puṟam poetry, Tolkāppiyam Poruḷatikāram speaks of a similar honour accorded by kings to their victorious swords. The uḻiñai puṟam situation deals with the siege of an enemy fort by a king and the defence of the fort by the king remaining within. The siege is resorted to when the authority of the attacking king is defied by the other. Both the kings at the start of the war place their swords under the decorated canopy at an auspicious hour and take them in procession. The soldiers defending the fort from inside and the ones attacking it from outside wage a fierce war against each other, either standing on or climbing over the ladders made of wooden planks which are placed on the fort walls. The spectacle of the soldiers inside and outside the fort fighting each other and retreating resembles the joining and moving away of the parasitic plant in the moat around the fort wall due to the strong winds or the vibration caused by the deed of war. The battle extends to many parts of the town too. Not completely relying upon the soldiers from both the sides and in order to demonstrate the steely resolve of their hearts, the warring kings fight on the wall of the fort themselves, without ever worrying about their lives. After all, the garland of victory is meant for only one of them! Before the defeat could stare large on his face, a king saves his dignity by embracing death. The purificatory ceremonies are performed for the sword of the victor king, as it is deemed to be responsible for his triumph. It was the ethos of those days to hold aloft the white canopy over the sword and thereby pay obeisance to the sword, which sealed victory in the war by being the deity in the santorum and the procession deity. Yes, it was the era which recognized and honoured valour. In spite of being an era of wars, it certainly was the golden epoch hailing the greatness of the Tamiḻ race, in that the victor king was being honoured with coronation in the name of the deceased king. Is not this a mark of magnanimity of our ancestors? Look at the Tolkāppiyam verse: > Uḻiñai marks twelve other substrands too: > Sending of the royal parasol and sword at an auspicious hour > Preceding the siege of the foe intended; > The raging fight of the soldiers > As they stand on ladders fitted to the fort; > The fierce, resolute battle > Intended to end the siege outside the fortress; > The mighty defence offered by the besieged within; > Breach of the defence by the besieging men; > Action in the moat of the fortress; > Carrying the battle thereon > Into the town of the besieged; > Triumphant scaling of the fort within; > The ceremonial bath of the victorious king > And his taking the crown of the vanquished; > The ceremonial bath of the sword of the victor; > And the absolute surrender of the vanquished. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Puṟattiṇai iyal, verse 13)

t: Persistence in War like an Unyielding Buffalo
x: The spectacle of the tumpai puram situation of a king taking on the enemy king of undaunted prowess and determination and putting him to rout is one of the finest examples of ancient Tamiḻs’ valour capable of moving even the stony hearts. In the battle arena, where the two kings cross swords, the enemy soldiers, afraid of going near a fighter, aim spears and bows at him from a safe distance. The warrior, carrying a sword and a shield, fights with all his might. His sword chops off many a number of enemies, but gets blunted after brushing against a stone. His shield also develops chinks and he offers his body as a shield to take on the innumerable spears and arrows shot at him. Alas! In the end, a sword shining like lightning powers its way towards him and in the same lightning speed rips apart his head from the body. But the severed parts of his body do not fall on the ground immediately; instead, his head, body, legs and hands keep moving and quivering. > It is in particular > The theme of undoing the might of an invading monarch > Burning with an overweening pride in his prowess. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Puṟattiṇai iyal, verse 15) > The life of the warrior in action departing, > With his body having been pierced thick and fast > By the rain of arrows and spears of foemen, > There is the wondrous spectacle of the man in two pieces - > The body standing erect without falling on the ground > In the manner of the leech cut into parts staying alive. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Puṟattiṇai iyal, verse 16) Men on foot, elephants and cavalry march on to the field, sending shivers down the spine of the enemy. The drums are played on both the sides to herald the start of the war. One of them sounds like the thunder of the summer season, while the other sounds like the storm, crossing through the sea, causing a great upheaval. The swords blaze through the warfield; the spears are launched from the mighty hands. The arrows, ripping through the air, pierce the stomach of a few lethargic men, announcing that a timid person has no place in the field of war. A few exceptional instances surface in which cowards, whose bodies shiver like strings of a musical instrument, running through in fear are identified and sidelined. A soldier fighting at a distance witnesses his king, dear to him like his own life, hemmed in by enemy soldiers and commanders like columns of fish. “What, is my king in danger?” he reacts with blood-shot eyes and with hands clutching on to his weapon, he pounces there, much like an injured tiger or rather like a stamped snake. On both the sides, soldiers form protective rings around their kings and safeguard them. The army commander moves around the columns of his army. In the event of any unexpected setback, he remains unfazed quite like a buffalo, only to single-handedly take on the might of the formidable army of the foe. The buffalo can bear anything. It is given such an honour in puṟam literature. The enemy king is seen fighting a surging elephant and ultimately getting killed by being trampled by it. In the end, when both the kings perish in the war, one of the soldiers rises up in rage on seeing the death of his king. He wrecks vengeance upon the enemy rank by killing a number of soldiers. In a precarious condition, wherein it could not be categorically established as to who finally won, this verse stands out eulogizing an individual soldier who beheads innumerable enemy soldiers to get even for his king’s death. Look at the following Tolkāppiyam verse: > The theme of tumpai > Ramifies into twelve substrands: > The three columns of infantry, elephantry and cavalry > That strike terror among the foemen; > The deed of mettle by a warrior > That leaves his charge aside > And puts the enemy soldiers to rout > Who come to surround his king > As he keeps daring them with his spear; > The chiefs of the two contending monarchs > Falling to death in personal combat > Besides their prop for their rulers in action; > The daring of an army chief > That comes up braving the odds like a buffalo > To stand at the head of the rear of his army > As it tends to retreat in disarray; > The grit of a warrior in action > Though he stands disarmed of his weapons; > The death of the warriors > That braved the charging elephants; > The clamour of singing and dancing > Of the warriors of the victorious king > Who felled his enemy king to death along with his elephant; > The annihilation of the two contending monarchs > Along with their kindred folk in deed > In their bloody conflict with swords; > The famed act of a warrior > Who finds his king felled in action > And rises in ire uncontained to fight the foe > And the feat exceptional of the warrior > That sends columns of enemy’s army into disarray > And goes about waving his brilliant winning sword. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Puṟattiṇai iyal, verse 19)

We can achieve victory by either vying with others or by striving on our own. Vākai does not refer only to the victory achieved in war. In fact, it is the attaining of a lofty goal in life through virtuous means. Tolkāppiyam, Poruḷatikāram explains the classifications of vākai as well as its defining traits and its grammar. That verse in question begins thus, “The sixfold occupations of the brahmins,” After reading it, one might feel like wondering, “What exactly is this Brahmin occupation? How on earth did brahmins appear in Tolkāppiyam?” They had indeed arrived but their arrival was portended in Collatikāram itself. Somehow, the Tamiḻs had lost sight of the fact that the sound of the bell would signal the advent of the elephant. In the cultivated fields weeds grow along with crop unannounced. Tolkāppiyam touches upon that in the verse below: > Vaṭacol comprises words (borrowed from Sanskrit) > That steer clear of the system of sounds in Sanskrit > And that come to be adapted to the native form and sound. > > (Collatikāram : Ecca iyal, verse 5) How many years ago was the door kept open for this phenomenon? Researchers fix Tolkāppiyam to the seventh century B.C. That is, approximately 2500 years ago, Sanskrit smelt the favoured environment and the way was paved for the entry of the Aryans into the Tamiḻ land. This verse in vākaittiṇai attests to their entrenchment. > The seven modes of vocations > Which the theme of vākai celebrates are: > The sixfold occupations of the brahmins > [Learning, instruction, performing sacrifices, > Making others perform sacrifices, > Munificence and being beneficiaries of munificence]; > The fivefold occupations of the kings > [Learning, performing sacrifices, munificence, > Protecting the country and administering justice]; > The sixfold occupations of the other [tradesmen and cultivating] classes > [Learning, farming, trading, rearing cattle, > Forms of worship and acts of liberality]; > The calling of sages and astrologers - > The flawless reading of planetary movements > In relation to their effects on the past, present and future -- > The eightfold functions of ascetics > [Bathing, lying on the bare ground, > Wearing leather covering, consecrated fire worship, > Keeping away from habitations of people, > Keeping undressed hair, > Eating forest produce and worshipping god]; > The demarcated skills of excellence of the warrior class; > And the myriad callings other than the above > [Such as music, drama and singing]. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Puṟattiṇai iyal, verse 20) The expression “so said the poets,” clearly indicates the Aryan arrival, either during Tolkāppiyar’s time, or even earlier. They had stamped their hold on our land and people, along with their codes of living which were alien to the Tamiḻ mores. According to Tolkāppiyar, Brahmins had six duties - to chant mantras , make others chant mantras , conduct homams, make others conduct homams, to give and to accept gifts. The king’s five cardinal duties were - to chant mantras, to conduct homams, to give gifts, to offer army’s support to allies, and to protect the subjects. The traders and peasants had six duties - to chant mantras, to conduct homams, to give gifts, to cultivate, to trade and to maintain the livestock. To calculate and monitor the events of the three times, namely, the past, the present, and the future, was the duty of persons endowed with wisdom. The recluse had the duties of upholding eight types of discipline. While being aware of these duties, the army leaders’ duty was to accomplish victory, not only through the might of sword or arms, but also through the means of these duties. Such a victory was supposed to be more enduring. Though many of these duties underlined could uplift one’s stature of life, the two duties of conducting homams, and making others follow the practice of conducting homams provided opportunities for the Brahmins and such people to resort to discrimination which was completely alien to the Tamiḻ land. Vēṭal means to conduct homams, while vēṭpittal is to make others conduct homams. The practice of offering sacrifice and conducting homams crept into the Tamiḻ land through the wiles of the Brahmins. It took roots and branched out among the Tamiḻs thanks to the cleverness of the brahmins. Victory could be amassed through bravery which required waging wars and perseverance. Real victory in life and happiness could be achieved by getting involved in various virtuous deeds, even cutting across national boundaries. What then was the necessity for these unavailing practices of conducting homams and offering sacrifices? There would have been reservations and protests. But would the priestly class allow this to be given up? If the subtle manipulation combined with versatile abilities worked, it was natural that even an emperor would be hypnotized in the meandering smoke of camphor. Therefore, conducting homams and the practice of making others conduct homams started slowly but gained momentum of a forest flood and breached the banks. Those who wielded arms like spear, sword, lance and trident and rode on horses and those who sang of the power of love and the breathlike passion for the motherland had to stoop before the fire pit of the homam, prostrate and remain in a hunched posture to drink the urine of cow, in keeping with the practice of conducting homams. Even that great Cēraṉ Ceṅkuṭṭuvaṉ of Cilappatikāram who successfully led the Himalayan campaign and brought the stone for carving the statue of Kaṇṇaki on the heads of the northern kings Kaṉakaṉ and Vicayaṉ had to fall in line. That renowned warrior was beaten squarely by the vedic rites and rituals. The invasion followed by the bringing of stone for the Kaṇṇaki statue was over. Kaṉaka-Vicayaṉ were also imprisoned. At that juncture, a person of the Aryan priestly class, Māṭala Maṟaiyōṉ, met the king and offered advice, which bore fruit. The kings of northern origin were set free. In keeping with the advice of the priest, the king made preparations for a homam. That work was entrusted to the army chief Villavaṉkōtai: > You, master of wisdom, listen to my words: > Vedic sacrifices prescribed for kings > You need to perform with priestly cooperation: > This will surely lead you to salvation, > That would gladden heavenly beings. > If you postpone it for tomorrow, who knows > For certain his last day? Supppose....” > Māṭalaṉ prayed for long life to the king, > His consort, and the brave king kneeling > Before him; he did sow thoughts of higher being > In the mind of Kuṭṭuvaṉ, the Cēra king. > The sowing resulted in abundant harvest; > The valiant king, eager to enjoy the best, > Engaged priests, who had studied the vedas, > And had all doubts cleared by their gurus, > To perform the sacrificial rites to conform > To the wise Māṭalaṉ’s prescription. > He released the Aryan kings from prison, > And lodged them in Velāvikkō mansion > Outside the city walls, and surrounded > By shady groves; he announced their freedom > To go home, after the sacrifices were concluded. > He instructed Villavaṉkōtai to show due courtesy to them. In his elucidation of Tolkāppiyam, Nāvalar Cōmacuntara Pāratiyār categorically rejects the presence of caste-based classification of Akattiṇai iyal and Puṟattiṇai iyal. The great scholar Veḷḷaivāraṇar subscribes to this view in his Tolkāppiyam studies and says: “The four types of caste observed in books of northern origin were unheard of among the ancient Tamiḻ people.” This was his categorical averment. He adds, “The practice of classifying people on the basis of caste was never prevalent in the ancient Tamiḻ country. The categorization was only on the basis of the geographical regions they inhabited.” Though these two learned academics claim so, it cannot be denied that the custom of classifying people on the basis of caste sneaked in either overtly or covertly and got established firmly. In came castes to begin homams and sacrifices heralding the advent of the Brahmins in vākaittiṇai itself. If one were to put it with a tinge of sadness, it would be rather more appropriate to describe vākaittiṇai as the ‘tiṇai of the Aryan advent’.

Even as the Aryan culture had come to entrench itself on the Tamiḻ soil as a tiny wart on a lovely face though refusing to go off except through a surgery, the Puṟam theme of vākai reflects an admirable dimension of the native cultural mores of the ancient Tamiḻs. Be it winter or summer, in war-camps there are the warriors and their generals closeted together working out the strategies of war and remaining ever alert for eventualities of martial campaigns. The peasants who provide for others’ sustenance through their labour get into joyous rapture on witnessing bumper crops. The enemy routed by acts of valour, the king in ecstasy joins his soldiers in their kuravai dance. Female dancers present a feast of dance by teaming up with the soldiers. The great heroes, who offered to sacrifice their lives on the warfield where occasion warranted, are seen inundated in the shower of adulation. The men of humanitarian propensities demonstrate their love even to their enemies. The good samaritans teeming with virtues get recognition, as they are felicitated by the king in his court. Those who claim to lead a fruitful life do so within the prescribed framework of discipline and stand out as the exemplars. Departing from the way of reforming wrong-doers through punishments, they derive pleasure in reforming them by pardon. They experience happiness by acts of munificence. The renunciation is not just giving up the conjugal life of the householder. There are rulers of land renouncing their all and merging into the sea of humanity. Here is that vākaittiṇai verse: > Eighteen are the ramifications > That the vākai theme marks: > Staying at the warcamp > In the cold season and the hot season > In fond devotion to the deed on hand; > The winning feats in the battlefield of warriors on chariots > Beside the attainments of ploughmen on the cornfield; > The circular kuravai dance in front of his chariot > Danced by his warriors > As their monarch stands victorious over his chariot-borne foemen; > The circular kuravai dance in the rear of his chariot > Danced by the kindred folk > As their monarch stands victorious over his chariot-borne foemen; > The deed of the spear that holds off massive charges; > The prowess of men that holds in mighty strikes; > The manly fortitude that disregards the burden of this unavailing existence; > The warrior offering his crowning life to fire > In fulfilment of his vow to the exalted > Putting the hostile foemen to shame thereat; > Extending hands of friendship to the enemy; > The eminence that attends possession of bulls and cows > By which to efface the evil of indigence; > The glory of abdicating the throne to take to renunciation; > The eight qualities that mark a courtier > [Nobility of birth, learning, virtuous conduct, > Truthfulness, purity, equity > And absence of envy and greed]; > Such modes of conduct as enjoined by sage works; > Unceasing acts of liberality that entail lasting renown; > Bearing no malice towards men that do evil unto one; > Being endowed with the wealth of the spirit; > Mercy and compassion as marks the detached mind; > And being freed of the fetters of want. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Puṟattiṇai iyal, verse 21)

t: Instability of Life and Things Worldly
x: What follows is the Tolkāppiyam verse detailing the situations of this poignant kāñcittiṇai theme, besides an illustrative verse of mine: > Peruṅkāñci that speaks of the inevitability of death; > Mutukāñci that indicates the great truths of life > Which men of sage wisdom bring home to the youth; > Maṟakkāñci that shows a warrior > Wounded in his breast in the battle > Tearing open that wound > And dying in utter disdain of life; > Pēykkāñci that refers to > The devils guarding the warrior wounded in battle > There being no kin to tend him; > Maṉṉaikkāñci that refers to mourning the death of the great one > Enumerating his deeds of virtue and valour; > Vañciṉakkāñci that indicates swearing a vow > That one would fall into such states stated > Were one to fail to accomplish a task chosen; > Toṭākkāñci that shows a loving wife > Guarding her wounded warrior-husband on the battlefield > Against devils laying their hands on him; > Āñcikkāñci that speaks of the wife > Killing herself with the spear > That took her warrior-husband’s life; > Makaṭpāṟkāñci that shows > Refusal by a chieftain of ancient lineage > To give his daughter’s hand in marriage > To another king of comparable valour > That has come to take him on in a war; > The wife of the warrior killed in the battlefield > Nestling up her face and breasts against his head > And seeing her life ended; > These are the ten substrands of kāñci theme, > Which the authority has decreed. > The bewildering wail of the kin around the warrior > Who met with a glorious end; > The lonely cries of uncontained distress; > Mūtānāntam, the awed expressions of tribute by onlookers, > As they find the wife ending her life > On the death of her husband in action; > Mutapālai, the bitter wail of the lonesome wife > On the death of her husband > As they traversed the killing arid wastes; > Kaiyaṟunilai, the helpless cries of anguish of the kindred folk > At the death of the ones who counted in their lives; > Taputāranilai, the piteous state of the bereaved husband; > Tāpatānilai, the misery of having been bereaved of one’s loving husband; > Pālai nilai, the words of resentment by the wife, > Who prepares to enter into the funeral pyre of her husband, > At those that tend to weaken her resolve; > Talaippeyalnilai, the supreme act of the mother > That went seeking death on the battlefield > On hearing that her son had a retreat in war; > And kāṭuvāḻttu, the glorification of the graveyard > That perpetually impresses upon the people of this wide world > The impermanence of the lives of men > And its own [graveyard’s] permanence - > These ten substrands of worthy treatment including, > Kāñci theme ramifies into twenty sub-situations. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Puṟattiṇai iyal, verse 24) > Be it the illumination of the little oil-lamp, > I have provided the expositions of all thematic situations > Included in Akattiṇai and Puṟattiṇai; > Although elucidations detailed of all these situations > I could not give in this study, > Could I afford to leave out Kāñcittiṇai? > Would not kāñci rebuke me albeit gently? > Don’t I know that honeyed heart? > > I am the one > Whose time of the day is split into atoms, > One atom of which is multiplied by a hundred > And is devoted exclusively to kāñci > And spent in all pleasure. > > The kāñci theme unmatched > Is to make a life of eternity > By being reminded of one’s instability of life > Bringing in the analogy of bubbles on water’s surface, > Providing an anchor to the mind vacillating > And standing on renown hill-like. > Kāñci theme is that > What tells folks > To preserve honour > Be it at the cost of one’s head. > > Kāñci theme tells men > To perform deeds virtuous on the earth > Leaving not a bit of it incomplete > With the realization that > ‘He that lived yesterday > Does exist not today’ > Even when there remains the threat > Of the power of Death around. > > Even if you stand uncared for, > Spirits too will come to your aid > Hailing your efforts large > To make the Tamiḻs flourish. > > Kāñci is routing the wily foe > In the manner of the Pāṇṭiya king > Who swore: “Let me not be the theme of Māṅkuṭi Marutaṉ’s song > If I don’t vanquish the foes and return! > > Kāñci is > That act of the woman > Who bathes with her tears > Her dead husband wounded in war, > Prohibits others from touching her > And stabs herself > With the sword that killed her husband. > > The unmatched kāñci is that > Where a father and mother in the evening of their life > See the suitor for their daughter driven away > With wounds on his back > Who came waging a war for her hand. > Kāñci is > Where the woman > Clasps her husband’s spear-pierced body > As does a creeper over the banyan trunk. > > Kāñci is > Where the wife leaps lightning-like into the flames > Detesting life beyond her husband > When he remained dead - apart > A sacrifice it is of womankind eye-like > To show that life is no sugar cane > And to hold honour dear as life. > Such is what kāñci is. > > No more energy I am left with > To elaborate further on this kāñci theme; > I stop it therefore at this.

> Look at the commentary of the passionate Tamiḻ scholar Veḷḷaivāraṇar > On the Tolkāppiyam verse on the nature of clandestine love! > We will understand > Why Tolkāppiyar refers here to the eight kinds of marriage in the Aryan land. > > These kinds stand flawed, > Unacceptable to the impeccable Tamiḻ mind; > They might suit only the Aryan culture > In their entirety; > And just one or two of them correspond to the Tamiḻ ethos - > So says the learned Tamiḻ commentator. > > What then are those eight kinds of marriage? > Piramam is gifting a girl of twelve > To a bachelor nearing fifty years of age; > Giving a girl in marriage to the brother-in-law by relation > With the mutual parental consent > Is what is called piracāpattiyam; > Āriṭam is taking a girl in marriage > Along with the gift of cattle; > Giving the girl’s hand to a performer of sacrifice > Before the sacrificial fire is teyvam; > Gandharvam is the union of love > Between a man and a woman running into each other; > Acuram is giving the girl learned to one adept in archery > Who tames a killer bull > And who is after gifts of wealth; > Irākkatam is coercive marriage of a girl by a boy: > And paicācam is union with a girl > Older by age, given to sleep and drink. > > Tolkāppiyar identifies these forms > As those of the Vedic Aryan culture > And rejects them subtly > And they do not go with the Tamiḻ mores, > So says our respected Tamiḻ scholar Veḷḷaivāraṇar. > > Kaḷavu is theft, stealing small things; > It is quite natural that it is despised as an act of wrong kind. > > But kaḷavu as a union of love -- > Between a man and a woman > Who are united by the union of hearts > With no hurry for physical intimacy, > Who do not transgress the bounds of propriety > And who meet clandestinely > Aided by their kindly companions, > Whose bond of union courses through > Ways of virtue and love > Combined with codes of worldly needs > The bond uniting the two as one > That comes in for acclaim > In Tamiḻ > Sweet as the strain of the lute > And the deep-sea pearl -- > Is no thing of a lowly worth > Even to men of lowly birth. Here is the Tolkāppiyam verse: > Examined rightly, > The union of love between a man and a woman, > Which embraces the fivefold love behaviour mutually realized, > (Union, forbearance, separation, sulking and lamentation) > And which draws on the pleasures of love, life’s plenty and righteousness, > Shares the nature of the love of the gandharvas adept at lyre play > Which is among the eight forms of marriage vogue among the vedic folk. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Kaḷaviyal, verse 1) Note: Tolkāppiyar had to make a reference to the vedic forms of marriage and contrast them with those of the Tamiḻ culture, for during his time, the vedic culture started taking roots on the Tamiḻ soil. The eight kinds of vedic marriage contrast with the three kinds treated in Tolkāppiyam, namely: mutual love (aṉpiṉ aintiṇai), one-sided love (kaikkiḷai) and abnormal sexual passion (peruntiṇai). Veḷḷaivāraṇar.

The confidant, though mischievous, is virtuous by disposition. His affection for the hero is boundless much like the waves of the sea getting gravitated towards the shore. At dusk, the friend saw the hero surging ahead. He called him by clapping, “Why such an undue haste as if you were heading for a feast? I am back after seeing an angel under the waning moonlight. She is none but a goddess; I witnessed the scene of her stepping out of the temple and standing near the entrance.” After hearing this from his friend, The hero resolved to see her. He literally flew towards the direction pointed at by the friend, like a kite pouncing upon a parrot. Without even an atom of doubt, she is a goddess! Decked in the ornaments, She appeared before him. Finding her as an embodiment of beauty, He surged quite close towards her, in measured steps. Since a goddess does not speak, There was no opportunity for him to speak out and clear his doubt. He dared to analyze her through eyes and see whether she is a goddess. Since a bee kept relishing the flowers From her hair flowing down And as only the flowers sported by the humans Emit fragrance, It dawned upon him that she was no goddess. He looked at the ornaments on the body And saw that they were all the ones made by the goldsmith of this world. Having finished his study on half of her body, He was in raptures understanding that she was not a goddess. The drawings on her breasts and shoulders seen, And the fragrance of lily flower held by her smelt, And known for certain That the eyes on her rounded moon-like face Were but the human eyes all flesh and blood, Also clearing his mind that If she were an angel, her eyelids would not twitch like this And seeing that she was perturbed after noticing him, a man, It was all obvious that She was not an angel but a pigeon Who came searching for him. The fact of her being a human fully dawned on him. And the prankster pal was embarrassed and hid himself near the bush Realizing the emerging scene of his friend and the lady united. > The swarming bees, the ornaments worn, > The ornamental lines drawn on the body, > The fading flowers, human eye, signs of disquietude > The winking of eyes and timidity > And such of these that mark the person > There manifest for the doubt to vanish. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Kaḷaviyal, verse 4)

The confidant was hiding beside the bushes for a long time Without causing any embarrassment to the lovers rendezvousing; He put a stop even to his cough That tended to come out of this throat, For that was not the hour to do so. He was all ears to listen to what they were speaking. There was no sound to be heard. “Where have they gone? Are they present or not?” Confusion reigned over his head. He stretched up a little, Both of them were seen standing like statues. What is the need for language, when the two eyes are there? They knew it well that Of no avail whatever are words of mouth Where eyes meet eyes in acquiescence true. The love which was like a flower has now grown into a green fruit. They knew that in keeping with the Tamil ethos, They should wait till their love turned into a ripe fruit. That is the way of the Tamils prescribed in Tolkāppiyam. “The union of two hearts is not a short story. I convey my greetings for it to become a never-ending saga; Depart for the day and come tomorrow.” So said the genial friend. Since it was time for the devotees to throng the temple, They decided that the day’s converse of the eyes was enough and parted. The confidant clutched the shoulder of the hero and said, “The woman is a beauty endowed with timidity, bashfulness and credulity.” The hero intervened and corrected the friend’s note: “The dame fell into fear as I touched her; Bashfulness is an inborn virtue unto women, And I don’t accept ignorance in women. If both of us were given to ignorance Wouldn’t it lead to physical relationship? We the birds of love Have a perfect understanding that The clandestine career is one Where the hearts unite With no room for fleshly congress, And so we parted after our hearts united into one.” After the hero finished his address The bosom friend responded with his eyes pulled wide apart in amazement: “You have conveyed your passion By signs healthy And by a language unspoken Thereby Fortifying male resolve and female reserve! May each day of your rendezvous Be as blessed as this day’s!” The confidant greeted the hero thus In keeping with the Tamil culture. > The meeting of eyes is the pointer sure > Suggesting the union of minds. > > Where the glances of the eyes reciprocate, > There marks the sprouting of a love career, > So has it been said. > > Nobility of bearing and fortitude > Are such stuff as marks the male [hero]. > > Timidity, bashfulness and credulity > Are the ruling traits in a woman [heroine]. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Kaḷaviyal, verses 5, 6, 7, 8)

He, lost in the thoughts of the beauty met by the Amman shrine, And she, carrying the image of him in her heart’s depths, Are looking forward to meeting again In anxious expectation penance-like. They won’t sleep, nor would they feel hungry, Like chilli powder sprinkled over the wound Their hearts pained, Which they suppressed by lips held tight together. For how many days would they keep it undisclosed Without the knowledge of parents? Would lightning get concealed in darkness? Or would darkness ban lightning tearing through it? Just as the hero has a confidant right, The heroine also has a beautiful maid for her companion. “He was startled as to whether you were a goddess; You called him a thief! With telltale evidences he came to know that you are a human lass Daughter of the earth, flower-like beauty, A woman filled with freshness-- All these you are though, Like the grass bending towards the stream’s course You are inclined towards love, as if it were your very existence. You are united as one in emotions and body.” The companions of the two pile up consolations one after another And yet their hearts remain weighed down. The confidante of the heroine loses on this score While the hero’s friend also doesn’t meet with success. It is not the failure in a battle fought though, Yet they fail in the task of reducing the momentum of love. The lady remains thinking about the hero all the time. What was his predicament? The hero with the body of teakwood-- He stood dispirited with emaciated form afflicted by passion’s extreme. Everything seen by the lady reminded her of him While the man found her in everything he saw. Not knowing what they could do, The male friend and the maid friend invoked the omnipresent God present in each pillar and particle To stand by them and bless them. The answer would be “I am in the heart of the man and the heart of woman In the form of love Though not in the form of the God.” Lost in love they forget the deed of the day and the inclination for doing too! Confusion, bewilderment, forgetting, Passions’ urge going to the extreme As to drive the partners to suicide Such is the intensity of passion Kaḷaviyal of Tolkāppiyam shows. Such are the hurdles the lovers need to overcome; But dispirited they are not, And they vow to succeed With their revolve and prowess. > The vicissitudes of mind > As marking the man and woman > In their clandestine course of love are: > Amorousness, persistent feel of one for the other, > Emaciation of the body, > Giving free vent to experiences of pleasure and pain, > Transgressing the bounds of modesty and propriety, > Every object of sight painfully reminding one > Of the features of the other, > Self-forgetfulness, stupor and death-like anxiety. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Kaḷaviyal, verse 9)

“Though she is not an angel, I would say even the angels cannot measure up to her. Even if one were to search vigorously And select the best among one crore women, Searching into the present and the future, There is nobody quite like this damsel beautiful as the moon On the earth or in the myriad worlds purāṇas speak of ; Definitely we cannot find one of her kind. You would not deny it I am sure! For you have seen her.” Sitting on the horse-drawn chariot stationary He asked his confidant dear as life a thousand times. No boredom writ on the face, The friend acquiescent said, “Yes, yes!” At that time she was standing unseen behind the surrounding wall. The hero pretending to be unaware of her presence Described her loveliness from head to toe: “She is the pinnacle of beauty; When she dresses her hair in five modes -- Bundling it up, Letting it flowing, Or decorating it in the curled fashion-- My darting eyes Would ask who this enchanting woman is! Is she the angel from heaven? Is she the one called Ramba or Urvaci? Dear friend, why don’t you say something to please my craving heart? Would your life-span decrease if you do so?” So saying The excited hero stamped on the plank of the chariot That spurred the scared horses to run along with the chariot And they were about to ram against the lightning-like heroine! He pulled her away and exclaimed “Oh! Is that you? I didn’t know the richly-hued peahen would be here around! O my goodness, you are spared!” “Dear, hope you are not hurt,” he asked with concern. Taking not his hands held around her, he said, “I have been yearning for it for a long time.” And bashfulness prevented her from responding, “I too.” “The Cupid has struck his arrow, now I don’t have any business here.” The dear friend said And he left the place within the bating of the eyelid, in the chariot, But not before winking at the hero And commenting that the rendezvous was fine; The towering trees, plants and bushes Dropped their flowers in the wind And did a good turn, For they made for a fine floral bed! Nobody was around, Only a bit of fear remained as companion for him. Guarded by culture native to womenfolk, That naive full moon of a damsel was feasting upon The external beauty of that man. He expected her to acquiesce in his desire for sex, As does a camphor, Without patiently waiting for the wet wood to dry out and ready to burn. Though she gave her consent to the union of hearts She didn’t acquiesce in bodily contact And sit aside she did. She then gave him an oblique look which drank his life He understood the underlying consent. He thought, “Why not take the fruit and relish it? I am granted the consent Not just for two souls to become one But also for two bodies to unite.” He tended to cross the limits. When she tried to stop him, He said, “I beseech you! We both are meeting amidst many a hurdle Do realize, dear.” His hands moved about caressing her. She gestured as if saying, “Leave alone the hurdles, now take away the finger probing my waist.” She moved a little away from him. He then made a request passionate, “I cannot bear it any more, my young parrot! Don’t let me die.” His entreaties melting her She threw off her bashfulness And let him close in. Though she initially consented to his passion’s compulsion, It turned out to be the desire of both for union. > Caressing the heroine’s limbs: > Contriving feigned excuses for the same; > Getting close to her and embracing her; > Speaking of her reserve as impediment to union; > His express regret at the union delayed; > The union that ensues thereon; > The joy of union realized in haste > And his lofty vow of unbroken intimacy -- > These eight situations of ruling import > Occasion utterance by the hero. > > ..... > > (Poruḷatikāram : Kaḷaviyal, verse 11)

“I am returning after seeing the lover”, said the heroine. “I understood that much-after seeing your dishevelled hair”, Was the quick reply of the confidante. “What happened to cause such things disorderly in your form, dear? Tell me how your mind has its composure lost.” For the confidante to see The heroine bared her shoulder. Bloodshot marks! Signs of scratches like the crescent moon! Even when the bruises healed, the scars deep remained intact. “My God! How bad! For heaven’s sake, don’t think I am insulting your hero; Does he belong to the species of animals or human beings? You got trapped by him; It would have been better even if he had gobbled you. But why did you permit him to maul you in frenzy of lust?” “You are weighed down in anguish, confidante! My sweet kindly man he is. He maintained his distance with me, like an ascetic. Though we met each other daily there was no overstepping on his part. While displaying decorum during this secret love career One or two streaks of eccentricity did indeed sneak in; But we never let that to lead us to fleshly affair.” “Then how come dear, your cheeks bear injury? Bruises on the hand? Swelling of fingers?” Responded the heroine: “Both of us met in the rendezvous as usual, Which was soon followed by parting. Since parents’ approval had been obtained for marriage Thanks to the help of a trusted friend like you, With the happiness that Marriage would follow soon, I was crossing the sandy upland, and treaded the way without realizing That the shortcut filled with mullai flowers was also infested with problems. A person with a grin approached me and said, ‘Have you finished the carnal affair one? Shall we get on with the next one?’ Since he sought to tarnish the very character of clandestine love career I had no desire to even look at that wretched man. Therefore, I added spring to steps and yearned to cross that garden Before he stretched his hands out to embrace me. ‘Don’t you worry about anything, Nobody would find out; Let go of shyness, woman,’ So saying he hemmed me in. Wriggling away from his probing embrace, I said, ‘Shyness is superior to very life You, a lowly creature worse than a dog! Be it known to you!’ ‘Does shyness have such a high worth? Young lady, don’t sport shyness; Give me your virginity for me to enjoy Giving up your bashfulness,’ he said. ‘You, the wolf of a man! Do understand one thing, Shyness is superior to life and chastity is superior to shyness. I declare right now, I am prepared to shed my shyness. Looking at shyness as a weakness in women You dare to defile me crossing me on the street, Don’t you? Here, I shed shyness to save my chastity on my own. I swirled like a whirlwind and hurled a big stone at him. He also didn’t remain silent, And transformed himself into a sword to subjugate me. If I had donned the shyness, Pondering, ‘Should one assault a man?’ I would have lost my honour and chastity. Now do you understand the reason for my injury, friend? Shyness is superior to life While honour is superior to shyness itself. That honour is woman’s chastity.” she concluded. The confidante stood up glad at my deed And she took leave of me then. > As the heroine goes herself > Seeking the hero she has fallen in love with, > Or as she says such words as are freed of wilfulness and guile, > Armed she is > With the saying of the ancients that > ‘Bashfulness is of greater worth than life itself, > And chastity unsullied stands superior to bashfulness too’ -- > And things lofty such as these > Constitute the thematic modes of Akam love proper. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Kaḷaviyal, verse 22)

Kōvalan the son of Mācāttuvān And Kaṇṇaki the daughter of Māṇāykaṉ Were united in wedlock On the auspicious hour of the auspicious day, The vedic rites being prescribed by the ripe brahmin priest And the bridal couple circumambulating the sacrificial fire. The auspicious time and day prescribed Did not guard against the separation of Kōvalan From the virtuous Kaṇṇaki, The woman on whom Kōvalan on the nuptial bed showered praises like ‘Gold with no blemish’ ‘Pearl with right-turned curls’ ‘Fragrance unadulterated’ ‘Sugar cane’ and ‘honey’; Nor did they protect the nuptial cord of Kaṇṇaki. They but pierced through his wedded life like swords and spears. Kaṇṇaki lost her husband and became a widow. The king hurled at her the charge of being a thief’s wife. The vedic mantras recited by the brahmin priest And the propitious time of wedding fixed on the planetary motion Didn’t protect the conjugal harmony of the couple. The epic Cilappatikāram is witness to this fact. The matchless Tolkāppiyam, That is the treasure trove of the Tamils And a fine flower-garden of language and literature, Preceded Cilappatikāram by a long span of time. The culture of the Tamils Didn’t see complete degeneration In the early days of the Aryan advent. The inroads of the alien influence nevertheless Were marked here and there. Why should it be denied? Tolkāppiyar himself makes pointed references to it. In the clandestine love career, That precedes the wedded life of the lovers, The hero does not eschew rendezvous with the heroine On account of the inhospitable path of the wilderness, The intense vigil of the heroine’s kin, The perils due to the wild animals, Or the thought of the long travel to make. And yet Commentator Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar presumes that The rendezvous used to be deferred For reasons of time and day inauspicious (ōrai). Another commentator Iḷampūraṇar too Almost concurs in this regard with the former. On the other hand, Veḷḷaivāraṇar’s Tolkāppiyam study Looks at the word ōrai As meaning sport and festivities. He says The hero takes part in the sports of the town In the company of his close companions, That would act as a cover Protecting him from the scandal of the villagefolk About his visit to the heroine’s place. And Veḷḷaivāraṇar provides us several instances, Not just one or two, Where ōrai refers to play and festivities. Going by which We can establish that Tolkāppiyar uses the term ōrai In the sense of play And not auspicious hour. Where we insist that Veḷḷaivāraṇar is unacceptable And that ōrai is observing propitious hour, It might then mean that Beliefs in day and time auspicious Are an intrusion into the Tamil life As is the visitation of snakes and scorpions. > During the clandestine career > The hero does not go by > Signs of the zodiac and auspicious day > For his rendezvous with the heroine. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Kaḷaviyal, verse 44) > > Deterred the hero is not too > From his rendezvous with the heroine > By the hardness of the path, > The dispiritedness (born of hostile men and things around), > And by the fear of perils and obstacles to his love. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Kaḷaviyal, verse 45)

The karpiyal (wedded love career) section of Tolkāppiyam Makes it clear that The term karaṇam signifies marriage. Commentator Iḷampūraṇar looks at karaṇam As belonging to brahmins, kings and traders, The reason being they are of the upper castes. He further says, A time there was When karaṇam was practised by the Vēḷāḷars down the ladder too. Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar too believed in The existence of caste distinctions. Many a scholar today Shows with evidences The three of the upper stratum As meaning the three crowned monarchs And the lower stratum their subjects. Look at the Tolkāppiyam reference: > ... the land of four extended boundaries, > The land abounding in cool groves > And under the reign of three monarchs of benign note. > > (Ceyyuḷiyal, verse 75) Just as Karpiyal section in Tolkāppiyam speaks of karaṇam “as taking the hand of the heroine in marriage as offered by those of a worthy line,” Kaḷaviyal, given the fact of elopement, refers to marriage as happening without the parental consent. > The wedded course is > The hero, who comes from a worthy lineage, > Taking the hand in marriage > Of the heroine > As she is offered by those of a line worthy and compatible, > With the rites and ceremonies attendant thereon. > > Even as the heroine’s kin do not consent to their union > There does occasion wedding solemnized > With the two taking to elopement. > > The ceremonies and rites > Attendant on the three superior social classes > [kings, brahmins and traders] > Came to mark the marriage > Among those down the ladder in the course of time. > So has it been said. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Karpiyal , verses 1,2,3) Note: What the commentator Iḷampūraṇar means when says that ‘the upper three’ comprises brahmins, kings and traders and the lower is the fourth caste, viz., Vēḷāḷar, is that in the ancient days marriage was common among all sections of the society and that it came to exclude the farming folks in the later days. Impliedly, the days when marriage was common among all sections represent the period of antiquity to which caste division was unknown. ‘The exclusion of Vēḷāḷar’ refers to the division of society into castes when each caste came to be governed by its own codes of conduct. During this period of social segregation, the Vēḷāḷars refused to toe the line of vedic prescriptions. From the line ‘the three monarchs of benign note’ (Ceyyuḷiyal, 75), it is clear that ‘the upper three’ is the trinity of ancient Tamil kings, which gives us to see that the ancient Tamils classified people corresponding to the fourfold division of land and not in terms of fourfold caste division. The lower section then refers to the subject people of the three monarchs. Veḷḷaivāraṇar

The well-meaning elders of the village Assembled at the public hall And had a brainstorming session: “I see that youth quite often By the pond, near the river bank, In the sandy plain where horses fall over. The young woman keeps waiting for the youth Without fail Even if the scabbard fish are not to be seen in the river, Even if the carp forget to pop up in the pond And even if the horses fail to make their visit. Day in, day out, These two frequent under cover By the hill, off the home In the jasmine garden, in the coconut grove, In the mango grove, in the teakwood jungle; They walk hand in hand tiptoe like shadows Speaking in hushed tones, Deceiving themselves That they do it all unknown to the village folk. We must catch them red-handed-- The boy who comes furtively And the maid of undefiled purity-- And put an end to their clandestine love career. We must see them man and wife married. The boy might desert the girl Despite his promise to her That he would forget her not Even if it be death to him. A time may come When falsehood and deception would rule the day; We cannot afford to lose the girl And go about crying over it. We must talk to them right today; We must take the matter to their parents.” As the elders were splitting their heads thus, The lovers made their presence right before them. The headman stately as the temple car addressed them: “See how worried the folks of the hamlet are! You keep meeting in rendezvous secret By day and by night, Near the house, by the fence And everywhere around. How would you convince us That you would not desert the girl eventually?” Fire of rage flew from the headman’s eyes. The boy responded, “Well said, sire! We would remain unseparated Even in the world after death. Do take it from me!” The headman said, “The times are changing And deceit looks raising its ugly head. Let’s summon the Aiyar.” The Aiyar appeared there forthwith Asking about the reason for the summon. One in the assembly wondered: “Should we need the Aiyar here? He belongs to an alien caste.” The village headman explained then: “Dear friend! He is not the Aiyar you suppose; Be it clear in your mind, He is the one venerable amongst us, The one fit to sit at the head Capable of prescribing things righteous And prohibiting ways evil. He has conceived of marriage That would guard against Falsity and deceit in love relations.” The Aiyar, unblemished, stood up and spoke then, “Bring here the relations of the lovers Including their parents.” Prompt they came. “Do you consent to the union of these lovers?” Aiyar asked. They nodded their heads in approval. “All is fine! No need for worry! The clandestine love career has come to an end.
