Let’s conduct the marriage called karaṇam That would be a celebration Of the love of these two.” > In so far as > The love career of the hero and the heroine > Unfolds to be inferred in discourses private, > And in so far as > It is thrown into the subject of gossip in public, > The acts of the hero must bear the prime responsibility for it. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Kaḷaviyal, verse 48) > > The hero and the heroine > Enter into marital union > Either after their clandestine union becomes public knowledge > Or before it happens. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Kaḷaviyal, verse 49) > > Sage men there conceived solemnized wedding > When falsity and breach of trust cropped up, > So has it been said. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Karpiyal, verse 4) Note: Aiyar is an indigenous Tamil word meaning a respectable elderly person of superior virtue and worth. Here this term refers to one of Tamil antiquity. There are misinterpretations of Aiyar as being derived from ‘Aryan.’ The Aiyar formulated the marriage rites to guard against love falling into deceit and falsity. This phase of marriage had been preceded by a culture when they did not visualize the need for marriage. It is obvious that the conduct of marriage should have come into existence before the days of Tolkāppiyar. The need for marriage then might have been necessitated after the advent of the alien cultures and races. Veḷḷaivāraṇar The History of Tolkāppiyam.

t: Clandestine Love Career and Wedded Course
x: Tolkāppiyam shows us that Karaṇam (marriage) is The hero taking the heroine’s hand in marriage As she is offered by those of a line worthy and compatible With the rites and ceremonies attendant thereon. He also shows that It is marriage As the lovers take to elopement Without the heroine’s parents offering her hand. In both the events The lovers enter into wedded course And make a blissful living to the acclaim of the world. The order of Tolkāppiyar’s day was that The hero stood on a higher plane In the domestic sphere and in other realms of activity too. Being so, In this flower-garden of Tolkāppiyam that I write, I make no attempt whatever to change that order. Tolkāppiyar steers clear of any controversy With regard to God or religion he believed in And holds forth God and religion universal. Such is the way Aiyaṉ Tiruvaḷḷuvar has chosen later, Keeping religion and God secular. The Akam lovers are seen running their household In tune with the norms of both Tolkāppiyar and Tiruvaḷḷuvar. The bud called clandestine love course Blossoms into the flower called wedded course By marriage. Malivu the ecstasy of union of the lovers, Pulavi the feigned reserve of the heroine, Ūṭal the sulking of the lovers leading to sexual fulfilment, Uṇarvu the resolution of sulking through the interceders, And pirivu the separation occasioned by the parting of the hero In quest of wealth and learning And for acts of valour for the country’s good -- Occur during the wedded course after marriage. “O my manna pure! Honey unsatiating! Do tell me without concealing. During those days of our clandestine career, When we were showering love unexhausted on each other, Why did you try to draw my heart apart And drown it in the flood of devotion to God?” Queried the hero. “It was my confidante’s counsel That we should worship and adore God For our love to come to fruition without hassles. But are you angry about it now?” So saying the heroine served food on his leaf plate And sat by him to eat together with him. “How is it that The food turns manna with your hand’s touch? Not just that. The flower too acquires a new fragrance! Are all these because of the bliss of God?” Wondered the hero. “It is all because my God dwells in my heart.” As she said thus, Both of them forgot the food cooked and served on the plate, Vied with each other And relished the lips of each other. Food taken They commented: “There is one thing that tastes sweet; It is not the manna but the lips!” Since it was the early days of wedded life They made no distinction As to whether it was morning, noon or evening Or day or night, And realized their dreams of passion Which they yearned for in their clandestine course. Realizing that He who lives a virtuous life is known as a brahmin, They decided by the dictates of their wisdom And followd the path of domestic virtue. But the dreams of their furtive career refused to die down! They went about recalling in joy those days When many a hurdle ran into their way Which they overcame using many a strategy And when their companions came to their aid unfailing. And they glossed over things unsavoury too When there intervened the beat of the drum called sulking. “One day I stood waiting there for you Till my legs threatened to break And you did not turn up!” The hero said in response quick: “None too good were you too! Another day I waited for you sleepless through the night And you failed to turn up!” All these accusations mutual Amounted at length to letters written on the air! The interceders stepping in, The false sullen mood Gave way to the bliss of joy ensuing. Should we need to tell those versed in this art That sulking adds to the joy of union? > [Thirty-three are the contexts structured > That find the hero of ineffable note > Marking his utterances:] > > When union occasions with the heroine > After they have come through the marriage solemnized, > A union freed of all reticence and reserve; > > As he stays immersed in the joy of union unbounded; > As there mainfests an awesome wifely rectitude in the heroine; > As they meet the charges of household > Guided by the worthy tradition of the old; > > As he weighs the days of disquiet of the furtive course > Against the abiding bliss of this wedded state; > > As the confidante adores the guardian deity > That stood them in good stead in days of adversity; > > As the heroine speaks now with passion’s fervour > With the days of care and distress withered away; > > As he wonders, > While taking food and wearing garlands, > How things taste sweet as ambrosia to him > When they pass through her hands; > > As he commends to her > Courtesies due to > Sages, learned men and others of exemplary conduct; > > As he addresses his heart > Reminiscing in a sorrowing mood > About those days of the clandestine-course > When they had union scarce and far between; > > As they revel in the bliss of wedded union > With the hardships and rigours of the clandestine course > Vanishing like letters inscribed on the air; > > As he comes forth with words of reassurance > ‘Go not dispirited’ and ‘Fear not the hardship of my journey;’ > > As there occurs the breach of his promise thereof; > > As he finds the heroine - > The one embodying fortitude and lofty bearing > And with discerning maids-in-attendance... . > > (Poruḷatikāram : Karpiyal, verse 5)

The home is all music; The hearts of the inmates all are things lustrous; Their minds are all books of knowledge; The letters of the books are marks of joy; The woods are a spectacle of dance. If it is so for crows, sparrows and cows Need we say anything about men? The revolutionary poet Pāratitācaṉ’s picture of a home it is! And our ripe author of antiquity Tolkāppiyar Has drawn a similar picture two thousand years ago. The Poruḷatikāram, Karpiyal section of Tolkāppiyam Shows the two lamps at home That like blossoms of a creeper diffuse fragrance around. The wedded life sweet suffers no want as it were; And yet the man tells his parrot-tongued wife, “Don’t you feel the want of a child at home?” A pointed finger was her reply to his concern. “Stop there! Are you threatening me?” Said the man in mocking jest “It has been a month since the period stopped”, said she. With a joyous roar of laughter He took her in his clasp Her resistance notwithstanding. “Mind your health, my dear! Conceived, you need to take much care,” Cautioning her thus, He kept moving behind her all through From month one to the ninth month of her pregnancy With care and concern undiminished. He parted from her with a sigh As the midwife came to attend to childbirth. As he heard the words ‘male child’ from the labour room He went about dancing in rapture. Allowed to see his wife, he went in And all her pain vanished without a trace. The flower of that woman wore a smile Holding the bud of the baby close to her. He wiped the sweat on her forehead, Saying, “You are reduced much like a twig, dear!” She blushed for a while And said with a streak of ridicule at the corner of her eyes: “Reduced in just one day’s pain?” She was showered in benediction by all kindred folk, Her parents and foster mother in particular. All kindly people thronged to greet her. She was bathed in oil. There was a celebration for the child When the martyrs who sacrificed for the freedom of the land Were remembered with grateful admiration. The lady was floating on the ocean of joy. Then she heard the tidings of her man Drawn in passion to an alien woman. It was a blow as if by an axe; She writhed in pain like a worm thrown into fire. He was worried about Her turning a tiger and a storm. The hill-like man stood reduced in his standing. He approached her companions With a request to quench The raging fire in the heart of the heroine. The efforts of them came to no avail. Eventually, He went to her in the bedchamber Held her legs in tight hold And begged her pardon. Could she say ‘no’ to him? Or could she erase his image from her mind? She did pardon him. “May the one who coined the word ‘pardon’ live long!” Thinking thus The hero moved closer to her And she moved off a little Saying, “There is the child!” > Bearing him a son worthy of his name; > > As gifts aplenty are bestowed on the sages > And worthy offerings on the celestials > At the hour of the heroine > Being given the ceremonial oil-bath > After she has borne him a son; > > As he comes after acts of debauchery > And entreats the bliss of heroine’s love > Holding her tender feet in his hands, > While she in a mood of variance > Stays lying despondent on the bed > With the soft pillow for her prop; > > As he brings in the intercession of other women > And resolves the sulking of the heroine > When she remains hard of access > In a mode of intense variance; > > .... > > (Poruḷatikāram : Karpiyal, verse 5)

The function marking the birth of a child Kumaraṉ and Kumari’s house Was visited by Vēḷaṉ from Kōṭṭai street. He joyfully gifted the chain made of cow’s horn. “What Vēḷaṉ? Quite uncharacteristic of you to have come all alone? Why didn’t you bring your woman?” They eagerly enquired. “We have not been on talking terms for some days. You have often been grumbling about my being issueless.’ So saying, She had gone to grandma’s house. Six weeks have passed since then.” To dispel the cloud of sadness from his face, On the very next day, Kumaraṉ accompanied by Vēḷaṉ, went to grandma’s house, And spoke to his wife: “Is it sulking or growling? If you remain separated for being issueless, Would you be gifted with a child? My parents used to say that I was born ten years after their marriage. If my parents had also remained parted in sulks for having been issueless, How could I have been born? Now also, there are quarrels and sulks marking our conjugal life. I ventured to a foreign country in pursuit of wealth. ‘My life would be shrouded in darkness, therefore I would also come.’ She insisted. How can I change the convention against women taking up voyage? With her eyes flooded with tears, She quarrelled and remained silent for a few days. I could not change the age-old custom of ancestors, But I changed my plan of going on a voyage, I travelled to the nearby capital city for training in warfare for ten days. ‘You assured me that there wouldn’t be any separation. I didn’t know then that you were lying.’ She fired a letter on the fifth day itself. Then, what work could I have there? I beat a hasty retreat midway, To wipe off her misery caused by parting. Compromise has never been a one way path in my house. I had committed a big blunder when she gave birth to my son. A fury she did become! But on my apology she forgot what had happened. Unlike in my case, No male chauvinistic blunder has happened here. Therefore you should forget the quarrel with your man. You should extend a whole-hearted cooperation. May you be blessed with the fruit of your thousand year crop, your married life!” Such of these arguments and many more I presented before her. “Nothing equals the bliss of married life. The life of the householder is a virtue unto itself. And a finer thing it would be were it to be freed of blame.” I also said. “Vēḷaṉ! This is for you also: ‘Even if there is no child in the house, We should toil like the child of the nation’. You should make a vow, And with a bright and beaming face, Lead a life like a sword and its sheath.” Vēḷaṉ and his wife expressed their gratitude to Kumaraṉ And said, “We shall live together ever.” > As he ends the affliction of the two women > [The heroine and his concubine] > Who stand grieving at his parting; > > As he stands in distress intense > Over his protracted separation from the heroine; > > As he ponders taking the hard tract > Which he had gone through in the past; > > As he realizes the overriding hold of love; > As he fears the heroine’s affliction > When parting from her intervenes; > > As he fails to keep his word to her > [As regards his promise of return in a given season > And as regards his promise of non-separation]; > > As he responds to the words of credulity of the confidante > Who urges him to take the heroine with him, > And who makes many a plea of this kind; > > As he feels the pain of separation > While setting off to a foreign land; > > As he ponders breaking his journey and returning home; > The feel of joy that attends > As he is homeward after the mission; > > .... (Poruḷatikāram : Karpiyal, verse 5)

The little one was moving in the direction of his mother After having run, played in the water and blown bubbles of foam. The anklets he wore and his child’s patter made wonderful music. Even as he was nearing his mother, The other woman in his father’s life stopped him to embrace and kiss him. Thinking that her son would reject the gestures and come to her, The mother waited along. Seeing that he didn’t, She became angry and exclaimed, “The sprout will follow the seed.” He my man keeps saying, “You’re the elder sister While the other women in my life are your younger sisters. You’re the genuine pearl while the others are the fake ones.” But he goes after the other pearls. She thought that if she remained silent not protesting, She might end up losing her relationship with her son as well. Just at this juncture, The son decked in ornaments came calling her ‘O mother!’. Her anger raging like a volcano subdued cool as snowfall. Spotting her husband she exclaimed, “Oh, here you are! Hereafter the boy alone would be the ray of hope dissipating my darkness; Today I start for my mother’s house along with him. Some men do exist, like the spots on the face of the moon, But you are a moon all in spots! Intiraṉ himself should take a lesson or two from you in the art of winning women. So long I exercised restraint with the fond hope of reforming you. You cannot bridle your habit of making merry every day. My son who looks like the full moon is enough to provide me solace. You spoiled the family with a mind perverse, Your blotted life would teach you a fitting lesson before long.” Bursting out thus, That speaking portrait was about to exit from the house Along with the soothing breeze on her lap. The husband cried out in pain within, With his legs trembling As if he were stabbed by a thousand spears and swords in the chest. “Let the bygones be bygones! You might leave me immediately if it were to happen again. I don’t fancy a life without you, my singing bird! Like the singing birds let us live without any worry. Let’s lead an impeccable life which nobody can fault. I will ever remain faithful to you hereafter.” Coming around, he fell at her feet. “It is not enough if the people here stand witness. Let your former concubines also see this scene”, she said. > As the hero’s concubine cuddles her son up in love > And lets him after play with him; > > As the hero approaches her unknown from behind > When she is absorbed in play with her son > And nestles up against her > In an act of virtuous conduct > And seeks to resolve her sulking; > > As she turns thereon to her son, > The source of unending joy that he is, > And holds him to reproach > Finding the adage ‘like father like son’ true; > > As she abides in the virtue of conjugal love > When she does not go dispirited > At the unkindly act of debauchery of the hero, > And takes the word of conciliation of the men of note; > > As she reveals her lofty trait of a wedded wife > When she tells him at his face > ‘It would look instructive (dishonourable?) > Were my younger sisters (the hero’s concubines) to see it’, > With the hero prostrating before her > And soliciting her pardon for his act of debauchery; > > .... (Poruḷatikāram : Karpiyal, verse 6)

Without being confined to the house like a cat that has littered, Without living like a caged parrot taking the cage for the nation, The hero and heroine would take to going out on tours at least once a year. They followed this practice even in those days. Taking their children along, they played in soothing ponds and beautiful parks, Enjoying the beauty in nature. How sweet it is to know that The Tamils lived a complete life Even in the infancy of their history, Which Tolkāppiyam shows In its section on the wedded life! > Seeking the pleasures of life, > Such as sports in rivers and tanks > And revelry in groves, > Beyond the bounds of their home soil, > Is part of the love career of the hero and heroine.

(Poruḷatikāram : Karpiyal, verse 50) When the elephants trample their way through the field Much like the mountains rolling down, The hero remains unperturbed and takes them head on. He would fight to keep his country’s flag aloft, Even if he were to lose his life in the process! The heroine had applied the tilak of blood on his forehead Bidding farewell and wishing him victory. In the thick of the battle he does not even think about her. Only after his country’s flag is unfurled on the enemy’s fortress Would the chaste warrior send the message By the breeze blowing across the countries: “My dear damsel! Victory is ours!” This is yet another portrait of ancient Tamil life in Tolkāppiyam. > No reflection of the heroine at home > Finds utterance from the hero away on his mission; > The task accomplished, > He wears her plight upon his sleeve. (Poruḷatikāram : Karpiyal, verse 45)

Those were the times Womenfolk were held in regard and concern And given due respect for their softness of disposition; They were therefore kept off places of danger. Their duties were restricted to work off the warfront And to war camps. The culture in this regard hasn’t changed; What is witnessed today is only a reformulation of things. > The union of love will be kept off > From the war-camp, the place of onerous charge. > > Women assigned to duties other than love > Would be there around in war-camps. (Poruḷatikāram : Karpiyal, verses 34, 35)

t: The Horse and the Bird would Stand Outsmarted!
x: Mission abroad accomplished, Vēḷaṉ was returning home on his fleeting horse Eager as he was to see his beloved wife. The tears shed by the sky would bring happiness to the peasants, While Vēḷaṉ’s return alone could infuse life into his woman. The flower doesn’t wither If the colourful beetle fails to visit to relish its honey, While the young woman’s heart might turn into a turbulent earthquake If the horse carrying Vēḷaṉ failed to be back home. She might breathe like a storm and writhe like a worm. The horse should understand that and gallop towards its destination Without taking a break in between, Without any hindrances on the way home. Vēḷaṉ spurred the horse on; The horse sped like a bird’s flight; And it was the bird From which he took the cue for his flight home. When Tolkāppiyar says The horse matched the speed of the bird, We cannot help entertaining a doubt. The bird flying in the sky should rapidly flutter its wing to fly fast, And the horse has to gallop to reach home, Both of which might take quite some time. But Vēḷaṉ’s heart Burning with passion intense for his lady Could be home to her The moment he thought he should be home. > No sojourn does the hero’s journey across the parched tract mark > As he is homeward after his mission accomplished; > For he had at his possession > A sturdy horse swift as a bird > That abides at his service > As does his benignant heart. (Poruḷatikāram : Karpiyal, verse 53)

The evening of life portrayed by Tolkāppiyar Could be compared with the perennial river merging into the sea Originating from the hills and flowing through the paddy fields, It renders benefits a thousand before reaching the sea. Since it writes its epilogue while merging into the sea, Nobody would conclude that the story of the river is all at a close. Even the lives of the dead continue through their progeny. The same is applicable to the river. Continuing to live even after death is an honour to great people. The sun is warm at rise and goes scorching at the peak, And before vanishing in the west, Thanks to the comforting south wind, Showers happiness upon the entire earth. Likewise, The aged who are in the last phase of their life, Having enjoyed the felicities of conjugal life And having reaped all that it offered, Will have their fortune realized As they live surrounded by pleasant children And comfort-giving kindred folks And live in serenity Taking to ways of virtue. > Having relished the felicities of the passion of love, > It is for the hero and heroine in conjugal union > To savour the protective presence of their children > And seek to live on things sublime, > With virtuous kinsfolk around, > Which makes for the fruits the wedded course entailed. (Poruḷatikāram : Karpiyal, verse 51)

The ailment called the passion of love Sprouts in the morning Develops through the day And blossoms in the evening. Is this a disease peculiar to the lady? Or does it afflict the man too Who wanders like a bee in search of a flower’s honey? Let there be no argument As to whether it is the man or the woman affected. Whosoever it might be Let’s see what their pleadings with their heart are like: > The monologic utterances > That issue from the mindscapes > Of the hero and heroine are: > > Addresses to the heart > As if it were a living body with sense organs endowed, > That manifest the eightfold emotions > [Laughter, weeping, despisedness, wonder > Fear, pride, anger and joy], > As if it breathed feelings alive and living, > And as if it offered denials and refutations -- > > Such addresses being informed of the passion of love, > The passion that alternates between pain and pleasure; > > Apostrophes to things personified > Attributing to them deeds they cannot perform; > > Taking the afflictions of the other > As if it were one’s own; > > Holding the mind and sense impressions apart; > > And finding similitude where appropriate > Between the three human class genders > And the two non-human class genders > In relation to their attributes and actions. (Poruḷatikāram : Poruḷiyal, verse 2)

The heart comes to realize that The corporal frame is gradually getting emaciated and life exhausted. Many days have passed since she met her husband on the bed. Therefore, she realizes that only a little amount of life is left in her. With the heart being kept unaware, She questions herself in anguish: Whatever has happened to my body? Whatever is the affliction to my life? Leaving the questions at that, She makes a resolution: ‘See him I shall not!’ > Even when the lonesome heroine turns dispirited > And wears withering, emaciated limbs, > She never goes out seeking the hero’s union, > But abides, exclaiming > ‘O whatever has befallen them!’ (Poruḷatikāram : Poruḷiyal, verse 9) Having resolved thus She asks her heart: ‘Is my resolution right?’ But her whining heart says ‘no’, “You only pretend to be indifferent to your body and life for society’s sake, Whereas your actual desire is to meet him at this very instant.” > Hero’s union she does think of > At those lonesome moments > When she addresses her heart. (Poruḷatikāram : Poruḷiyal, verse 10)

There is a complaint that ancient works, be it literature or Tolkāppiyam, the treasure-trove of grammatical theories, treat women as if they were dumb and servile beings. Even in this era, which is known for the awakening of women, when war-cries for the rights of women are resounding from every nook and cranny, it could be observed that freedom of women remains a question mark. We also see that among the intellectuals, there are women just as there are men. What is more, it is a proven fact that women fare better than men in school and college examinations. Today, one can see them vying with their male counterparts in governance and administration. In spite of making such strides, here and there women do find themselves a disadvantaged lot thanks to assertions of male superiority. The number of women who are victims of superstitions, who fall into the pit of orthodoxy, who writhe in ignorance and who are deluded into magic and witchcraft far exceeds the menfolk of such kinds. Be that as it may, women’s progress is witnessed in fields like science, education and even in the field of defence. Ancient works of literature and culture should not be criticized unjustly and denounced by juxtaposing the status of women of modern age and the rights enjoyed by them with that represented in these works. Such works should be viewed only as documents from which to learn about the social conditions of an ancient past. Such an approach should inform our study of ancient works. A piece of literature which reflects the conditions of that age need not be considered as containing norms of behaviour applicable for today. Instead, we should understand the basic idea the ancient works attempt to project. We should also be clear about the extent to which it should be taken and on what basis. We must see how these ideas and attitudes bear on the current realities. If we were to undo the foundations of the past in our pursuit of newness, then in our homes the pictures of our grandparents and parents and the articles used by them along with the other traces of the yesteryears would have to be jettisoned as useless objects. When ancient literature projects the improbable as real, it may be left aside and need not be believed in. In the modern age, the trains which are powered by electricity or for that matter aeroplanes which fly with the assistance of technology have wheels. The chariots of kings of yore had also run on wheels which might have been different in size or shape. Even today, bullock carts with wheels can be seen in small hamlets, just as we find buses and cars running on wheels. In the same manner, though significant changes have surfaced in culture, ethos and lifestyle, the fundamentals remain unchanged. At this juncture of this book when I have already penned sixty chapters, I must mention that there is a need for us to look back and then proceed further. Tolkāppiyam, Poruḷiyal speaks of certain characteristics specific to women, which, if we look at objectively, deserve to be appreciated rather than condemned. > Temperance, fulness of bearing, uprightness, > Facility of the tongue, discrimination and discernment > Are traits marked in women. (Poruḷatikāram : Poruḷiyal, verse 15)

The smithy forging implements for war it was Where soldiers from the army camp were at work. There came a young maiden running, holding a letter of palmyra leaf. A warrior-hero engaged in the work exclaimed: “You are the woman who can bathe the fox without getting it wet! I presumed you would come tomorrow. But today just as I am making this sword, You have arrived to gladden my heart. What letter did my flower-eyed woman give? Give it!” So saying he received the letter Without minding the taunts and comments from those around. The text of the letter ran: I expected your visit during daytime yesterday and waited with hunger; Then only I realized that all your assurances are like letters written on thin air. I even became apprehensive of a friend’s prediction that our love would fail. Dear, if you are afraid of coming in broad daylight You can as well come lurking in the darkness of night. Are you afraid of the wretched moon’s light? At dusk, once the sun vanishes you can plan your visit. Obstacles may abound in thwarting your visit. But only you possess the medicine for my withering heart. Even the flower I sport loses its fragrance in your absence. Have you not learnt the art of outwitting the local guards Who are active throughout the day? The path you have to tread is full of stones and thorns I do know how difficult a path it is. Maybe it is well That your journey is not taken keeping in mind the nature of the path. But it will be a pleasure for me If you were to come here to wipe the tears off my eyes. Many a time have we planned to meet, But on thinking we know it to be risky. And what remains is confusion. Even our families have become apprehensive; As one alleviates one’s hunger without waiting for one’s turn, Rushing into marriage is the only way out. Folding the palmyra letter, The hero gave a tender twist to the emissary’s ear. “I told you then itself that you can bathe the fox without getting it wet. Tell your friend I shall not fail my word. Let the month of Thai be born, A way out will have been born too,” he said. The young woman responded, “A child would also be born in the tenth mouth.” She asked further, “What does bathing the fox without getting it wet mean? I ask you out of ignorance. Please do let me know it.” He replied, “The fox is none but me. You have brought the love letter from my love and showered me with happiness, Without getting me drenched in the process.” * > Pointing to the perils attendant on > The hero’s coming for union at inopportune time, > The hazards of the tract that he comes through, > The rigours of watch around, > Speaking of her anxiety and concern therein, > Expressing her apprehension of harm to the hero, > Changing the hour of trysting > From day to night and from night to day, > And instructing him not to come for trysting > Drawing on things righteous and evil > To bring her point home, > And things such as these [by the confidante] > Are all the ones marked with the intent > To see the hero take the heroine in marriage, > Thus has it been ruled. (Poruḷatikāram : Poruḷiyal, verse 16)

Is the word ilakkiyam of Tamil origin? Or does it belong to the Sanskrit language? This was the topic of a big debate. This issue necessitated more or less a forum for debate. It came up in the function on Muttamiḻ (Threefold Tamil) organised in May 1949 at Coimbatore. Pāvēntar Pāratitācaṉ presided over the function. I was also present at the function in which Ariñar Aṇṇā, Avvai Duraisamy Piḷḷai, the multilingual scholar Appadurai, the great critic Veḷḷaivāraṇar and many others participated. Hardly was there any discourse on the development of Tamil or the rise of the Tamils. In the huge gathering of ten thousand people, the only question that dominated the proceedings was ‘Is ilakkiyam a Tamil word or not?’ Speaking on the second day, I observed thus: “Having mobilized ten thousand people and spent thousands of rupees to conduct this function to which renowned scholars and academics are invited, you have wasted two days’ time and deliberations by focusing upon the single issue of deciding as to whether ilakkiyam is a Tamil word or not. Instead, a group of eight or ten of these scholars could have assembled in a separate place and done this research. One of these scholars then could have conveyed to us the result of your deliberations.” My speech created a big sensation. I referred to this Muttamiḻ Viḻā function to drive home the point that the debate as to whether ilakkiyam is derived from ilaṭciyam (objective) or from ilaṅkutal (shine forth as an example) still continues. We have such a debate in Tolkāppiyam also: > Usage > Being the word of the learned, > Propriety in poetry > Draws on conformity to the usage. Iḷampūraṇar’s commentary on this verse is that poetic diction should adopt the usage that comes to be the standard from the use of the learned. Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar, on the other hand, adds the conjunctive particle um to uyarntōr kiḷavi (the usage of the learned) and says that the learned usage going in accord with the vedic usage becomes the poetic diction. Here, the word vaḻakku (usage) does not refer to any case filed in a court of law! Instead, it refers to usage of words and sentences. Iḷampūraṇar claims that only the words of learned men can become the standard of usage. The conjunctive particle of Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar may imply that there exists iḻintōr kiḷavi (the diction of the lowly) too, which goes against the norm in Tolkāppiyam Marapiyal section that > Usage is > What is in vogue and use > Among the learned. Quoting this in his Tolkāppiyam commentary, the great Tamil scholar Veḷḷaivāraṇar points out that vaḻakku (usage) is linguistic usage, and reference to vedic usage is out of place. Another commentator Pērāciriyar agreeing with Iḷampūraṇar says that usage is the use of language by the learned because it is from that the events of popular speech issue. The use of the lowly, such as > eṉṉaṭā tapāykkiṟē (What man, trying to escape?) > eṉṉammā moṟaikkiṟē (You woman! Why staring at me?) can never become norms of usage. * > Usage > Being the word of the learned, > Propriety in poetry > Draws on conformity to the usage. (Poruḷatikāram : Poruḷiyal, verse 23)

‘To fear what ought to be feared is given to the wise’ (Tirukkuṟaḷ) A dictionary compiled by a team of scholars records ‘humility’ and ‘reserve’ as the meanings of accam (fear), and nāṇam (modesty) means fear, humility, regard, shyness, etc. In case our action brings with it disrepute, then it is necessary that we should fear it. Throwing fear overboard under such circumstances is never acceptable. When loss of honour is imminent, fear one should. Likewise, modesty (feminine reserve) does not mean women lowering the gaze at the sight of men. Tolkāppiyam prescribes that in any explanation of virtue, wealth and happiness, modesty has a role to play. Since the virtue of modesty is dear to great men as if it is their very life, it should never be lost sight of. Such great men embody inner and outer realities exemplifying the ideal that the world is what such men make of. They are not the people who merely preach munificence, virtue and bliss, but hold modesty to be a supreme virtue. The modesty discussed here is not the one that occurs between a lover and the beloved. It is about knowing under what conditions the practice of modesty exalts that very virtue, and organize our lives accordingly. * > Propriety of demeanour of the heroine > Shall be deemed indispensable > In compositions of Akam mode > That embody contents of a lofty nature. (Poruḷatikāram : Poruḷiyal, verse 25)

Though the feeling of pleasure is common to all living beings, it is, in particular, that special feeling felt by man and woman united together. Iḷampūraṇar elaborates on it stating that even a natural instinct like happiness requires union of hearts. He points out that, if good rapport exists, one can experience pleasure significantly even in the company of a prostitute. But in the absence of good rapport, one cannot derive joy even from his wife. While explaining the term “all living beings,” Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar makes it clear that happiness experienced by male and female in union is common to all living creatures - people, gods, demons, animals and birds. When Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar brings in the celestials and the demons while referring to all living beings, one cannot be oblivious of the fact that the purānas abound in stories of male gods taking the female form and enjoying sex with the male beings. As such, we need to steer clear of the joy of union belonging to the worlds of harlots and gods and must look at the Tolkāppiyam verse with reference to the human male and human female united by mutual love. This alone goes in accord with Tamil culture. > Joy is > The joy of union between the sexes > That every living being accomplishes > As it unites in passion with its loving mate. (Poruḷatikāram : Poruḷiyal, verse 29)

“Keeping you by me, The fiery sun felt cool; Parted from you The cool moon did scorch me. We bared out our hearts And communicated with each other. Without pouncing upon me, much like a tiger, Do give a thought to my parents’ concern for my state. Our clandestine love career has been exposed. The entire town is resounding with words of scandal about us. I conveyed to you my willingness to elope with you. But you insisted upon marriage to the knowledge of one and all. Let the act of caressing cheeks and stamping on them follow later. Tell me what your response to my concern is! Is it elopement or immediate marriage? Why do you enact a dumb skit? Would your lips remain glued for ever? Would they refuse to open even for an instant to answer my question? Do come out with an answer, at least before my death,” she said in despair. He said, “You know how to read, Look here, the wedding invitation on the palmyra leaf.” * > The heroine’s mindscape encompasses: > Privileging her right of love for the hero, > Apprehension of separation by the hero, > Fear of her clandestine love career > Coming to be inferred by folks > And becoming the subject of idle talk around, > Her longed for rendezvous with the hero > Running into impediments, > Willing desire to go on elopement with the hero, > And wanting the hero to take her in marriage. (Poruḷatikāram : Poruḷiyal, verse 31)

The land throbs with valour, The eyes of women express chastity. The shadow of the rising flag would conquer all enemies. The anthems are pregnant with pride. The fort of warriors is teeming with myriad talents. The golden walls of their fort have the silvery clouds for their canopies. The sea which kisses the walls of the fort is in penance, The people of this land hold not life too dear. Behold Rāvaṇa, the one with eternal fame! The beacon light of Lanka, The flame of self-esteem, The leader of the great Tamil race, For whom protecting the subjects is the norm of the reign. A passage in Kamparāmāyaṇam portrays Rāvaṇaṉ’s sense of honour and valour with awe-struck admiration. Before pointing it out, let us look at the pride of place given to the sulks between lovers in Tolkāppiyam Poruḷiyal. Tolkāppiyam shows that however proud and manly a person might be, in the event of the feigned quarrel between husband and wife, the husband would have to stoop to pacify his wife. > The dominance of the wife > And the suppliant postures of the husband > Are seen to mark > The moments of tiffs of passion between the two. Bearing this in mind, let us take a look at Rāvaṇa’s speech demonstrating his self-esteem. The wisemen, ripe counsellors and the learned approach Rāvaṇaṉ at his court to counsel him, “Defeat is imminent! Therefore, it is better to surrender than inviting destruction.” On listening to this, Rāvaṇaṉ declares: Even at the time of sulks in marital life, it is not my wont to yield. Surrender is unknown to Rāvaṇaṉ. “ I will not give in even in sulks with my wife in the bed-chamber, will I? In Teṉṉavaṉ Kātai authored by me, years ago, I noted: “It was only in the bed-chamber before his wife where the music of Rāvaṇaṉ’s harp faced defeat.” My opinion was prompted by these lines from Tolkāppiyam. > The dominance of the wife > And the suppliant postures of the husband > Are seen to mark > The moments of tiffs of passion between the two. (Poruḷatikāram : Poruḷiyal, verse 33)

t: The Truth Unknown to the Devotee
x: It was the wont of that Saiva adherent to invite a guest to a feast on all the important Saivite festivals. That Saiva devotee didn’t need the assistance of any almanac to realize that it was Mahāsivarāttiri. He wandered around looking for a guest to be fed on that day. His search proved futile. At last, he was heartened to see somebody slumbering in the choultry. He heaved a sigh of relief. Overcome with joy, he approached him. He addressed that devotee of Lord Siva, who was dozing off with the ritual sacred ash sported on his forehead, chest and folded hands. “Sir, the one of ripeness!” he called a bit loudly. “Who is that? I am lying here sapped of vitality due to hunger and fatigue. Why are you bothering me?” So saying the devotee got up. The host replied, “I invite you not to appease your hunger. It is to cleanse myself of my sins. I invite you to a feast in my house.” “Is it so? Are you offering food? Why the invitation? I don’t require one,” So saying the devotee started walking with the Saivite friend. On the way, the guest enquired, “Is it vegetarian food or non-vegetarian?” “How come you have such a doubt? Today is the day of Lord Siva--Sivarāttiri. God is Love. How can you forget all these and ask me such a question?” “It is okay! In any case it is better to clear the doubt in advance. That is exactly why I enquired.” “Okay, sir, you need not doubt at all. Dishes made of brinjal, drumstick, unripe banana and other such vegetables combined with rice of excellent quality await you. Please eat to your heart’s content.” “Let it be so”. “Hara Hara Siva Siva, Sambo Mahadeva! Let me squat on the veranda. Please invite me after the food gets ready.” The guest lounged on the veranda of the house muttering Siva, Siva. A few moments might have passed, when a voice assailed the ears of the guest, Iṟaicci (meaning ‘meat’ among others)! Iṟaicci! though the explanation that followed was barely audible. “What is this? A queer conversation is ensuing.” The guest became apprehensive. Again the word iṟaicci loudly uttered fell on his ears. The guest peeped inside the house. Again the matter related to iṟaicci reared its head though the context remained unclear. It was time for food--but the persistent sound inside was, iṟaicci, iṟaicci, iṟaicci! The startled guest got up abruptly. “How dare he cheats me after inviting me for a vegetarian food;” He raged, and left the place in a huff and doubled up. What had happened actually? The host in his anxiety to look for a devotee as a guest left his teaching of a chapter of Tolkāppiyam to his son incomplete. Then the host was engrossed in clearing the doubts of his son. > Iṟaicci is > The suggestive import > Paralleling the Akam thematic strand explicit. > > That from iṟaicci > There emerges an implied subtext > Beside its evocative designation of flora and fauna > Will be obvious to men of discernment. > Designating sights of flora and fauna in nature > That are evocative of love and tenderness > Is intended to bring comfort and reassurance > To the heroine in lonesome anguish. These are different layers of meaning of the term ‘iṟaicci’ listed in the verses 35, 36, 37 in Poruḷiyal. The father and son were discussing them. 1. ‘Iṟaicci’ refers to the suggested meaning. 2. The parallel meaning suggested is context-specific and is obvious to the learned. 3. Iṟaicci functions to privilege love in times of distress and it underlines forbearance. > Iṟaicci is > The suggestive import > Paralleling the Akam thematic strand explicit. > > That from iṟaicci > There emerges an implied subtext > Beside its evocative designation of flora and fauna > Will be obvious to men of discernment. > > Designating sights of flora and fauna in nature > That are evocative of love and tenderness > Is intended to bring comfort and reassurance > To the heroine in lonesome anguish. (Poruḷatikāram : Poruḷiyal, verses 35, 36, 37)

Our forefathers advise us to rein in anger (ciṉam), as anger spoils relationships, destroys unity, and mars friendship. That is why anger is vicious. It should be avoided. Anger cannot be accepted in any form. But there are instances where the word ‘anger’ is used in a positive sense. For example, when an army of brave youth rises to defend the Tamil language, we go in for expressions like the one below: > Look at the upsurge of the angry tigers > That march up > Beating the drum of racial honour! Though the emotion of anger is generally not accepted, the term attains a significant status in this context. Pētaimai can be interpreted as ignorance. The dictionary defines pētai as a young woman. There are women who witness with glee the plight of a woman ‘possessed’ being thrashed by exorcists. While denouncing such women as pētai, we are not using the term in any positive sense. But if an old man who marries a young woman dies within six months of the wedding, we take pity on the young widow and call her a poor, unfortunate girl. When we use the word pētai for the young widow, the meaning changes. The word here does not denote folly but her pathetic condition as a young widow. Therefore in this context, pētaimai gains in stature as a special term referring to pathos. When we call a person jealous or compare that person to Gandhari (Duriyodhana’s mother in Mahābhārata) we are using the term poṟāmai (envy, jealousy) in its derogatory sense. But when the film Parācakti scripted by me became a roaring success, my good friend poet Kannadasan visited me. After hugging me, he exclaimed, “Sir, I feel really jealous of you.” He kissed me on the forehead. In this context the word parts with its negative sense to become something endearing and appreciative. Thus the word develops a special sense. Poverty is not acceptable in any form. Eradicate poverty. This is the war-cry of progressive people and the vow of those in governance. Poverty no doubt is a cruel thing. “I withered every time I chanced upon withered crops.” These are the words of Vaṭalūr Vaḷḷalār Rāmaliṅka Aṭikaḷār, a saint who had a great compassion for the poor and the downtrodden. As in the case of the two words discussed above, the word vaṟumai (poverty) too undergoes a kind of regeneration through Vaḷḷalār comparing it to withered crops. Anger, ignorance, jealousy, and poverty are to be avoided by us. Be that as it may, there are contexts where they have a positive worth. > The four traits of the hero and heroine-- > Anger, ignorance, envy and penury -- > Do occur in them > As attributes (implied) of their positive worth. (Poruḷatikāram : Poruḷiyal, verse 51)

We talk about like-minded couple, or the son taking after the father or the daughter the mother. The comparison is called oppu which can only be felt intuitively. It does not lend itself to any understanding based on realities without. Much like oppu, uru means a mind event caused by viewing something never seen before. This again is felt only through faculties within. The word veruppu which commonly means hatred has another meaning listed in the dictionary, cerivu, which also means, abundance or modesty. Whatever might be the meaning, hatred could only be felt through the heart. Chastity is also related to the heart. Chastity cannot manifest itself in a material form. Both ēr (beauty) and eḻil (splendour) fall under the category of words which don’t lend themselves to be differentiated in concrete terms. Nāṇ bridles the feelings. Maṭam is a characteristic of women. Nōy is a medical condition. Vēṭkai and nukarvu are the urges to get the object of desire, and quite like them, love, jealousy, modesty and wisdom can only be felt. Thus they fall under the category of abstract things. * > Likeness, awe and abundance, > Fidelity of the loved to the lover, growth and loveliness, > Delicacy, coyness and credulousness, > Affliction, longing and enjoyment > Are all terms of the abstract kind > Discernible to the mind’s eye; > They elude definitions of a concrete nature. (Poruḷatikāram : Poruḷiyal, verse 53)

Five and twenty years ago, When Pūmpukār had been recreated With beauty and splendour blending, With art and artist at their best, At a function marked by grandeur, In the assembly of poets celebrating Tamil The lines I recited from my poem I recall And make them a beautiful archway to Tolkāppiyam Meyppāṭṭiyal. The eight kinds of manifest emotions treated therein are: Laughter, grief, disgust, wonder Fear, pride, anger and joy. By treading the path shown by The father of grammar in Tamil, Let us happily relish the eight sentiments: Laughter, grief, disgust, wonder, Fear, pride, anger and joy. I say This section on sentiments does really transport us to ecstasy. Laughter is what emerges when we obstinately work at a person given to fear. The valiant are astonished at people who are not infuriated by humiliation. Happiness and weeping are the children of the same mother. > For us to be served to the fill > These > Eight sentiments > In Tamil > Like curd delicious, > We shall further see > In the ‘blossoms’ succeeding > The way Tolkāppiyar, > Who was hailed > By poets of threefold Tamil > In the courts of > The crowned monarchs > Where fluttered > The silken banner > Aloft the royal canopy, > Looks at them. * > These eight kinds of manifest emotions are > Laughter, grief, disgust, wonder > Fear, pride, anger and joy. (Poruḷatikāram : Meyppāṭṭiyal, verse 3)

Meyppāṭu is an inner feeling manifesting on one’s body for others to see and hear. Watery eyes, beads of tears, bristling of hair, perspiration, shivering and other such overt signs are the meyppāṭus arising out of the mind’s response to an external event. Suppose a person faces a python coming to swallow him, it is natural for him to be subjected to shivering of the body, anxiety to escape and perspiration. The python here is the external event (cuvaippaṭuporuḷ) that causes the manifestation of the emotions (cuvai) on the person, whose tripidation and bewilderment are the signs (kuṟippu) and perspiration and shivering are the physical expressions (viṟal). These things together, as they come to be known to others are described by the term meyppāṭu. It has been the part of literary conventions from the ancient times to represent these sentiments arising out of our inner life and external life situations and experiences in dramatic usage and imaginative usage. The Tolkāppiyam verse in this regard occurs as the first verse of the Meyppāṭṭiyal section: > As the literate men say, > Thirty-two are the sources > That represent spheres of human sport > Wherein are born the eight emotions > With each emotion having four sources. (Poruḷatikāram : Meyppāṭṭiyal, verse 1) There are thirty-two sources of human sport wherein are born things sixteen when classified. Music and dance enjoyed in those days by the three crowned monarchs and the chieftains, the emotions that they experienced as they witnessed these ‘sports’ (paṇṇai), the objects of these emotions (cuvaippaṭuporuḷ), the inner responses they felt (kuṟippu) and their external manifestations (viṟal) - these four expand into thirty-two as is seen in the Tolkāppiyam verse above.

( The term eḷḷal (ridicule), one of the sources of laughter, has been in vogue for a very long time) Commentators bring in the example of a lame person while talking about the situations where ridicule is due. ( Humane considerations prohibit ridiculing others especially the handicapped. The fast spreading social awareness in the modern world rules out ridicule of a handicapped person’s staggering being a source of laughter.) However, I would like to share with you an incident I have heard of as an example of the source of laughter. It was an incident that occurred in a city. Even as civilization has seen great advancement with the advent of industrialization and electrification, people were travelling in bullock carts and carriages driven by horses. There was a vegetable vendor who did business on the roadside. People regularly bought vegetables from him. Whenever a cart passed by, the vendor would become enraged and challenge the occupant with swear words. He would shout, “Hey, horse carriage, bullock cart, go slowly. Why on earth do you raise dust while whizzing past the road? If I get up and come there, you might have to meet with dire consequences. I would whip you severely.” Though none of the vehicle owners cared to listen to him, the vendor never stopped hurling abuses. One fine day, the vendor shouted and threatened the driver of a horse carriage as was his wont. “Do you know what I would do? I will break your carriage to pieces. Why do you stare? Do you know what will happen if I come there?” Just as the vendor was at his abusive best, the driver stopped the carriage and dared him to come near. The vendor was dumbstruck. The reason being his inability to do so, as he was handicapped, without legs. This evoked laughter from all quarters. (Ridicule suits only such particular situations. It does not suit the disabled in general, neither should it do so.) (Since Pāṇṭiyaṉ Neṭuñceḻiyaṉ was young, he was mocked at by the other kings. An undaunted Neṭuñceḻiyaṉ rose up in arms against them. My poem below celebrates the exploits of this youth: ) The jingling anklet on the leg of this tender youth Was replaced by a string of bells marking heroism. The plaited lock was cut off. He was a boy-king holding a dazzling sword. He took off the bangles from his tender hands And sported the bow on his shoulder. He was still an adolescent wearing amulet. Therefore, holding him too young, The two crowned monarchs, Cēra and Cōḻa. Together with the five mighty vēḷir chieftains challenged him for a war. The famous army of the five chieftains paired with The kings holding the banners sporting arrow and tiger, The young Pāṇṭiyaṉ was never perturbed At the event of crossing swords with the alliance of the seven. Looking at the message from the enemy, “Better be chastised, otherwise you may have to part with very life,” He laughed aloud and roared: “It is not in our tradition to hide from war. Do you think that the Pāṇṭiya kingdom is a place of recluses? No, no, it is not so. Our presiding deity Mother Pāṇṭi has not begotten cowards. Oh! Countrymen! Virtuous souls! Trust me. This young Neṭuñceḻiyaṉ would add to the fame of our motherland Thus did the young king instil valour into his subjects. The foes looked down upon the youth and mocked him. He in turn laughed at their arrogance and it was he who had the last laugh. A person preferred a written complaint to the police station about the theft of a metal pot (tavalai) The police official peered through and burst out laughing, “But then your head is very much intact.” Owing to poor knowledge, he missed the letter ‘va’ and has instead written talai in his complaint. Just as the official explained, he also joined in the laughter, got back his petition and made the correction. The official laughed again and enquired, “Pray, from which well did the frog disappear?” Again, instead of tavalai he had mistakenly written tavaḷai meaning frog. So ignorant was he that after having made the pot a head, he now has made it a frog. These four are then situations and objects that have the potential to provoke laughter. Here is the Tolkāppiyam verse: > The four sources of laughter are > Ridicule, childishness, stupidity and credulity. (Poruḷatikāram : Meyppāṭṭiyal, verse 4)

Socrates, the thinker par excellence, stands trial in the Greek court of law. The charge against him is that he instigated the youth against the state by his speeches. A group of three persons raise a furore proposing and seconding those charges in the court. These three persons-Anytus, Lichen and Meletus-level charges against Socrates which are in the nature of contempt of the great thinker. Anytus: Seething volcano! Turbulent ocean! More terrible than all these is Socrates! ... Weapon of Wisdom! All the world would surrender to this missile, it is said!... If that weapon were to be manufactured in Greece, we would not be able to raise our heads, Meletus! What do you say, Lichen? Lichen: I am a sculptor who carves God out of stone...! Once even this Socrates was a sculptor like me! But now he has metamorphosed into a sculptor of thoughts! It’s all right! After the three of us - me who create God out of stones, Meletus the poet who with his Midas touch gives divine shapes to bundles of imagination, and a political genius like you - once we have colluded together..., Socrates is nothing more than a worthless particle upon an ocean, isn’t he, Anytus...! Meletus: Hurray, Lichen! Kudos... ! Only as long as people are like donkeys would they patiently bear the burden of falsehoods we place on their backs! Only if they are blind will they follow the way we show! We must put an end to him before he succeeds in opening the intellectual eyes of the masses who dare not cross the line we draw... These were the barbs directed at a peerless man of wisdom and a revolutionary thinker, which constitute an attempt at disgracing Socrates. India’s first Prime Minister, Nehru, who ruled for 17 long years, was hailed by all sections of the society - right from the common men to the elite. Here is a poem composed in the form of the grief of the rose which he sported on his coat on the death of Nehru, the light of Asia and the white dove of peace. The nobel one! The man of principles! Where is that Death which robbed us of you? Today, you took me and put me near your heart. But you have left me and gone far away. Is it fair? You lent honey to my petals. Don’t you remember as to how I reciprocated that? Has your heart turned into a stone, Depriving me of my joy overflowing? On hearing the dirge, the other flowers approached the rose. Finding it in the flood of tears and is about to faint Jasmine went close and asked: “What Rose, why do you keep crying so long? A good person lived for the nation to benefit from. A munificent person lived to embrace us all, Could we ever get him back? Stop your wailing. The queen of flowers! Do smile.” The Tamiḻ race stands tall today with pride and self-esteem thanks to the efforts of Periyār. When Periyār breathed his last, the Tamiḻs all over the world felt completely dispirited which is reflected in the following lines. As a volcano, As a scorching fire, As a thunder striking terror among the foes, As a burning torch of ethnic pride, As a billhook felling things disgraceful, As an Ingarsal refuting the very divinity, As a Socrates who never minced words, As a Voltaire in questioning things, Did our Periyār live his life! Behold him lying on the lap of death! He didn’t die young, a full life had he lived though If Taj Mahal were to be engulfed by the earth, Would we comfort ourselves saying, “Well, it was an old building?” Would we bear if the Big Temple of Tanjavur were to fall Saying it is an aged structure? Like these unforgettable monuments Periyār too has history made! An emotion of this kind is what Tolkāppiyar calls decline (acaivu) that would cause grief and distress. (Poverty had driven the purāṇic Nallataṅkāḷ and quite a number of mothers of the modern age as well to either sell the children begotten by them to eke out a living or drown them in a pond or river only to follow suit, later. The flooding tears at such spectacles of poverty constitute the sentiment of weeping.) * > The four inexorable sources of grief are > Contempt, deprivation, decline in stature and indigence. (Poruḷatikāram : Meyppāṭṭiyal, verse 5)

She bore him for ten months, and suckled him. After sending him to school, she took pride upon his growth. She became ecstatic on seeing her son in groom’s apparel. Now she is gifted with grandchildren too. Sapped of vitality with hair all grey, toothless and hunchbacked, she dreamt of spending her last days under the protective and loving care of her son. Her own son now denounces her, “Why are you still alive? Do you wish to make life miserable for me? Get lost and go to an old age home.” But even at this point what the mother regrets is her senility and not the behaviour of her son. In his youthful days, he slogged it out and earned money in abundance; all of a sudden, he was struck with epilepsy. Each day was marked by seeking medicine and treatment. The woman who joined him as his lifemate savoured every moment of their sunny days. Once he became an invalid, she became sick of marital life. Whenever he called out to her affectionately, she retorted derisively, “What the hell do you want? Speak out.” She kept scorching him. But he never reprimanded her. Instead, he was furious and would vent all his anger at the disease. Like the birds that desert the dried-up pond, selfish people leave their friends when the latter lose their wealth. Such victims direct their ire not against the former friends but at their own miseries. Is it not because misery becomes their companion that their friends left them? When the rich lead a simple life, it is valued as simplicity. If simplicity is taken to the extreme and the person takes to wearing torn and crumpled clothes, it is miserliness causing a sense of disgust to others. * > The four abiding sources of disgust are > Decrepitude, sickliness, vexation and incapacitation. (Poruḷatikāram : Meyppāṭṭiyal, verse 6)

Even now, mothers beseech the distant and bewitching moon through songs to come down and play with their children. The moon has never accepted their invitation and come down. Even though the moon hasn’t descended to the earth, thanks to the marvels of science, an American astronaut, Armstrong, put his feet on the moon, hoisted his national flag and came back to the earth bringing with him stone-like things from the moon. Isn’t this ‘newness’ a thing of wonder for us? Gandhiji who went to South Africa as an advocate stood his ground in the struggle against the racism practised there. Transcending from being the ‘Saint of Wardha’ he, through his intelligence, energy and selfless effort, gained in stature and esteem not only in India but also in the international arena. Through his perseverance and relentless practice of non-violence, he secured freedom for his country, an astonishing feat indeed, achieved through his hugeness of effort and dedication. The flag of peace hoisted by him flutters still. Scholars hail Tirukkuṟaḷ as having drilled a hole in an atom and stuffed into it knowledge equivalent to seven seas. Yes, an atom is that small. But bombs made of such atoms not only brought curtains upon the Second World War but also extinguished the flame of life in millions of people. The immense potential of the tiny atoms stupefies everybody, doesn’t it? The ancient people of the country remained helpless and were subjected to humiliation from all quarters. Ambedkar the great emerged as the ring of protection for them, crossing swords with the all-powerful ‘Varnashra Dharma’ and coming out victorious. The spectacle of K. R. Narayanan occupying the chair of the President of India is an example of the evolutionary development of the principles of Ambedkar, the architect of the Constitution of India. Such a social transmutation achieved by Ambedkar is but a matter of wonder. The following is the Tolkāppiyam verse in this regard: > The four sources of wonder that overwhelm one’s mind are > Novelty, hugeness, minuteness and transmutation. (Poruḷatikāram : Meyppāṭṭiyal, verse 7) Note: Men of wisdom are capable of comprehending the true nature of newness, hugeness, minuteness and transmutation. As such, the emotion of wonder is that of others who are witness to these four phenomena. Perhaps for this reason, Tolkāppiyar in the verse above speaks of these phenomena as overwhelming ones.

A youth with the resolve to converse only in chaste Tamiḻ, adhering to the tenets of literature and grammar, confided to an elderly person of his hamlet possessing profound knowledge of Tamiḻ, that he would very soon tie the knots. The person greeted him with a heartfelt wish, “May you get an aṇaṅku most suited to your life!” Incidentally, the youth had browsed the dictionary just that day and found out that aṇaṅku meant ghost. “Sir, why do you wish me to be tied up with a ghost?” The learned elder explained, “Don’t you know that the dictionary details aṇaṅku as ‘a woman’, ‘a ghost’ and a ‘mohini’ (a devil in the guise of a beautiful woman)?” Even in this hi-tech era, there are people horrified by such things as ghost, apparition and black magic. Therefore, in Tolkāppiyam, aṇaṅku is shown as a being evoking fear. Owing to the fear of lion, tiger, bear and other dangerous animals and being unequal to them in strength and valour, the primitive man hunted them with arrows and spears, while his modern counterpart uses bullets. Of course, they do so from a safe distance. Laymen as well as the learned are naturally subjected to fear on either hearing about or encountering thieves, groups of robbers or highwaymen. In this list of things evoking fear, wrong deeds of a serious nature are also included. Many commentators state that iṟai refers to the king. If iṟai is not taken in isolation and read together with the prefix as tam iṟai it becomes tammiṟai, which means ‘one’s wrong deeds of a grievous nature’. It is quite natural that such wrong-doers dread punishment Veḷḷaivāraṇar also points to the double entendre involved in tam iṟai and tammiṟai. * > The four sources of unmitigated fear are > Demoniac beings, wild animals, thieves and depravity. (Poruḷatikāram : Meyppāṭṭiyal, verse 8)

There is education where one learns about the world in a book and also the other kind where the world itself is the book to be read. Anybody excelling in both these types of education will naturally stand at the peak of knowledge. Such people had excelled in the past and do so at the present time as well. When the entire world showers praise upon them, we, as do these people, are filled with a sense of pride. Those with an unflinching resolve with the flame of truth burning within can stand up to any challenge without fear. They are very brave indeed. Such people find a place among men of prowess. With the golden saying, “If at all you live in this world, do so with fame” as their motto, people from all walks of life yearn for recognition and fame. Fame follows only those who don’t covet it. It is the Koṅku land Where The women wear smiles bud-like That are sweet like mellifluous Tamiḻ Mixed with honey bees collect from flowers, And walk with a sense of pride Saying, “Even the tiny particles of food Carried by ants Are gifts from our king Kumaṇaṉ the munificent.” Such is the emotion of pride as arising from the feeling that Kumaṇaṉ’s name is synonymous with liberality. * > The four sources of rightful pride are > Learning, prowess, unsullied fame and munificence absolute. (Poruḷatikāram : Meyppāṭṭiyal, verse 9)

In a scenario where anybody wielding a stick becomes a ruler, a reign of terror is unleashed--like chopping people’s heads through violence and suppression, vicious acts of severing hands and legs, refusal to even appreciate the cause of opposition and mercilessly trampling them down with spouse and children, incessant beating and acts of terrorism with the approval of the government, murder committed without anybody raising even a muffled protest or making efforts to prevent it, with the people writhing like worms in a fire, unable to bear the injustice--where people rise like tigers. This transformation is what is called anger. * > The four sources of hate-born anger are > Cutting one’s limbs, harming one’s kin, > Inflicting pain and anguish and ‘killing’. (Poruḷatikāram : Meyppāṭṭiyal, verse 10)

Though not as mammoth as a mountain, the required yield from the paddy fields to one’s heart’s content, the ripeness of mind acquired through learning, the communion of the hearts of men, the villagers assembling to dance and sing together in rapture-this is happiness earned to one’s own heart’s fill rather than the sadistic pleasure derived from others’ misery. This happiness manifests itself in all its serenity on the day of Taip Poṅkal which the Tamiḻs celebrate as a day of happiness with lots of emotions. The following musical verse captures the sentiment above: Hail Poṅkal, hail Poṅkal! Poṅkal which exudes mirth everywhere. Hail Poṅkal, hail Poṅkal Toiling gods of folks! Tens of thousands of people you prop up. The world has placed the crown upon your head - Your roar of resolution can dwarf even the peaks of the Himalayas. Let us all speak of the greatness of the peasants, And wish them for their prosperity! We shall shout, “Let milk (pāl) overflow!” That Pāl is the one Vaḷḷuvar has gifted us— The Pāls of Aṟam, Poruḷ and Kāmam. What more do we need? Let’s cleanse our homes, cows, calves and get rid of dust and dirt. This is the real Bhogi! Let’s uproot superstitious beliefs and remove their stench, Chisel our grey cells and rational thinking and gather knowledge. Let’s twist our moustaches And work for the empowerment of our womenfolk. Let our women’s lips wear buds of smile - The women who love turmeric, ginger and sugar cane lofty And lands fertile! Bull-fight for our youth was a child’s play then. Righteousness and fair-play are essential in public life. The joy of such a new life will cross the boundaries of the earth. Hail Poṅkal! * > The four sources of unmixed joy are > Riches, mind’s might, sexual union and play. (Poruḷatikāram : Meyppāṭṭiyal, verse 11)

t: Fivefold Akam Love: The First Stage of Physical Manifestations
x: While looking at the physical manifestations proper to the fivefold Akam love, it seems that the Meyppāṭṭiyal section of Tolkāppiyam may have inspired and aided the great bard Kampar. While describing the scene of the first meeting between Cītā who was standing on the terrace of the palace at Mitilai and Rāma who was ambling along the streets accompanied by the sage Viswamitrā, Kampar states: The Lord looked at her, which she also reciprocated. I must add a further gleam to Kampar’s imagination: The Lord looked at her Which she also reciprocated, Which the sage, an absolute renunciate, also noticed. Encounter belongs usually to the warfield. But here it is the arena of love’s union. In the lanes or gardens wearing a deserted look, The flower of a girl and the tiger of a young man run into. They are mature enough to understand the language of the eyes. As their four eyes exchange their glances - Beads of perspiration appear on the forehead of this woman fit for poetry. Her head drooped weighs down by abundant shyness. Whereas the man doesn’t fail to drop his hints. That queen of beauty grasps his intension - immediately. How eager she is to converse with him! Here is the picture of this encounter as it constitutes the first phase of the love career of the Akam hero and heroine: The states of mind that there aptly manifest As the hero and the heroine are drawn by passion In their clandestine pre-marital course are: Her receptive posture as the hero’s passionate eyes fall on her, Her forehead wearing beads of sweating, Her coyness concealing her inward longing and delight And her keeping off from others, Her heart having been lost to him. (Poruḷatikāram : Meyppāṭṭiyal, verse 13)

t: Fivefold Akam Love: The Second Stage of Physical Manifestations
x: The physical manifestations of the first stage of Akam love Consist of the dilemma as to who would initiate the act; She wipes off the beads of sweat on the forehead, Unties the tresses of her hair which add to the beauty of her person, And then ties them up immediately. Her body seems emaciated in no moment owing to the passion of love. Pretending to have lost an ear-stud, She walks the street and the garden under the pretext of looking for it. She gropes for the ring on the finger and bangles on the wrist To reassure herself that they are intact, though they remain in place. Swayed by the strong winds of the conflict between passion and modesty, She removes her dress and rewore it thinking it to have come off. Thus these four are the physical manifestations of the second stage. They are truly the beginning Leading to the ecstasy of love union. * > Her tresses flowing in loosened strands, > Dropping off an ear-ornament of hers, > Holding her ornaments fast worn in order though, > And keeping on setting her dress to order -- > The second phase of the states of mind of the lovers, > As they are through clandestine love career, > Stands betrayed in the deeds of passion above. (Poruḷatikāram : Meyppāṭṭiyal, verse 14)

t: Fivefold Akam Love: The Third Stage of Physical Manifestations
x: As her dress gets loosened, She goes behind the fragrant creeper by the stream To adjust the clothes. Be it so that he would be her husband in future, Shyness prevents her from doing it under his gaze. The lustrous lass stands behind the creeper Loosens the attire all and rerobes it. She plaits the wear under the navel And tucks it up Running her palm down to the hip. Just then A gush of strong wind snatches away her upper garment. Crossing her elbows over the chest And placing the fingers ten on the shoulders, She conceals her breasts As does one That hides the stolen lotus buds From the guards of the pond. These four Along with displaying non-existent strength, Constitute the bodily manifestations Of the third phase of love union. They then leave the rendezvous With two bodies but with hearts unseparated. * > The third phase of the clandestine love manifests in: > Her seeing her hips down off from exposure as the garments slip, > Correcting the waist-ornaments thereon, > Her pretence to be unassailed by slings of passion, > And her hands rising, her pretence notwithstanding. (Poruḷatikāram : Meyppāṭṭiyal, verse 15)

t: Fivefold Akam Love: The Fourth Stage of Physical Manifestations
x: The sweet clandestine union having enjoyed, The lovers part With hearts full of love. Another day -- The kindred folks spot them. With an open-hearted praise of the lady, The hero said: “I have resolved to marry her”. But the people of the village are not amused. Taunt and rebuke mark their words “How dare you inform us after everything is over?” Seeing the kinsmen in frenzy, The lady casts off her shyness and speaks with resolve: “After the decision of ‘he for me’ and ‘I for him’. Why should there be a wall in between? Let it be shattered to pieces.” “How could she wag her tongue so After having led a secret love course?” They bare their fang. Dismayed, the lady’s heart is filled with woe. She then accepts the gift of the hero as per the ancient custom. “What is left now Is only fixing the marriage date.” Saying so She leaves the place Wishing her critics well. * > The heroine’s ecstatic recollecting and praise > Of the hero’s acts of love towards her, > Her utterances shorn of her native credulousness, > Being down with coyness at the gossip > The unkind tongues of the town indulge in about their love, > And her willing acceptance of the hero’s gifts of love -- > Such are the externalizations of the fourth phase > That mark the clandestine love career of the two. (Poruḷatikāram : Meyppāṭṭiyal, verse 16) Note: Once marriage is confirmed, the hero will offer a gift to the heroine which is called kaiyuṟai.

t: Fivefold Akam Love: The Fifth Stage of Physical Manifestations
x: The clandestine course on With the consent of the heroine, And in tune with the convention of The heroine’s acceptance of the hero’s gift of love. She takes the gift of the hero with passion, Hands it to her parents submissively And looks for their consent to marriage. “You have brought disgrace to our clan! We have become the object of ridicule of folks around! People laugh at us everywhere! Having already publicized your bond of passion, You have come now to us Saying the marriage awaits to be performed. Our kinsmen, the townsfolk and all know of it already! Is it proper that You bring it to us, your parents, so late?” The heroine’s confidante speaks In a tone soliciting, “O mother! Things have gone beyond reckoning; Pray, don’t put any obstacles now! She will keep the honour of the family unimpaired! And will bring no disgrace to your standing!” Speechless, the mother glances at the father. “Like mother like daughter; Do nod your head without any hesitation,” the father retorts. “My head has been nodding all these days,” so saying she smiles. Isn’t she the old lady who years ago had that bewitching smile? With the mother giving consent, the father follows suit. “Now, what prevents us from caressing each other, come” Was the invite of the hero. “Take to your heels, it won’t happen now,” The heroine says like a gentle breeze. “How come the shyness and reserve that have been in hiding have surfaced today?” He was surprised. “To refuse to frolic around is an experience sweet to me. Whence the shyness and tenderness?” Though refusing fleshly union, She relished the beauty of her lover to her heart’s content from where she was hiding. Not to be outdone he tiptoed to where she was to hug her. * > The fifth phase of their clandestine love career manifests in -- > The heroine’s consent for her clandestine course > To be revealed to her kin at home > Having weighed the consequences thereof, > Her shunning sports and such acts of pleasure > With her clandestine career revealed to kinsmen, > Her willed solitude off her lover’s access > As she is subjected to rigours of watch at home, > And her feeling of ecstasy > As there occasions her meeting the hero. (Poruḷatikāram : Meyppāṭṭiyal, verse 17)

t: Fivefold Akam Love: The Sixth Stage of Physical Manifestations
x: The lover could draw her unto him Like the flavour of sugar cane, juice of the fruit and a piece of magnet. But how could she forget the memories of her lying on her mother’s lap Growing under the protective care of her parents? That is why -- The imminent parting from parents -- She wears an anguished countenance As she is decked in bridal wear. Though a sea of kinsmen swarm around her, She feels like being on an island. And she is deeply worried over not sighting her lover even for a single moment. She is disturbed and asks her confidante as to where he has gone? The angst scorches her like the latent heat of the sun. She stands helpless and in quite despondency. When one is at the extreme of either melancholy or mirth, One becomes helpless and confused. This is not peculiar only to her, but natural to one and all. * > The states of mind that are revealed in > The sixth phase of the clandestine course are: > The lonesome heroine turning heartsick > At her person bedecked with ornaments, > Her falling into a mood of despondency, > Her utterances of dismay and distress, > And her wearing a sense of helplessness. (Poruḷatikāram : Meyppāṭṭiyal, verse 18)

> Four are the grounds for comparison > Between the tenor and the vehicle: > The deed done, the effect thereof > The form and the complexion. (Poruḷatikāram : Uvamaiyiyal, verse 1) A simile compares something with something else using the words like or as, for example, a row of teeth like a string of pearls Here ‘a row of teeth’ is the subject of comparison, and ‘a string of pearls’ is the simile or the standard of comparison. In Sanskrit, the subject of comparison is called uvamēyam and the standard of comparison is known as upamānam. These terms are frequently used in the teaching of similes. Comparisons are made between things on the basis of four common characteristics, viz., complexion, form, deed and effect. The comparison markers in Tamil are aṉṉa, āṅka, pōla, etc. (meaning like or as) e.g. mayilaṉṉa cāyal - peacock’s like grace māṉ pōlat tuḷḷiṉāl - she hopped like a deer. Tolkāppiyar in the verse quoted above speaks of the classification of similes. This classification comprises (i) comparison of things that are accessible to the eyes, and (ii) comparison of things that are accessible to other sense organs or to the mind.
