We shall illustrate these classes and the grounds for comparison. She flew off as a sparrow (comparison based on deed) • munificent like rain (comparison based on effect) • neck like a conch (comparison based on form) • gold-like complexion (comparison based on colour) Look at the following examples: flute’s like speech (through hearing) • sweet like honey (through taste) • scorching like the summer sun (through bodily feeling) • fragrant breeze (through smell) • O lovely moon! Is the joy of your sight Like the joy of sighting A potful of white rice While looking for A little gruel in hunger? (through the mind) Apart from these that we have drawn on the first verse of Tolkāppiyam : Uvamaiyiyal, the second verse speaks of the mixed categories of similitude: > The grounds for comparison above > Do get intermingled too. (Poruḷatikāram : Uvamaiyiyal, verse 2)

The excellence of the simile adds to the worth of the thing compared. > As we examine them, > The vehicles of comparison > Do stand loftier than the tenors. (Poruḷatikāram : Uvamaiyiyal, verse 3) When we say, ‘the face is as beautiful as a red lotus’, the thing compared is the face. The standard of comparison, the red lotus, gives here an added significance to the face. The simile should be worthier than the thing compared. He stood like a lion. In this simile, we don’t research as to whether the lion or the man is greater. Such an argument will only undermine the importance of the simile. However, in this case, the emphasis is on the strength and majesty of the lion. Thus the thing taken for comparison gains pre-eminence over the thing compared. The simile becomes efficient when an attribute like “pouncing tiger” is given to a character like Paṇṭāraka Vaṉṉiyaṉ by way of comparative description. On the other hand, in the expression ‘Shivaji mountain mouse like,’ the significance of the simile goes down as the person compared is of a high stature. We have to consider this rather an exception.

> Pre-eminence, loveliness, love and might > Are the four characteristics > That abide as sources of similitude. (Poruḷatikāram : Uvamaiyiyal, verse 4) This verse shows that though the simile in a comparison is loftier than the subject, it has excellence, beauty, love and valour as the sources. In this context, I would like to bring in a few illustrations from the historical novel Rōmāpuri Pāṇṭiyaṉ written by me. In the beginning of the year 20 BC, one day, the city of Pūmpukār ruled by the Cōḻa king Karikālaṉ wore a festive look. The Cōḻa and the Pāṇṭiya flags fluttered together over the palace near the Maruvūrppākkam seashore of Pūmpukār. On that day Pāṇṭiyaṉ Peruvaḻuti and Cōḻaṉ Karikālaṉ met and established their friendship. On that occasion, the poet Kārikkaṇṇanār sang in praise of the two monarchs: > You are the cool-watered Cauvery’s lord, and he... Starting thus, it goes on; > With water and grain easily available to everybody, > The king reigns with a cool sceptre the Tamil-flourishing Maturai, > Where witness sandal from mountains, > Pearl from the sea and the resounding drum. The poet lauds the unity and friendship between the two kings. Just as the two kings were seated together in the court, music and dance combined to fill the city with joy and festivities. This simile has excellence as its basis. Here excellence is not a natural trait, but something added. The nalam (loveliness) mentioned in the verse refers to a natural aspect arising from a thing. It is like the water spurting naturally while a well is dug. Excellence, on the other hand, is like making a pond and digging canals from the river to facilitate flow of water into it. The excellence is the basis for the simile of music and dance going together becoming the standard for Cōḻaṉ Karikālaṉ and Pāṇṭiyaṉ Peruvaḻuti seated together in the court. The residents of Maruvūrppākkam - traders, yavaṉars, weavers of silk, cotton and woollen clothes, goldsmiths, flower vendors, sculptors, sailors, physicians, brahmins, officials of the palace, bards, songsters - added to the beauty of the city. Already, the Grand Arch which the king of Avanti constructed as a gift to Karikāl Cōḻaṉ, the Auditorium of Pearls, a present from the monarch of Vajra, and the Pavilion, a tribute from the ruler of Maghada added lustre to the city of Pūmpukār rendering it a picture gallery and a treasure house of sculpture. This simile then serves as a source of loveliness. In another chapter of the same historical novel, Ceḷiyaṉ, a character, wonders at a beautiful woman named Juno in the city of Rome: > Oh! Seeing this Juno, I feel as if my Tāmarai has descended on the city of Rome after having flown winged angels-like by a boon from God. This imagination flashing across the mind of Ceḷiyaṉ reflects the deep affection he has for his love residing in Tamiḻ Nāṭu. Therefore, the source of this simile is love. In the same novel, a poem about one of the important characters, Karikāl Cōḻaṉ, written by Kaṭiyalūr Uruttiraṅkaṇṇanār finds a mention: > The spear of Karikāl Tirumāvaḷavaṉ hurled at his foes is ferocious; > But even more horrible is the forest ventured into by the lovers. > But the shoulder of the lady seemed more comforting than Karikālaṉ’s sceptre. Here, the horrible forest functions as the simile for the ferocity of Karikālaṉ’s spear. Therefore, valour is the basis for this simile. Obviously then, a simile arises primarily on the bases of excellence, loveliness, love and might.

> Five characteristics the sources of similitude come to > As one includes things lowly. (Poruḷatikāram : Uvamaiyiyal, verse 5) Apart from the four sources of simile -- excellence, beauty, love, might -- mentioned earlier, there is a fifth one too. That is the comparison of the subject with the lowly things. The Tamil term kiḻakkiṭu poruḷ used in the Tolkāppiyam verse is a trivial thing or something degrading or lowly. In a big village, a person was working as a washerman assisted by five donkeys. On an eventful night, one of those donkeys was found missing. He went searching for it throughout the night. At the approach of dawn, the washerman thought he heard a donkey bray from a house. “Hurray! I have traced my donkey”, he exulted and entered that house. Actually, it was the singer in the house doing his early morning practice. The singer was surprised to see this man sprint in, and enquired, “What is the matter?” He replied, “I have lost my donkey and I am searching for it. Since your music sounded like my donkey’s voice I rushed in here.” “Now get lost! Stop barking like a dog and get out!” he shouted in rage. The tempers became frayed which ended up in a big ruckus. A person from a nearby house approached them and asked, “What men, why are you howling like foxes?” Now, both these men joined together to take up cudgels against the third person. Fortunately, a grammar teacher who happened to pass by pacified them and explained: > Making similes using the donkey, dog and fox is an instance of the fifth > basis of simile referred to in the Uvamaiyiyal. This is done to make clear the > inferiority of a particular thing. It is natural to expose its characteristics > through such similes. Hence these are called trivial things. Though they could not comprehend what he was stating, they could grasp that he was pacifying them through some good advice. They stopped shouting and the quarrel ended. Thus we see that the sources of a simile come to five when a thing of lowly signification is added.

> The vehicle and the tenor in similitude > Must be in accord with norms of propriety. (Poruḷatikāram : Uvamaiyiyal, verse 8) The simile and the thing which is compared must be comparable enough to make the listeners happy and accept them. For example, in the expression tuṭi iṭai (slender waist) tuṭi means a small drum. It describes the slender waist placed in between the broad chest above and the broad lower abdomen below being compared to the drum tuṭi. Since the upper and lower parts of the body remain broad and the middle part of the body thin, the simile of tuṭi iṭai stands appropriate and pleasing. Since the shape is broad at the top and the bottom and slender at the middle, can we bring in a grindstone for the simile? No, such a simile is not acceptable. That is why this verse states that whether in the case of the simile or the thing which is compared to, they should be acceptable as well as comparable. The commentator Pērāciriyar states that while the comparison of tresses to the feathers of a peacock is acceptable, its comparison with the feathers of a crow would jar. The national Tamil poet Bharati sings, “Hey, Lord Krishna, I can see your pleasant dark colour on the wings of the crow!” The colour black on the crow’s feather is not used for a simile here but we witness it being presented in a positive light. The expression, “cascading tresses” should not be interpreted as representing grey hair. It must be understood that it represents only thick and long hair. In the phrase, “eyes-like black beetle”, we don’t get apprehensive that the eyes might have legs like the beetle’s or that they fly. It would only demean the importance of the simile. One cannot use a simile indiscriminately. This opinion of Veḷḷaivāraṇar is worth remembering.

> Where the tenor is made the vehicle > [And the vehicle the tenor], > It is the mode of comparison proper > Insofar as the vehicle-turned tenor > Abides as one of a loftier note. (Poruḷatikāram : Uvamaiyiyal, verse 9) It is clear from this verse that even though the subject of comparison is represented in the form of a simile, the simile stands out unambiguously, given the fact that the simile-turned subject is shown as one of heightened estimation. Pērāciriyar, a commentator, quotes the following Cirupāṇāṟṟuppaṭai lines and explains it thus: > The solid bud > Lovely face-like, > Resembling the maturing breast > Breaking open, > There unfolds > The divine lotus. Here the breast and the face are similes and the bud and the flower the subjects. Because the breast and the face are shown to be loftier, they are the standards of comparison. Turned into metaphors, they are ‘the bud of the breast’ and ‘the lotus of the face’. Given the fact that the simile stands on a higher pedestal in relation to the subject, there is no obscurity with regard to the subject and the simile. Pērāciriyar’s explanation runs along these lines. Later rhetoricians term ‘the lotus of the face’ a metaphor and classify it as a separate figure of speech. Veḷḷaivāraṇar, basing himself on the commentaries of Iḷampūraṇar and Pērāciriyar, looks at it as a variety of the simile.

Veḷḷaivāraṇar observes: > Conventions regarding the organization of morphemes and prosody apart, conventions vis-a-vis the male and female species and the offspring of human and non-human classes, conventions on the fourfold social classes of the human world, conventions on grass and trees, conventions as regards the features of the physical world and literary conventions - all these come under ‘Conventions’. I shall discuss Veḷḷaivāraṇar’s views on the social classes later in this essay. A look at Tolkāppiyar’s description of male and female species and the offspring of the human and non-human classes shows that they have gone through extensive changes in worldly usage. > Kuṭṭi is the offspring designation of > Mongoose, wild cat, rat and three-striped squirrel. (Marapiyal, verse 6) This verse states that the young ones of mongoose, wild cat, rat and squirrel are called by the name kuṭṭi. But in usage today, there are no such designations as kirikkuṭṭi or aṇilkuṭṭi; instead, they are called kirippiḷḷai, aṇilkuñcu, etc. The young of cat alone is called pūnaikkuṭṭi. This changed usage applies to other designations in Tolkāppiyam like narippiḷḷai, paṉṟippiḷḷai, etc. which the commentators too have pointed out. Wherever due, Veḷḷaivāraṇar does not fail to deny the existence of caste system in those days. He shows in his scholarly and objective study Literary History of Tolkāppiyat Tamiḻ that the social castes was a much later development in Tamilnāṭu. He observes: > Tolkāppiyam Marapiyal verses 71-85 that deal with four castes are the interpolations of a later period. > > Tolkāppiyar classifies people in terms of the landscape divisions, and not on the basis of their colour (varṇam) anywhere in his treatment of the living modes of people in the earlier sections. The Marapiyal section deals with only the conventions vogue in his day relating to male-female distinction and young ones (vide verses 1-70 and 86-90). Verses 71-85 on castes represent a break in this order being added later. > > Where Tolkāppiyar classifies people in terms of their Akam love conduct and in terms of their Puṟam conduct in vākaittiṇai, the classifications are based on division of land and types of occupation, and he does not designate them by caste as Vēḷāḷar or Vaiciyar. And the term vaicikaṉ does not occur anywhere in Caṅkam literature. Given that Tolkāppiyar does not speak of four castes, it is incorrect to say that he has referred to kings and traders as the intermediate class (iṭaiyiru vakaiyōr). Besides, the interpretation (of verses 77 and 82) that the other two castes have no martial traits runs counter to the life portrayed in Caṅkam works. Tolkāppiyar does not mention vēḷāṉ (peasant) people as a caste. Such of these references in Tolkāppiyam are proper to Akam and Puṟam themes and do not fit into the section on conventions. > > Therefore, it is to be clearly understood that these verses 71-85 must have been included in the text only after the caste system took roots on the Tamiḻ soil at a much later period; that they have been wrongly put into Tolkāppiyam when alien rulers like Kaḷappirar held sway in Tamilnāṭu trampling down the native Tamil consciousness and the Tamil mores; and that commentators like Iḷampūraṇar and Pērāciriyar misinterpreted Tolkāppiyam caught helplessly as they were in the milieu of their days when the northern fourfold caste system nurtured by Sanskrit writers like Manu slowly entered into the social fabric of Tamilnāṭu. (Veḷḷaivāraṇar, Tolkāppiyat Tamiḻ Ilakkiya Varalāṟu : Marapiyal Viḷakkam (The Literary History of Tolkāppiyat Tamil: Conventions of Poetry))

Tolkāppiyam embodies, both suggestively and explicitly, qualities and characteristics of things, modes of living of the ancient days and basic structures of phenomena which are relevant to the present time. Even though some of them may not bear on modern customs and the new world thinking, they, nevertheless, remain valuable treasure troves of history left by the ancient Tamils. The following verse represents the acme of ancient Tamils’ scientific knowledge base: > Single-sense organisms have the sense of touch; > Two-sense organisms are endowed with touch and taste; > Touch, taste and smell go with three-sense organisms; > Four-sense organisms have sight added to the three; > Five-sense organisms are gifted with hearing in addition; > Mind’s faculty is the sixth sense known, > Thus goes the classification by discerning men. (Poruḷatikāram : Marapiyal, verse 27) That is, beings with one sense feel through the body. Two-sense beings use body and mouth. Three-sense beings have the faculties of body, mouth and nose. Four-sense beings employ body, mouth, nose and eye. Five-sense beings enjoy the faculties of body, mouth, nose, eye and ear. Six-sense beings have the gift of mind in addition to the five above. Thus all living things on the earth have been classified into six categories. This classification apart, Tolkāppiyar identifies the beings that are endowed with each of these six classes of faculties. That the ancient Tamils have written the grammar of life on the earth on scientific basis just amazes us. The division of living things into six categories on the basis of the five senses and the sense organs has been done in terms of their hierarchy of intelligence and power - which demonstrates the scientific knowledge and scientific perception of phenomena of the ancient Tamils. This knowledge and perception constitute the core of the grammar of life propounded in Tolkāppiyam. Look at the following verses: > The grass and tree are single-sense organisms; > Other species of the flora there are too > That are limited to this faculty. (Poruḷatikāram : Marapiyal, verse 28) > The snail and shell-fish are two-sense organisms; > Others of their species there are too. (Poruḷatikāram : Marapiyal, verse 29) These verses show that grass and tree are one-sense beings using the faculty of the body. Be it noted that Tolkāppiyar states that there are other species too that are one-sense organisms. Such of these instances show Tolkāppiyam to be a treasure-house of scientific knowledge and information. Look at the following verses where Tolkāppiyam gives examples of the beings that are endowed with two, three, four and five faculties. > The snail and shell-fish are two-sense organisms; > Others of their species there are too. > The termite and ant are three-sense organisms; > There are others of their kind confined to these faculties. > The crabs and beetles are four-sense organisms; > Others of their species there are too. > The beasts and men sans discrimination > Are creatures with five senses; > There are co-sharers among their species too. (Poruḷatikāram : Marapiyal, verses 29, 30, 31, 32) Human beings have six senses. If some people are deficient in one or two of these or if they do not use them properly, Tolkāppiyam is in no way responsible for it.

The comic script that follows explains that many a word found in the dictionary is not in use today, and a few of them have completely disappeared. Look at the verse below: > Mōttai, takar, uṭal and appar > Designate the male sheep. (Poruḷatikāram : Marapiyal, verse 48) In Aṇṇā’s play Nīti Tēvaṉ Mayakkam, Rāvaṇaṉ files a case against Kampar. He takes umbrage at Kampar describing him as “a merciless demon” in his version of Rāmāyaṇa and he himself argues his case before the judge. “I didn’t even touch Cīta, and safeguarded her in the garden of Ashoka. Juxtapose my chivalry with Intira’s who raped Akalya, Cantiraṉ who raped his teacher’s wife, Lakcumaṇaṉ who chopped off the nose and breast of Cūrpaṇakai, Lord Civa who misbehaved with the wives of the sages in Tārukāvaṇam and Rāma, who assailed Vāli hidden from a vantage point. How could I be termed merciless?” This is Rāvaṇaṉ’s defence. The judge, out of his inability to pass a judgement against the gods, faints. In the same manner, here comes another piece of imagination. Appar, Campantar, Cuntarar and Māṇikkavācakar were the four renowned Caiva devotees. They were also great poets in Tamil. Among them, Tirunāvukkaracar who was known as Appar brings a case before the judge. His contention is that his name included under non-human beings (akṟiṇai) in Marapiyal of Tolkāppiyam must be deleted. The judge observes, “It doesn’t seem that Tolkāppiyar included your name wantonly to denigrate your reputation, since Tolkāppiyar lived in an era much before that of yours. How could he contemplate maligning your name as you live in a later period? Appar replies, “I accept your explanation regarding difference in the era. Therefore, I do not indict Tolkāppiyar personally. It would be enough if my name be deleted.” The judge passes the judgement ordering that the name of Appar be deleted. Therefore, the term appar grouped with mōttai, takar, uṭal ceased to be there in the list. Thus was the word appar that meant a he-goat made to disappear from the list. The account above is only an imaginary, humorous anecdote. Pērāciriyar, the commentator, points out that the convention of using the word appar for a he-goat fell out of use in later years.

t: The Cultural Programme and the Gift of Kaḷiru
x: > The male of the elephant is kaḷiṟu. > Kaḷiṟu denoting the male pig > Is not disallowed too. (Poruḷatikāram : Marapiyal, verses 35, 36) > Kalai is the male of the deer too; > Kalai is also the male of the langur (mucu). (Poruḷatikāram : Marapiyal, verse 47) Narrated below is a humorous incident by which to remember kaḷiṟu, kēḻal, kalai and mucu used in the verses. The king returns home after victory in a war. The soldiers are indulging in fun and frolic. The court jesters are singing the victory song and dancing with the soldiers inebriated with toddy. After some time, they stop singing and one of the court jesters says to his counterpart, “Sir, Court Jester, you can make use of your good offices to arrange a cultural programme by beautiful damsels.” “Not a big deal at all. I will arrange it, right now.” The other court jester replies and leaves the place. He returns then parading a black langur by holding the rope tied to its neck. The jester thrusts a stick into monkey’s hand and gestures it to dance. The soldiers burst into peals of laughter, whereas the other court jester enquires in rage, “What is this, sir? Is this a beautiful woman? Do you call this a cultural programme?” The court jester who has arranged the monkey dance replies, “As per the rules prescribed in Tolkāppiyam, kalai means mucu. Kindly refer to the dictionary, where you will find the meaning of mucu to be a black langur. Leave that alone. I promptly arranged the cultural programme heeding to your request . Now, why don’t you give me a reward?” “What reward do you want?” “Recommend to the king, I may be given a kaḷiṟu (male elephant) as a reward.” Why recommendation to the king? I will myself give you a kaḷiṟu as a reward. Please wait a moment, here, I will come.” He reappears after some time, dragging a male pig along with him. “Dear jester, here is the kaḷiṟu which you asked for as a reward. In the very same Tolkāppiyam which you cited as a reference, a male pig, along with a male elephant, is referred to as a kaḷiṟu. Here, do accept your beautiful kaḷiṟu,” he says. This triggers an infectious roar of laughter among the soldiers. The cultural programme and the reward of kaḷiṟu have made them laugh to such an extent that their ribs have started aching. It turns out to be a perfect revelry on victory in the war. The meaning of the verses is: 1. The male elephant is known as kaḷiṟu. The male pig is also known as kaḷiṟu. 2. Kalai is the apt word for deer, Which designates mucu the black langur too.

> A structured blend of > Earth, fire, water, air and space > As the world is, > The use words are made of > Must be undistorted, > Undeviating from the norms > That go with the classifications of > The human -- non-human generic distinction, > And the five genders thereof. (Poruḷatikāram : Marapiyal, verse 91) By way of interpreting this verse, Iḷampūraṇar observes that the world is composed of the five elements, viz., earth, fire, water, air and space. He then goes on to explain the two words in the verse kalattal and mayakkam. The former is a mix, as of pearl, coral, sapphire and ruby. The latter signifies the one like the melted blend of gold, silver and copper. The world, therefore, exists at two levels - one as a mixture, and the other as an undifferentiated one made up of the five elements, which the compound term in the verse kalanta mayakkam signifies. Thus goes the explanation of the commentator. Now, what does the expression in Tamil kiṇaṟu veṭṭap pūtam puṟappaṭṭatu (the elements surfaced as the well was dug) mean? As one digs up the well, the ‘earth’ piles up - one element. The ‘air’ shut up in the earth comes out - second element The ‘water’ gushes forth - third element The ‘sky’ is reflected in the water - fourth element The sun’s ‘fire’ purifies the water - fifth element. Thus remains the world as the structured fusion of the elements. The phenomena of the world must therefore be denoted without deviation from the norms of usage, and in terms of the human--non-human generic distinction and the five genders informing them. Violation of the norms of usage would result in distortion and variation of meanings of words. The things of the world must be represented without deviation from the established conventions and in accord with human--non-human classification and gender distinction. Thus goes the import of the Tolkāppiyam verse. Pērāciriyar’s explanation is that the five elements remain individual entities and at the same time they remain fused with the things of the world.

t: Those Who Realize will Know, Those Who Know will Realize
x: > Compositions admit of > No violation of the conventions in vogue; > Use of diction tested through tradition > Should inform the usage therein. (Poruḷatikāram : Marapiyal, verse 92) This verse emphasizes that words not breaching the established conventions must go into the making of a verse. I am not adept in the grammar of poetry. I brought out, sixty years ago, a book of verses titled “It is No Poetry”, wherein I have openly admitted my verses being metreless. I have presided at many poetic meets of eminent poets through years. And this is what I wrote as my presidential address in the poetic meet, on the theme ‘Freedom Fighters’ broadcast on the All India Radio, Tiruchi, in the year 1967. > He in prison lived, and pulled the oilpress, > To drive away the Whites who ruled the land. > Many were killed before the prime of their lives. > He fought like a sword drawn from out of the sheath, > With no care for his life. > Of his glory to hear, > We are all arrayed here today. > > But to describe the greatness of all those > Who have their lives laid down for freedom, > I have neither the poetic ability acquired, > Nor the art of poetry learnt. > > Though my verses might poetic metre lack, > Guided as I was by the sole principle > That our land, language, honour and feelings > Should not go undefended, > I make poetic lines of my feelings, > That from my heart do gush forth, > To let those treacherous ones, > The turncoats of principles, gain awareness > I shall say this. > > Freedom was gained, > By the loss of so many lives, by the loss of so much blood! > After great loss and labour on earth, > Freedom, like purest gold, was earned. > Can we throw it away? > Good is it to hand over this rose beautiful, > To a monkey wild? > Our freedom let us zealously guard, > Let us add glory to those freedom fighters. Thus is the age of new poetry, an age when novelties like haiku are being composed. To put it in other words, it is the age when words and sentences are juggled or lines broken and they are paraded as rhythmic poetry. I do not claim that I am the one versed in prosody, and yet my verse portraits are no eyeless needles. I have the sense of pride to proclaim that my poems have remained the magnetic particles drawing even eyeless needles unto their fold. Here are a few examples: > The world to be one with all lands united, > Mankind to be knit as one by human love- > Are the noble thoughts articulated by the poet. > > But even he, he as a poet did live > With his place name, Pūṅkuṉṟam, after his name. > And he was known as Kaṇiyaṉ Pūṅkuṉṟaṉār. > > When we contemplate this carefully > Doesn’t it strike as true > That even this man of eminence > Was bound by the love of his land? Another poem: > He was the lion of a Tamil with self-respect > Who wouldn’t bend > Even to kiss his toddling child; > Instead he would get the child lifted over his head > And go about fondling it. > > He was not used to looking down to the ground, > And he would plant a kiss > On the forehead of his love of moon-like face > With the face straight up. > He wouldn’t bend like a question mark on the bed > But would lie down erect like an arrow with legs stretched out. > > Is he one with a backbone unbending? > Is his heart a field > Where the crop of obeisance never grows? > Amazed thus were many > With gaping mouths and fingers on the nose. Yet another poem: > There came a woman > Swinging like a jewelled chariot, > Walking on the verdant grass > Where the eggs of snow were being hatched. > > She was an adept in the flow of fruit-like Tamil words; > She was the elder sister of Kākkaippāṭiṉi Poṉmuṭiyār; > She sang the praises of > Atiyamāṉ Neṭumāṉañci and the munificent Pāri, > Cēramāṉ Māveṅkōvaṉ, > Kānapper tanta Vaḷuti > And the Cōḻa king Perunaṟkiḷḷi, > Thereby adding many a jewel to Tamil, > She is Avvai, the light of wisdom! Another instance: > Honour! That’s the lullaby my son listened to; > Death! That’s the sport he played; > I taught him the art of using lances > Even as he was a suckling; > > He turned a worthy son to his father > As aerial roots to a banyan tree; > > He rose against the foes in rage, > The foes with stunted minds like the goat’s tail, > Who dared to usurp our throne, > He flayed them and saw them routed > And he gave his life in the deed. > He is now the ruler of fame winning. > Look not at my eyes raining tears! > Look at my heart in joy immersed! One more of my poems: > Such a joy she did not experience on her marriage; > Son’s birth too did not give her as much happiness. > > Look! there he lies dead > With a spear piercing his chest! > She saw this and her heart leapt in joy. > > O, I was about to pluck away my breasts that fed him > O, where is that wicked man who told me a blatant lie > (That he died with a spear on his back)? > Here is the sword! Where is the tongue of that man? I keep dedicating at the feet of Mother Tamil such of these poetic portraits that are a blend of the sound of the sword’s sway and the music of the harp, and that have infused my fellow Tamils with a new vigour and a sense of amazement. I might have strayed away from the established conventions of versification. But my mind has all along remained undistracted. The readers who have had a feel of the import of the blossoms of Tolkāppiyam presented so far by me would understand this truth. And those who have understood this will feel it in their heart of hearts.

> Usage is > What is in vogue and use > Among the literate > From whom issue > The events of popular speech. (Poruḷatikāram : Marapiyal, verse 93) > Primary or original works > Are those compositions > By men of sage wisdom > Whose consummate faculties stand unsullied > By the mire of turpitude. (Poruḷatikāram : Marapiyal, verse 95) > Secondary works comprise four modes. (Poruḷatikāram : Marapiyal, verse 97) > These four modes are: > Summarization, elaboration, > Synthesis of summarization and elaboration > And translation in conformity with the tradition of the receptor tongue. (Poruḷatikāram : Marapiyal, verse 98) The explanations of these four verses are as follows: (1) Given the fact that the events of popular speech draw on the use of language by the literate, what is called linguistic usage is the usage of the literate. This apart, this usage defines and informs the worldly usage, poetic usage and the normal, grammatical usage. Following the literate usage and simplifying the poetic usage and the worldly usage for the people at large to access it will go a long way in the development and protection of the language. (2) The present work gave me the opportunity to engage myself in the protection and preservation of the Tamil language. (3) When it comes to the meaning of verse 95 given above, a misinterpretation will give room for assumptions and questions like Tolkāppiyam is the primary work. • It was composed by a person of consummate wisdom. • He was also the one of unblemished mind. • Will Tolkāppiyar go to describe himself in such terms? Primary works are those that precede and that form the basis or the source of secondary works. Dr Ilakkuvanar in his Study of Tolkāppiyam observes as follows: > It is said that Tolkāppiyam is the earliest extant work in Tamil. No other work predating Tolkāppiyam has come to us. It does not mean that no work was written before Tolkāppiyam. Tolkāppiyam is a work of grammar. In any language, literature precedes grammar. Tamil is no exception to this. Here too grammatical works came to be written only after the advent of literary works. Tolkāppiyam was written after not only works of literature but also grammatical treatises, which is attested to by Tolkāppiyam itself. Therefore, Tolkāppiyam must be seen as the earliest extant work and not the first, primary work. Even before we arrive at an answer to the question of whether Tolkāppiyam is the primary text, there have come up false mythic accounts like, Akattiyar was the teacher of Tolkāppiyar. Akattiyar was the one who wrote the first book in Tamil. Pāṇini had written a grammatical text in Sanskrit before Tolkāppiyar. Tolkāppiyar was the son of the Aryan sage Camatakkini. Camatakkini was the father of Paracurāmaṉ. Paracurāmaṉ and Rāmaṉ were contemporaries. Akattiyar belonged to the period of Rāmaṉ. Tolkāppiyar too belonged to the same period. What is strange here is that Rāma’s age is fixed before 2000 BC. Pāṇini’s period was 350 BC. Had Tolkāppiyar lived after Pāṇini, Paṉampāraṉār in his prologue to Tolkāppiyam might not have described Tolkāppiyar as the one versed in Aintiram. He would have called him versed in Pāṇini’s treatise. As such, it is obvious that Tolkāppiyam preceded Pāṇini’s work. Now, let’s come to the Tolkāppiyam verse referred to above. It does not speak of whether Tolkāppiyam is a primary text or not. On the other hand, it discusses the nature of secondary works. A secondary work implies that there must be a primary work. The verse in question just outlines the what and how of a primary work. But some of our scholar-commentators tend to give the impression that the author of a primary work is God. Not just that. Shouldn’t we realize the wily misdirection behind such assertions like Akattiyam is the primary work of the ancient era, and Tolkāppiyam is based on this work. As I have shown earlier, we must ignore such things as to whether Tolkāppiyam is a primary work and whether the primary work was authored by God. And we must treat this and the following verses in Tolkāppiyam as describing primary and secondary works. The verse > viṉaiyiṉ nīṅki viḷaṅkiya aṟiviṉ > muṉaivaṉ kaṇṭatu mutal nūlākum must read as > viḷaṅkiya aṟiviṉ muṉaivaṉ kaṇṭatu > viṉaiyiṉ nīṅki mutal nūlākum which means that men of consummate wisdom write what are called primary works, works that are faultless and that precede secondary works. Verses 3 and 4 speak of the four kinds of secondary works: synthesis, elaboration, both synthesis and elaboration, and translation.

If we were to establish a garden, we should decide which trees and flowers should adorn it, think of and implement the amenities needed for the comfort of those who come for a stroll and also carefully avoid things which should not find a place in the garden. Since the establishment of a garden can have parallels with the making of a book, a verse in Tolkāppiyam throws light on the defects to be avoided in a book. Traffic rules prescribe whether we should keep to the right or the left though it differs from country to country. Although this is an important issue, even more important is the fact that without obtaining the permission or observing the signal one should not cross the road. In the same manner, though a swimming pool is essential in a park, one should not dig a deep well in another corner of the park. The reason is that children who come to the park, accompanied by their parents, should not fall into the well by accident. A few would come to the garden holding a book with the intention of reading it there. For their sake, bright lamps should burn in a few places. In the same way, lamps should not be there in places where men and women can relax enjoying privacy which is necessary after a day’s work. If light is required there it should be dim. Though the toilet is essential to answer the call of nature, it should not be constructed in the centre of the park. Such dos and don’ts are in order in a book too, which the following verse lists: > A study sharp-eyed > Points to defects that stain a composition: > Tautology, inconsistency, understatement, > Overstatement, verbiage, obscurity, > Cacophony, contemptible things in unworthy diction, > Persisting in one’s own pet ideas, > Incomprehensibility of varied sorts > And failings that issue from these. (Poruḷatikāram : Marapiyal, verse 109) Tautology is saying the same thing again which is unnecessary. Inconsistency is saying things which are contradictory to one another. Understatement refers to making something seem less important or less impressive than it really is. Overstatement is its opposite. Verbiage is the use of too many words or of more difficult words than needed to express an idea. Obscurity is being difficult to understand. Cacophony is a mixture of loud unpleasant sounds. Such of these defects will not add to the worth of a book. A book free from these shortcomings will be like the bright lamp on a hillock enlightening minds. Now what are the features of excellence of a composition? > Brevity and perspicuousness, > Pleasing, worthy diction, > Pleasing sounds, > Depth of thought and ideas, > Right organization, > Acceptability in a large measure, > Sublimity > And coherence. (Naṉṉūl)

The previous chapter looked at the defects of a composition as listed in Tolkāppiyam. This verse speaks of thirty-two devices in a composition by which to achieve structural unity, coherence, critical validity and acceptability. It could also be viewed as a collection of norms and conventions informing scholarly writing. This verse constitutes the hundredth flower of my ‘Garden of Tolkāppiyam’. > The devices in a composition [utti] > That go in tune with the norms of thematic unity expand into: > Stating one’s theme before dealing with it in detail; > Placing the chapters in a logical, meaningful order; > Summarizing, detailed exposition of what has been briefly stated; > Conforming to the norms or conclusions of the earlier authorities; > Exegesis being added by way of exposition of a proposition; > Expressing what has not been treated earlier in the general statement; > Complementing what has been said in the general statement; > Going backwards over the sequentially presented material > To illuminate the earlier portion and to realize the unity; > Application of a rule relating to one thing > To other things of a similar character; > Statement of absolute certainty of a proposition > That is marked by plurality of meaning; > Taking one’s own view of the perspective of the text; > Not deviating from the order that inheres in the text; > Acquiescence in the conclusions drawn by others; > Presenting what has not been there earlier in the text; > Anticipating things to be treated later in the text; > Mention at the commencement > Of what needs to be stated frequently > In the course of the text; > Drawing attention to a subject > That has already been explained; > Constant use of one’s own technical terminology; > Showing that a convention bearing on a proposition > Extends to cover others also; > Assertion of an idea by personal authority > Rather than by any objective illustrations; > Choosing the best among the possibilities; > Yet another proposition that emerges > In the course of treatment of a proposition; > Establishing one’s own view > By refuting the opposing views of others; > Bringing in the views of others; > Going with the views of others one is unaware of; > Things new being interspersed > In the treatment of a proposition; > Norms and conventions being formulated for posterity; > Stating a fact in such a way > As to imply other things not shown explicitly; > Bringing a term from the preceding or following verse > To bear on that in between; > Making a statement > Pregnant with two interpretive possibilities; > Pondering a meaning > More appropriate than the one on hand; > Such are the devices > And others apropos thereto too > As must go inhering in the text of composition, > Brevity and perspicuity marking them all -- > So do the literate men speak > Of the defining features of a composition. (Poruḷatikāram : Marapiyal, verse 111) Tolkāppiyam predates both Pāṇini and Kaudilyar. Having enjoyed myself in the literary and linguistic riches of this great work, I did invite you to go into this richly endowed garden of flowers. Because it is against the Tamil culture to send back the visiting guests empty-handed, I have generously placed on your nectarous hands a hundred blossoms.
